2a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah rules that anyone may slaughter validly, excluding the deaf-mute, imbecile and minor, and that slaughter observed by others is valid.
Gemara notices an apparent contradiction: the opening phrase suggests slaughter is permitted ab initio, while the closing phrase only validates it after the fact.
Rav Aha asks Rav Ashi whether the word everyone always signals ab initio permission, and extends the doubt to parallel mishnayot about substitution.
Rav Aha objects with a verse forbidding exchanging a sacrificial animal, showing the word everyone cannot indicate permission.
Rav Ashi replies that the mishna in Temura only uses everyone because it immediately states that substitution is forbidden and punished with lashes.
Rav Aha counters with a mishna on vows and valuations that uses everyone, asking whether those cases are also ab initio permitted.
Rav Aha cites a verse saying there is no sin if one refrains from vowing, implying vowing is not something to permit.
A second verse in Ecclesiastes states it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay.
A baraita reports differing views of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda on whether one who vows and pays is better than one who never vows.
Rav Aha limits Rabbi Yehuda's view to a case where one explicitly designates an animal, so no risk of failing to pay arises.

2b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Aha concludes that even Rabbi Yehuda forbids a vow of incumbent-upon-me, so the mishna's everyone language does not signal ab initio permission.
Rav Ashi objects that everyone also appears where obligations like sukka and fringes are described, which are plainly not ab initio, so the inference fails.
Rav Aha replies that he is not speaking of cases describing an obligation, since fulfilling any obligation is obviously permitted ab initio.
Rav Ashi presses that the everyone who places hands on an offering is also not ab initio, citing Leviticus on the burnt offering being accepted.
Rav Aha holds that everyone sometimes signals ab initio permission and sometimes after-the-fact validity, depending on context.
Rav Aha argues that the mishna's everyone should be read as after-the-fact validity, so no contradiction arises there.
Rav Ashi argues that the phrase whose slaughter is valid would be redundant if everyone were only after-the-fact, so the first phrase must be ab initio.
Rabba bar Ulla resolves the contradiction by reading the mishna as teaching that everyone, even an impure person, may slaughter ab initio.
The Gemara asks what the point is of teaching that an impure person may slaughter non-sacred animals, since no prohibition applies to that.
Rabba bar Ulla explains that the case concerns non-sacred animals prepared under sacred-food strictures, which take on the impurity restrictions of sacrifices.
The Gemara asks how an impure person can slaughter without rendering the flesh impure.
He uses a long knife to avoid contact, cannot slaughter sacrificial animals ab initio for that reason, but his after-the-fact slaughter stands if he swears he did not touch.
The mishna excludes a deaf-mute, imbecile and minor even after the fact, lest they interrupt, press the knife, or conceal it during inverted slaughter.
The Gemara asks which case the clause about anyone who slaughtered and was observed by others refers to.
The Gemara rejects candidate readings: deaf-mute and minor do not fit, nor impure person with non-sacred or sacred animals, since a sworn denial would suffice.
Supervision is needed for an impure person slaughtering sacrifices because he may not be present to be asked whether he touched the flesh.
The Gemara asks whether the halakha about an impure person slaughtering sacrifices is learned from this mishna or from the one in Zevachim.
The Zevachim mishna is quoted: all disqualified persons who slaughter an offering have valid slaughter, provided the impure do not touch the flesh.
The Chullin mishna is primary, since it lists the impure case for non-sacred animals and so also includes sacrifices; alternatively the Zevachim mishna is primary.
The Gemara asks what kind of impurity is meant, and rejects corpse impurity since the Torah specifies impurity from one slain by the sword.

3a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: By analogy from slain by the sword, an impure person's knife would itself become impure and render the meat impure, objecting to his slaughter.
Rather, the impurity may be from a creeping animal, which leaves the knife pure, or the knife may be a reed stalk checked for smoothness, which cannot become impure.
Abaye resolves the mishna's contradiction by reading everyone as including a Samaritan, valid only when a Jew stands over him and supervises.
If a Samaritan slaughters unsupervised, a Jew may eat only if the Samaritan first eats an olive-bulk of the meat, showing he slaughters carefully.
The mishna excludes a deaf-mute, imbecile and minor even after the fact, lest they interrupt, press the knife, or conceal it during inverted slaughter.
The Gemara asks which case the clause about anyone who slaughtered and was observed refers to, given the adjacent exclusion.
The Gemara rejects a Samaritan reading, since the mishna's wording would then be difficult even on the view that a Jew standing over him permits ab initio.
Rava argues from the mishna on a gentile in a wine store, where a Jew exiting and entering suffices, that supervision by exiting and entering is enough ab initio.
The Gemara rejects that proof: the mishna teaches leaving a gentile only after the fact, so it does not show ab initio permission.
Rava instead cites a mishna on barrels of wine where a supervisor who exits and enters still leaves the wine permitted, showing this suffices ab initio.
Rava resolves the contradiction the same way, reading everyone slaughters as including a Samaritan, with the condition that a Jew exits and enters.
If the Jew merely came and found an animal already slaughtered by a Samaritan, he may eat only if the Samaritan first ate a piece of that meat.
The mishna again excludes deaf-mute, imbecile and minor even after the fact, for the same reasons of interruption, pressing the knife and inverted slaughter.
The Gemara asks again which case the clause about anyone who slaughtered and was observed refers to, given the adjacent exclusion.
The Gemara objects that if a Jew who exits and enters permits a Samaritan to slaughter ab initio, the mishna's wording is again difficult.
Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by reading everyone as including an apostate who eats unslaughtered carcasses for appetite, following Rava's ruling.

3b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A transgressor's slaughter is permitted only if his knife is checked beforehand or afterward, and the mishna again excludes deaf-mutes, imbeciles and minors even after the fact.
The Gemara asks which case the clause about anyone who slaughtered and was observed refers to, given the adjacent exclusion.
The Gemara rejects a transgressor reading: if the knife was checked, he may slaughter ab initio; if not, the knife's condition is unknown, so the mishna is still difficult.
Ravina resolves the contradiction by reading everyone slaughters as experts who are known to know the laws of slaughter, with examination after the fact.
The mishna once more excludes deaf-mutes, imbeciles and minors even after the fact, for the same reasons of interruption, pressing the knife and inverted slaughter.
The Gemara asks again which case the clause about anyone who slaughtered and was observed refers to, given the adjacent exclusion.
The Gemara rejects the reading that they are not experts, since examining the slaughterer afterward would suffice.
Supervision is necessary because the slaughterer may not be before us to examine, and another version says those established as steady and not fainting may slaughter ab initio.
The baraita's exclusion of deaf-mutes, imbeciles and minors even after the fact is restated with the same reasons.
The Gemara asks yet again which case the clause about anyone who slaughtered and was observed refers to, given the adjacent exclusion.
The Gemara rejects the reading that they are not established as steady and not fainting, since a post-slaughter statement that they did not faint would suffice.
Supervision is needed where the slaughterer is not before us, so that we can ask him whether he fainted.
The Gemara notes that Ravina and Rabba bar Ulla do not adopt the resolutions of the other amoraim, because the phrasing of the mishna is difficult for them.
The other amoraim reject the readings of Rabba bar Ulla and Ravina, arguing that the Zevachim mishna is primary and that a majority of slaughterers are experts or steady.
Rava, Abaye and Rav Ashi each decline to adopt the others' resolutions, based on their views of Samaritans and transgressors.
The Gemara asks why Rava, who holds that a transgressor may slaughter if his knife is checked, did not explain the mishna that way himself.
Rava gave the Samaritan explanation to answer Abaye's difficulty, but he does not personally hold that explanation.
A baraita teaches that a Samaritan's slaughter is valid ab initio under a Jew's supervision, and that eating his meat depends on the Samaritan eating an olive-bulk first.

4a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A Samaritan's bird is eaten only after the Jew cuts a head and sees the Samaritan eat it, and Abaye and Rava derive different conditions from the baraita.
The Gemara objects that Abaye's reading makes the baraita's latter clause difficult, and Rava's reading makes the first clause difficult.
Each can answer: the Jew who exits and enters is treated as standing over the Samaritan, so the baraita's clauses are consistent.
The baraita continues with the case of a string of birds in a Samaritan's possession that the Jew cannot verify, with the same test of eating.
The Gemara asks why we need not worry that only the one bird whose head was severed was properly slaughtered while the rest are carcasses.
Rav Menashe answers that the Jew hides the birds under his garment and hands over a head, so the Samaritan cannot know which bird it came from.
The Gemara objects that the Samaritan may have marked the proper bird, so the answer fails.
Rav Meshar sheya answers that the Jew crushes the head he hands over, making it indistinguishable from the others.
The Gemara objects that Samaritans may hold that the Torah has no ritual slaughter for birds, so eating the head proves nothing.
The Gemara replies that many disqualifications are not written in the Torah either, yet once Samaritans accepted them they are relied upon, and the same applies to bird slaughter.
A baraita states a dispute among tanna'im: a Samaritan's matza is permitted and one fulfills the Passover matza obligation with it.
Rabbi Elazar forbids a Samaritan's matza because Samaritans are not expert in the details of mitzvot, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel permits it since they are exacting.
The Gemara asks whether it is not obvious that a permitted matza allows fulfilling the obligation, and what the baraita adds.
The baraita teaches that Samaritans are expert in guarding the matza, and explains Rabbi Elazar's view that they lack expertise in guarding it.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that Samaritans are more exacting than Jews in any mitzva they accepted upon themselves.
The Gemara objects that this view is identical to that of the first tanna.
The tanannaim differ on a mitzva written in the Torah that Samaritans did not accept, and on whether their acceptance of a written mitzva makes them reliable.
The Gemara objects that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's wording is imprecise and should have said if they accepted, to address the first tanna's view.
Rather, the tanna'im differ on an unwritten mitzva that Samaritans accepted, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel relies on them once acceptance is known.
Rava states that a transgressor who eats unslaughtered meat may slaughter if his knife is examined and given to him, and his meat is then permitted.
Rava's reason is that the transgressor would not intentionally choose the prohibited option when a permitted one is available, and the examined knife makes the meat presumptively permitted.
The Gemara objects that if this is so, then even where the Jew did not examine the knife, the transgressor's meat should be permitted.
The meat is prohibited without examination because the transgressor, finding the knife flawed, would not trouble himself to replace it.
The Sages cite a baraita supporting Rava: leavened bread of transgressors who did not remove it before Passover is permitted after Passover.

4b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita permits leavened bread after Passover immediately, because transgressors exchange their forbidden bread for gentiles' permitted bread.
The Gemara infers that the transgressors do not forsake the permitted for the forbidden, assuming the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, who treats post-Passover leaven as Torah-forbidden.
The Gemara asks where the baraita proves this, since it may instead follow Rabbi Shimon, who treats the prohibition as rabbinic.
The baraita states the exchange as fact, and if transgressors avoid rabbinic prohibitions, all the more so they avoid Torah prohibitions.
The Gemara cites a baraita that everyone slaughters, including a Samaritan, an uncircumcised man and a Jewish transgressor, to support Rava.
The Gemara asks what the uncircumcised case means, since a man whose brothers died from circumcision is simply a full Jew.
The uncircumcised man is a transgressor only in refusing circumcision, and the baraita holds that a transgressor in one matter is not one in the whole Torah.
The Gemara asks what the latter clause, the Jewish transgressor, refers to.
If the transgressor is in the same matter of eating carcasses, the baraita would support Rava's view that his slaughter is permitted ab initio.
The Gemara rejects that proof: a transgressor in the same matter is invalid, since habituated transgression makes it permitted for him and he is careless.
Rather, the baraita concerns a transgressor in idol worship, following Rav Anan's statement of Shmuel that his slaughter is permitted.
Rav Anan restates Shmuel's view: a Jew who transgresses in idol worship may be eaten from when he slaughters.
Jehoshaphat ate the feast of Ahab, a transgressor in idol worship, as Chronicles records Ahab slaughtering animals for him.
The Gemara objects that Ahab may have slaughtered without Jehoshaphat eating, and that incitement must be through words, which is then rejected.
The Gemara asks whether incitement with words exists, citing Deuteronomy and Job, and answers that incitement with people involves food and drink.
The Gemara challenges that Jehoshaphat may have drunk but not eaten, and that drinking and eating are treated the same way for transgressors in idol worship.
The Gemara asks how the cases are comparable, since wine of gentiles was not yet prohibited, while the meat of a transgressor is forbidden.
Jehoshaphat must have eaten, since a king does not drink without eating, and the verse shows Ahab incited him through slaughter, so the meat is permitted.
The Gemara suggests Obadiah, a righteous man, slaughtered the animals, but rejects it because Obadiah could not have slaughtered so many.
The Gemara suggests the seven thousand righteous slaughtered, and rejects it because they were hiding from Jezebel and would not have gone to the palace.
The Gemara suggests Ahab's servants were upstanding and slaughtered, and rejects it based on the verse that a ruler's servants follow his character.
The Gemara suggests Jehoshaphat's servants were not upstanding, so he ate only Obadiah's animals, and this is also treated as an implausible reading.
The Gemara rejects that suggestion, since the verse about wicked servants implies that righteous rulers have righteous servants.
The Gemara suggests each king ate only from his own servants' slaughter, leaving the question of Jehoshaphat's permitted meat unresolved.

5a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Jehoshaphat did not separate himself from Ahab to eat and drink alone, because he fully relied on him.
Asks where this claim is derived from.
Proposed source: Jehoshaphat's words that he and his people are like Ahab and his people.
If that meant reliance, the horses phrase would also mean reliance, which is absurd.
The horses phrase means whatever befalls one side befalls the other, so the reliance reading stands.
Rather, Jehoshaphat's reliance on Ahab is derived from a different verse.
Quotes the verse describing both kings seated on a threshing floor at the gate of Samaria.
Asks what the word threshing floor means in this verse.
If it was a real threshing floor, that makes no sense for the gate of Samaria.
It was shaped like a half circle, as a Sanhedrin was, so the two kings could see each other.
Suggests that a verse about Elijah supports the opinion of Rav Anan.
Quotes the verse where ravens brought Elijah bread and meat morning and evening.
Rav said the meat came from Ahab's slaughterers, and Elijah ate it only by divine command.
Elijah's case is different, so it proves nothing about ordinary slaughter.
Asks what the word orevim, ravens, means in the verse.
Ravina says they were actual ravens.
Rav Adda suggests they were two men named Oreb, so the word is a name.
Quotes the verse about slaying Oreb at the rock of Oreb, showing Oreb is a personal name.
Ravina replies that it would be a remarkable coincidence for both to be named Oreb.
Suggests the name refers to a place called Oreb.
Quotes the verse about a young maiden taken captive from the land of Israel.
Asks why the verse calls her both a young woman and a minor, which is difficult.
Rabbi Pedat says she was a minor from a place called Naaran.
If so, the verse should have used the form that means people from a place called Oreb.
Suggests a baraita supports Rav Anan.
Quotes a baraita stating that everyone slaughters, including a Samaritan, an uncircumcised man, and a Jewish transgressor.
Asks what the circumstances of the uncircumcised slaughterer are.
If his brothers died from circumcision, he is a full Jew, so the baraita is not about a transgressor.
Rather, the uncircumcised man is evidently a transgressor who refuses circumcision.
Asks what the circumstances of the Jewish transgressor in the final clause are.
If he transgresses one matter, that is the same as refusing circumcision, so he must be an idolater, supporting Rav Anan.
No, the transgressor is one who worships idols, which the baraita says is not accepted, upholding Rav Anan's view.
Quotes a teaching that idolatry is so severe that denying it equals denying the entire Torah.
Rather, the transgressor is one who transgresses only one matter, following Rava.
Raises a baraita on Leviticus 1:2 that rejects offerings from transgressors and accepts those of Jewish sinners who are not idolaters.
Points out that the baraita itself appears contradictory, since it first excludes transgressors and then accepts offerings from them.
The first clause refers to transgression of the entire Torah, the middle to a single matter, so there is no contradiction.
Asks about the final clause, which excludes libation wine and Shabbat desecration, in the same terms.
Asks what the circumstances of this transgressor are.
If he is a transgressor of the entire Torah it matches the first clause, and if of one matter it contradicts the middle clause.
Rather, the mishna means the exception applies to libation and Shabbat desecration, showing idolatry makes one a transgressor of the entire Torah.
This is a conclusive refutation of Rav Anan's view.
Asks whether the rule about not accepting an offering from a transgressor is derived from the verse here or from there.

5b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita infers from the words of the common people that a transgressor's sin offering is not accepted.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yosei transmits a teaching in the name of Rabbi Shimon.
Quotes the Leviticus verse on unwitting sins and infers that only one who repents upon learning of his sin brings an offering.
Asks what the practical difference is between the two opinions.
Rav Hamnuna says the difference arises for a transgressor who ate forbidden fat and then brought an offering for consuming blood.
The two baraitot are both needed: one addresses the sin offering and one the burnt offering, since each could otherwise be thought to be a special case.
Asks whether the word animal always indicates a deficiency.
Cites a Psalms verse where man and animal are mentioned together as a sign of praise.
Rav Yehuda says in Rav's name that these are clever people who humble themselves like animals.
In the Psalms verse man and animal are written together, whereas the animal word alone is used here.
Asks whether the combination of man and animal always indicates a virtue.
Quotes the Jeremiah verse on the seed of man and the seed of animal and notes that they are distinct.
A mnemonic is given for the names of the sages who follow.
The court of Rabban Gamliel counted opinions and prohibited eating the slaughter of a Samaritan.
Rabbi Zeira suggests the ruling applies only when no Jew is standing over the Samaritan slaughterer.
Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi replies that this is the mistake of someone unfamiliar with the halakha, since the prohibition holds even without a Jew watching.
Asks whether Rabbi Zeira accepted that response, and says a proof will be brought to resolve the matter.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzhak reports that Rabbi Asi saw Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Asi eat from a Samaritan slaughter.
Rabbi Zeira wondered whether they had not heard the prohibition, or heard it but did not accept it.
Rabbi Zeira concluded for himself that they heard it and did not accept it.
Argues that if they had not heard it, or would have accepted it, such a mishap could not occur, and even the animals of the righteous are protected, so the righteous certainly are.

6a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If Zeira had not accepted the ruling, he could have explained the case differently, so we conclude he did accept it.
Asks why the Sages, led by Rabban Gamliel, decreed that Samaritan slaughter is forbidden.
Explains through the story of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, warned by an elder about Samaritan wine, whom Rabbi Meir then made the basis of a decree.
Asks what the reason is for deeming the Samaritans unreliable.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak cites the dove image found on Mount Gerizim, and Rabbi Meir decreed out of concern for the minority that worshipped it.
Asks what matter the verse about putting a knife to the throat actually concerns in its plain sense.
Cites a baraita reading the verse as addressing a student before his teacher, and explains how the student should act depending on the teacher's ability.
Rabbi Abbahu sent Rabbi Yitzhak ben Yosef for wine, and sages then ruled that Samaritans are full gentiles.
Asks which matters the ruling covers, since slaughter and libation wine were already prohibited earlier.
The earlier decree was not accepted by the people, but when Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi decreed it, the people accepted it.
Asks what it means that Samaritans are fully gentile.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak says it means that a Samaritan is treated as a gentile for renouncing or transferring rights in a shared courtyard on Shabbat.
A baraita states that a Jewish transgressor who publicly keeps Shabbat can renounce or transfer courtyard rights, but one who does not cannot.
Only a Jew may verbally transfer or renounce domain rights, and an open Shabbat desecrator is treated like a gentile, so an example of a valid transfer is given.
Rabbi Zeira and Rav Asi visited an inn where eggs cooked in wine were served; Rav Asi ate them while Rabbi Zeira abstained.
Zeira asks Rav Asi whether he was not concerned about a mixture that might contain doubtfully tithed produce.
Rav Asi replies that the concern did not occur to him.
Zeira reflects whether the Sages could have decreed against such a mixture and whether Asi thereby ate forbidden food, concluding that the righteous are protected.
Zeira later examined the matter and found a baraita stating that wine or vetch bought from an am ha'aretz is obligated in tithes as demai, yet the mixed products are permitted.
Asks whether the Sages really did not decree against mixtures containing demai.
Cites a baraita on a neighbor's dough and pot: no concern for leaven or spices replaced by her own, but if he asks her to use his own, concern applies.
Two replies: when he asked her to prepare it from his own ingredients it is as if he mixed it himself, and leaven and spices always impart taste, which is not nullified.
Asks whether we are not concerned about replacement of the ingredients the neighbor used.
Quotes a mishna requiring tithing of food given to a suspect mother-in-law, because she may have replaced spoiled ingredients.
Rabbi Yehuda explains that the mother-in-law wishes her daughter well and is ashamed to tell her son-in-law about the replacement.

6b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether we should not be concerned about replacement of ingredients in general, not only with a mother-in-law.
Cites a mishna requiring tithes on food given to an innkeeper who is an am ha'aretz, because she may replace the ingredients.
The innkeeper's intentions are good: she rationalizes the swap by saying the Torah scholar should eat her hot food while she eats his cold food.
Asks again whether we are not concerned about replacement of ingredients.
Cites a baraita on a haver's wife grinding grain with an am ha'aretz's wife, permitted only when the haver's wife is impure.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar holds that the haver's wife may not grind even when impure, because the other woman gives her grain to eat.
Asks whether, given the suspicion of theft from her husband, the am ha'aretz's wife must surely be suspected of replacement too.
Rav Yosef says the am ha'aretz's wife rationalizes her behavior by thinking the ox eats from its own threshing floor, so the case is special.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Zeruz testified that Rabbi Meir ate untithed produce in Beit She'an, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi then permitted all of Beit She'an's produce.
Rabbi Meir's brothers objected that he was permitting what his fathers had forbidden, asking whether he would now treat it as permitted.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi responded by citing a verse to support his ruling.
Quotes the verse on Moses's copper serpent, which the Israelites had burned incense to and was named Nehushtan.
Asks how a righteous king like Asa or Jehoshaphat could have left the idol in place if it had been worshipped.
Asks whether Asa and Jehoshaphat did not in fact eradicate all idolatrous objects in the world.

7a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Hezekiah's ancestors left him room to gain prominence, just as the speaker's ancestors left him room by permitting Beit She'an produce.
From this we learn that a Torah scholar who issues a new halakhic ruling should not be removed from his position, with differing wordings of the principle.
Explains the three different wordings by citing verses and a baraita about conceited hearts causing disputes among the people.
Yehuda, son of Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi, objects that Beit She'an is clearly part of Eretz Yisrael, since the verse says Manasseh did not drive out its inhabitants.
Explains that the earlier statement escaped Yehuda's notice: cities were conquered by those who came from Egypt under Joshua, not those who came from Babylonia, and Beit She'an was among the former.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds that the sanctity of the land lapsed in the exile, and Beit She'an was left unsanctified so the poor could rely on it during the Sabbatical Year.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks how Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi could rely on testimony that Rabbi Meir ate only a leaf, which is permitted incidentally.
Rabbi Zeira replies that Rabbi Meir ate the leaf from a bundle, which requires tithing.
Cites a mishna that a vegetable typically bound in a bundle is obligated in terumot and tithes once it is bound.
Yirmeya suggests Rabbi Meir may not have been thinking about tithing when he ate the leaf.
Zeira argues that if the righteous animals are protected from mishaps, the righteous themselves surely are.
Yirmeya suggests Rabbi Meir may have tithed those leaves from produce in another place.
Zeira replies that haverim are not suspected of separating terumah from produce that is not adjacent to it.
Yirmeya suggests Rabbi Meir may have focused on one side of the vegetable while eating a leaf from the other side.
Zeira replies that such a great man as Rabbi Yehoshua ben Zeruz is reliable in his testimony about Rabbi Meir.
Asks what is meant by the animals of the righteous, through whom God does not bring mishaps.
Illustrates with the incident of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair, who was on his way to redeem captives and encountered the Ginai river.
The river parted for Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair after he threatened that it would never flow again if it did not.
The river parted for a man carrying wheat for matza and again for a traveling Arab, at Rabbi Pinchas's request.
Rav Yosef says Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair was greater than Moses, since the waters parted three times for him and only once at the Red Sea.
Asks whether the waters may have parted only once, and concludes that he was as great as Moses and the six hundred thousand.
Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair stayed at an inn where barley was put before his donkey, but the donkey would not eat it.

7b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The hosts try sifting and cleaning the barley, but the donkey refuses until Pinchas suggests it may be untithed and it is tithed.
Asks whether one who buys demai grain to feed an animal must tithe it, given a mishna exempting such purchases.
Rabbi Yohanan limits the mishna to goods first bought for animals; goods first bought for people and later diverted to animals must be tithed, as a baraita confirms.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi goes out to greet Pinchas and invites him to dine, and his face lights up because Pinchas rarely accepts invitations.
Pinchas denies any vow against benefiting from Jews, explains he avoids meals where the host cannot afford them or does not want to host, and says he must first perform a mitzva.
When Pinchas returns, he notices the white mules at the entrance and says the Angel of Death is in the house, so he will not eat there.
Rabbi Yehuda offers to sell the mules, and Pinchas objects that this violates the prohibition against placing a stumbling block before the blind.
Rabbi Yehuda proposes declaring the mules ownerless and removing their hooves so they cannot kick.
Pinchas objects that this causes suffering to animals, which is prohibited.
Rabbi Yehuda proposes killing the mules.
Pinchas objects that destroying items of value is prohibited by the verse against destruction.
Rabbi Yehuda urges Pinchas to come home, but a mountain intervenes; he weeps and says the righteous are greater after death than in life.
Rabbi Hama bar Hanina is cited as holding that the righteous are greater after death.
Cites the story of the man revived by touching the bones of Elisha as proof that the righteous are greater after death.
Rav Pappa says this proves nothing, since it fulfilled Elijah's blessing of a double portion; Abaye objects that a baraita says the revived man did not go home, which undermines that reading.
Asks how Elijah's blessing could have been fulfilled in that case.
Rabbi Yohanan says it was fulfilled by curing Naaman's leprosy, since a leper is like a dead person, as the verse about Miriam shows.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains why the white mules are called yemim, because their terror is cast over all creatures.
Rabbi Hanina says no man has come to him with a wound from a white mule and survived.
Asks whether we have not seen people survive such wounds.
Suggests that the statement should be read as saying the wound from a mule heals.
Asks again whether we have not seen such wounds heal.
Says the dangerous wound is only from a mule with white legs at the top.
Rabbi Hanina cites the verse that there is none beside Him, teaching that even sorcery is ineffective against God's will.
A woman tried to take dust from beneath Rabbi Hanina's feet to harm him by sorcery, and he replied that it would have no effect since none is beside God.
Asks why Rabbi Yohanan calls sorcery keshafim, since it denies the heavenly entourage, given that Rabbi Hanina was unaffected.
Rabbi Hanina is different because his merit is great, so sorcery has no effect on him.
Rabbi Hanina says a person is injured on earth only if he is decreed for injury on high.
Cites the verses that a man's steps are established by the Lord and that a man does not understand his own way.
Rabbi Elazar says that the blood of a wound effects atonement like the blood of a burnt offering.
Rava says this applies to a wound on the right thumb, or a second wound before the first heals, when one is going to perform a mitzva.
It is said of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair that he never recited a blessing over bread that was not his, and never benefited from his father's meal.

8a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel rules that a knife heated white hot is valid for slaughter if its sharpness precedes the heating.
Asks whether the sides of the knife, which also burn, do not render the slaughter invalid.
The slaughter area is spread open by the cut, so the sides are not seared.
Raises a dilemma: is a mark from a skewer struck while heated classed as a leprous boil or a leprous burn?
Asks what practical difference the classification makes.
Cites a baraita that a boil and a burn do not combine to form the measure of leprous marks.
Cites a baraita defining a boil as a wound from non-heated objects and a burn as one from fire-heated objects.
Cites a baraita that the later of a boil and a burn on the same spot determines the nature of the mark.
Asks what the circumstances of the dilemma are.
The case is one where a half-bean boil was present first and then a half-bean burn was added by the heated skewer.
Asks which halakha applies: whether the blow comes first and the heat nullifies it, or the reverse, so the marks join.
Suggests resolving the dilemma from Shmuel's ruling about the white-hot knife, which implies the blow comes first.
Replies that cutting with a sharp blade differs from striking with a blunt object.
Suggests resolving the dilemma from a baraita that the mark from a heated skewer is a burn, implying the blow comes first.
Replies that there too the skewer stabbed the skin like a sharp blade, which is a different case.
Rav Nahman, citing Rabba bar Avuh, rules that an idolatrous knife may be used for slaughter but not for cutting meat.
Rava adds that slaughter is forbidden with such a knife for an endangered animal, and cutting is permitted for a gift animal.
Objects that the prohibition on the knife may instead be explained by residual forbidden fat on the blade.

8b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Nahman's ruling concerns a new knife, which has no residue on it.
If the knife is new, it is only an accessory of idolatry, which is forbidden only once actually used for worship, so the earlier ruling needs explaining.
Either the knife cut a branch for idol worship and so left no residue, or it was an old knife burned white hot in fire.
Rav says to peel off a layer of flesh where a gentile's knife touched it, while Rabba bar bar Hana says to rinse the spot.
Suggests the two Sages disagree about whether the slaughter area is cold or hot, which would account for their different remedies.
Rejects that reading: everyone holds the slaughter area is hot, and rinsing suffices because the simanim are occupied with blood.
Others say everyone holds the area is cold, and the difference is that pressure from the knife on the throat lets flesh absorb residue.
Rav Aha and Ravina dispute how to clean a knife used on a tereifa; the halakha allows rinsing in cold water, and a cloth to wipe suffices.
Asks why one who requires hot-water purging insists on it, since a knife used for a permitted animal might absorb residue too.
Absorption is a concern only once the throat warms, which happens at completion of the slaughter, when the animal is already permitted.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, says the slaughterer needs three knives: one for slaughtering, one for meat, and one for forbidden fats.
Suggests one knife could be used for meat and then fats, with no harm if it is cleaned between uses.
The Sages decreed separate knives to prevent cutting fats and then meat with the same knife.
Objects that after such a decree confusion between the knives remains possible.
Since two knives are required, one bears a distinguishing mark that prevents confusion.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, says the slaughterer needs two water vessels, one for rinsing meat and one for rinsing fats.
Suggests one vessel could be used for both, rinsing meat and then fats.
The Sages decreed against using one vessel, to prevent rinsing fats and then meat.
Objects that confusion between the two vessels remains possible even after the decree.
The two vessels are required, so one carries a distinguishing mark that prevents the mix-up.
Ameimar, citing Rav Pappa, says one should not place an animal's flanks on other meat, since the fat liquefies and the meat absorbs it.
Objects that the concern would arise even when the flanks are placed in their usual position, with fat above the meat.

9a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Membrane above the meat splits when the slaughterer's hand touches it, so the forbidden fat flows onto the meat.
Rav Yehuda cites Rav: a Torah scholar must learn three skills, writing, ritual slaughter and circumcision.
Rav Hananya bar Shelamya adds, in Rav's name, tying tefillin knots, the grooms' blessing and tzitzit.
The rival Amora holds these skills are so common that they need no special training.
Shmuel's rule: one ignorant of slaughter halakhot may not be eaten from, followed by a list of those halakhot.
Why does Rav need to teach this, since all these halakhot were already taught in the Mishnah?
It is needed for a slaughterer who was reliable earlier but may still err, unknowingly invalidating a slaughter.
Shmuel's rule: the slaughterer must examine the simanim after completing the slaughter.
Rav Yosef cites Rabbi Shimon's mishna: an interruption as long as an examination invalidates, implying simanim checks.
Abaye rejects Rav Yosef's reading of the mishna.
Abaye cites Rabbi Yohanan: the interval is the time to examine the knife, by a Torah scholar.
Rav Yosef objects that this makes the rule depend on circumstances, since the scholar's distance varies.
Rather, the interval is the time of examination by a slaughterer who is himself a Torah scholar, which is fixed.
What is the halakha if the slaughterer did not examine the simanim after slaughtering?
Rabbi Eliezer ben Antigonus, citing Rabbi Elazar: such an animal is a tereifa and forbidden, but does not impart impurity.
A baraita states such an animal is a carcass that imparts impurity by carrying.
What is the underlying point on which the two opinions disagree?
They dispute Rav Huna's principle: a living animal is presumed forbidden until its slaughter is known, then presumed permitted until its tereifa status is known.
One Sage holds the animal stays presumed forbidden, so once dead it is a carcass that imparts impurity.
The other Sage holds presumed forbidden applies, but presumed impurity does not, since a living animal is not impure.
Rav Huna's principle is restated: a living animal is presumed forbidden, a slaughtered one presumed permitted.
Why not say that once slaughtered it is simply permitted, rather than presumed permitted?
It teaches that a flaw arising in the animal does not remove its presumed permitted status.
Rabbi Abba asks Rav Huna: if a wolf took the innards of a slaughtered animal, what is the halakha?
Taking is impossible since the innards are absent, so the question is: what if the wolf perforated them?
But a perforation is visible, so the dilemma as framed has no uncertainty either.
What if the wolf took the innards and returned them perforated: must we fear the perforation was preexisting?
Rav Huna says we do not fear a preexisting perforation, because we rely on the presumed permitted status.
Rabbi Abba objects with a baraita about a bird pecking a fig or a mouse gnawing melons, apparently challenging Rav Huna's view.

9b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Abba's objection: a bird or mouse may have perforated a snake-made hole, so the fruit is forbidden due to venom danger.
Rav Huna replies that danger cannot be compared to prohibition, since danger is treated differently.
Rava asks why danger-based doubts are ruled stringently, when prohibition-based doubts are also ruled stringently.
Abaye says there is a difference, citing a mishna where doubtful impurity in public leaves things pure but exposed water is forbidden.
Rava replies that the public-domain impurity rule is learned by tradition from the sota case, applying only in private domains.
Rav Shimi objects with a mishna about a weasel carrying a creeping animal's carcass over teruma loaves, where doubt leaves them pure.
The Gemara answers that the sota derivation applies: doubt matters only for an entity with consciousness that can be questioned.
Rav Ashi cites a mishna on purification water: a flask left exposed then found covered is impure; a weasel, snake or dew disqualifies it.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi asks the reason there is no concern that an impure person exposed the waters and made them impure.

10a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Creeping animals typically expose liquid to drink, while covering exposed vessels is not their habit, so the baraita's cases are distinguished.
From the baraita's ruling that exposed water is forbidden, the Gemara infers that danger is more severe than prohibition.
A mishna states three liquids are forbidden when exposed, for the time a snake needs to come from nearby and drink.
Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Yehuda says nearby means a snake could come out from under the vessel handle and drink.
If the snake drinks in the time it takes to emerge, the owner would see it, so the period must be longer.
Rav Huna holds that a slaughter with a notched knife is invalid, since the notch may have come from the hide.
Rav Ḥisda holds the slaughter is valid, since the notch may have come from breaking bones with the knife.
Rav Huna's view follows from his earlier principle, but what is the reason for Rav Ḥisda's ruling?
A bone certainly notches a knife, while hide is only doubtful, and uncertainty does not override certainty.
Rava cites a baraita on immersion where a later-found interposition invalidates it, arguing doubt overrides certainty, against Rav Ḥisda.
The Gemara rejects the proof: there one may presume the impure person did not immerse properly.
Here too one could presume the animal was not slaughtered properly, based on its presumptive prohibition.
That presumption is undermined because the slaughtered animal is before you, and most slaughters are valid.
Here too, the immersed person is before you, so the presumption of impurity should be undermined.
A flaw developed in the validity of the immersion through the interposition, so the cases differ.
Here too a flaw developed in the slaughter's validity, since the knife became notched.
The knife became flawed but the animal did not, so the animal keeps its presumptive permissibility.
A baraita on bird slaughter, with one siman cut and then displacement, is cited as an objection to Rav Ḥisda.
The baraita continues with a case of uncertain displacement, and the Sages rule any uncertainty in slaughter invalidates it.
What does the general rule about uncertainty in slaughter add, if not a case like the knife notched before or after?
It adds uncertainty whether the slaughterer interrupted the slaughter or pressed the knife, or whether the knife was pressed on the simanim.

10b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What distinguishes uncertainty about interrupting or pressing the knife from uncertainty about a notch before or after slaughter?
In the first case a flaw develops in the animal and the slaughter is invalid; in the notch case only the knife is flawed, so the slaughter stands.
The halakha follows Rav Huna when no bone was broken and Rav Ḥisda when one was; this implies Rav Ḥisda accepts validity even without a broken bone.
If no bone was broken, where could the knife have been notched to make the slaughter valid under Rav Ḥisda?
The notch may have occurred on the neck bone after the slaughter was completed.
Rav Yosef once declared thirteen animals tereifot after finding the knife notched following the last slaughter.
Which opinion did Rav Yosef follow, given that he ruled even the first animal forbidden?
Alternatively, Rav Yosef follows Rav Huna, since on Rav Ḥisda's view one cannot tell which neck bone caused the notch.
Rav Aḥa bar Rava reports that Rav Kahana requires examining the knife between each slaughter.
Does Rav Kahana follow Rav Huna, invalidating the first animal, or Rav Ḥisda, validating it?
If examination is needed after slaughter, why not by a Torah scholar too? The answer: a slaughterer's testimony suffices, and the scholar's review was for deference only.
What is the source for the principle that a matter is established on its presumptive status?
Rabbi Yonatan derives from the leprous house verse that the priest quarantines the house after viewing the mark.
Perhaps the mark shrank as the priest left, so how could he quarantine based on it, unless the presumptive status governs?
Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov objects that the priest may have left backward, so he still saw the mark when going out.
Abaye refutes this: leaving backward is not leaving, and in a dark house one may not open windows to view the mark.
Rava counters with the High Priest on Yom Kippur, who leaves backward, and says the window rule applies only when the mark was not yet established.
The window restriction applies only before the mark is established; once established, the priest may open a window to view it.
A baraita, not following Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov, derives from the verse's wording how the priest quarantines the house, including from within it.
Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov reads the baraita in line with his own opinion.

11a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continuing the example: a row of standing men each reporting that the leprous mark remains unchanged to the next.
From where is the Sages' principle of following the majority derived?
The Sages' principle: one follows the majority.
From where do we derive that rule?
The verse Exodus 23:2 says to incline after the majority, which supports the rule.
For a quantifiable majority, such as nine kosher shops out of ten, the question never arises; it arises only for unquantifiable majorities.
For an unquantifiable majority, such as minor boys and girls, from where is the majority rule derived?
A mnemonic lists the Sages who addressed this question, from Rabbi Elazar through Rav Ashi.
Rabbi Elazar derives it from the burnt offering: the head is not cut into pieces, by inference from Leviticus 1:6.
Rabbi Elazar argues that the brain membrane may be perforated, so the majority of non-tereifa animals must be relied on.
Perhaps the proof refers only to splitting the head fully, and not to cases where its sides remain joined.
Mar bar Ravina derives the rule from the Paschal bone-breaking prohibition, again relying on the majority of non-tereifa animals.
Perhaps the baraita's bone-burning case shows the head can be examined, so the proof fails.
A baraita holds that cutting sinews or burning bones of the Paschal offering does not violate the bone-breaking prohibition.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak derives the rule from the intact fat tail of the peace offering, relying on the majority of animals.
The tail is severed above the spine in a place that does not make the animal a tereifa, so the proof stands.
Perhaps the tail is split to examine the spine, so no proof can be drawn from it.
Rav Sheshet bar Rav Idi derives the rule from the broken-neck heifer, which must remain whole apart from its neck.
Rejecting that proof: the heifer is not eaten or sacrificed, so why does its tereifa status matter, since it is compared to sacrifices?
Rabba bar Rav Sheila derives the rule from the red heifer, which must be slaughtered and burned while whole.
Rejecting the red heifer proof: it is called a purification offering, like a sin offering, which a tereifa cannot be.
Rav Aḥa bar Ya'akov derives the rule from the two goats of the scapegoat, which must be equal.

11b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Perhaps one scapegoat is a tereifa, since it is cast alive; and rejecting the proof, the lot only applies to fit animals, so examination is pointless.
A mishna says the goat was torn limb from limb before reaching halfway down the mountain, showing it is examined after the fall.
Rav Mari derives the rule from the verse on striking one's father or mother, relying on the majority of a married woman's relations.
Perhaps the father and mother were jailed together at conception, so paternity is certain and no majority is needed?
Even so, no guardian exists to restrain sexual immorality, so paternity is not certain.
Rav Kahana derives the rule from the law on killing a person, relying on the majority of people who are not tereifot.
One could examine the corpse, but that mutilates it, and the risk of a sword perforation still requires relying on the majority.
Ravina derives the rule from the law of conspiring witnesses, who are executed as they intended to cause death.
Perhaps the accused was a tereifa, so the witnesses should not be executed; rather the majority is relied on.
A baraita on conspiring witnesses executed only if the accused was not yet killed, which rejects the examination argument.
Rav Ashi derives the rule from the slaughter law, relying on the majority of animals, and reports his teaching before Rav Kahana and Rav Shimi.
The Sage replies that where examination is possible, the majority is not followed, which limits the principle.
If the majority is not followed, Rabbi Meir, who takes the minority into account, would forbid all slaughtered meat, which is absurd.

12a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What can be said about the Paschal offering and sacrificial meat, given the rule on examination?
Rabbi Meir's view is the only consistent one: examine where possible, rely on the majority where examination is impossible.
Rav Naḥman cites Rav: if a person saw a slaughterer throughout the whole act, the meat is permitted; otherwise it is forbidden.
Which case is meant: an onlooker who knows the slaughterer is expert, or one who does not know, in which case the majority of slaughterers are experts?
A baraita states that finding a slaughtered chicken in the market, or sent-agent slaughter found done, is presumed properly slaughtered.
Apparently we rely on the majority of experts, so here too, when the slaughterer's knowledge is unknown, the majority should apply.
The case is one where the slaughterer is known to be ignorant but properly cut one siman; the other siman may have been interrupted or pressed.
Rav Dimi bar Yosef asks Rav Naḥman about an agent sent to slaughter a chicken and found it already slaughtered.
Rav Naḥman rules the presumption is that the chicken was slaughtered properly.
Rav Dimi asks the same about an agent sent to separate teruma and found it already separated.
Rav Naḥman rules there is no presumption that teruma was separated.
Rav Dimi objects: whichever way, the rulings conflict, since the agent presumption should cover both teruma and slaughter, or neither.
Rav Naḥman replies jokingly, then explains the difference: a slaughter is valid by majority, while an unauthorized teruma is not teruma.
Perhaps the majority-of-experts rule is a tanna dispute, as the Gemara suggests.
A baraita: if lost young goats or roosters are found slaughtered, Rabbi Yehuda forbids and Rabbi Ḥanina son of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili permits, depending on location.
Is the disagreement not whether the majority of experts is relied on?
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak says everyone agrees about the house and marketplace cases; they disagree only about a scrap heap in the house, depending on whether a person would discard a carcass there.
What does the scrap heap in the baraita refer to, and what does the house refer to, given the rulings?
The two rulings of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi contradict each other: one follows Rabbi Yehuda, the other Rabbi Ḥanina, on the same case.

12b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's ruling: each Rabbi agrees with the other in the case where he himself would concede, so only the house scrap heap is disputed.
The mishna: anyone may slaughter validly, except a deaf-mute, imbecile or minor, lest they ruin the slaughter.
The Gemara notes the wording is future tense, and Rava explains that non-sacred animals are not given to them to slaughter ab initio, even under supervision.
The mishna continues: if others watch, the slaughter by such people is valid, even without their intent.
Which tanna holds that intent is not required for slaughter?
Rava identifies Rabbi Natan through a baraita about a thrown knife that slaughters validly, and Oshaya rules in accordance with Rabbi Natan.
How can the thrown-knife slaughter be valid, since the knife must move back and forth across the throat?
The knife cut the throat, rebounded off the wall, and cut again in the proper manner.
Rabbi Yoḥanan's dilemma is whether a minor's thought is halakhically effective, and why he does not raise the same dilemma about a minor's action.
A mishna on minors hollowing shells or affixing them to scales: their action makes vessels, but their thought does not.

13a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ḥiyya explains that bare thought is not the issue; the dilemma concerns cases where the minor's intent shows in his actions.
Illustration: a burnt offering standing in the south is moved to the north and slaughtered there, so intent is shown through action.
Did the minor intend the northern slaughter, or did he move the animal north only because no southern spot was free?
Ami notes that Rabbi Yoḥanan already resolved this type of question once before.
Mishna on produce dried on a roof: the intent of a deaf-mute, imbecile or minor for dew does not make the produce susceptible.
Yoḥanan limits the mishna to a minor who did not turn the produce over; turning it over shows effective intent.
Is a minor's apparent intent effective by Torah law or only by rabbinic law?
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak transmits the exchange differently, with Ḥiyya reporting Yoḥanan's dilemma about a minor's capacity to act.
Does a minor have the capacity to perform an action that is halakhically effective, or not?
Ami objects: why would Yoḥanan not raise the same dilemma about a minor's thought?
A mishna is cited: a minor has no effective thought but does have the capacity to perform an action.
Is a minor's effective action by Torah law or only by rabbinic law?
Yoḥanan resolves: action is effective even by Torah law and thought is not, while apparent intent counts by rabbinic law.
Shmuel asks Rav Huna where the disqualification of an unintentional slaughter of sacrifices is derived.
Rav Huna derives the requirement of intent from the verse about slaughtering the young bull.
Shmuel replies that intent for slaughter is an accepted tradition that is indispensable, so the verse must teach something else.
Shmuel asks where the indispensability of intent after the fact is derived.
The verse about slaughtering according to one's will is brought to show intent is required even after the fact.
Mishna: slaughter by a gentile renders the animal an unslaughtered carcass that imparts impurity through carrying.
Gemara: the slaughter makes the animal a carcass, but a carcass does not carry a prohibition on deriving benefit.
Who is the tanna who taught the mishna?
Ḥiyya bar Abba reports Yoḥanan: the mishna is not like Eliezer, who would otherwise hold a gentile's unspecified intent is for idolatry.
Eliezer's view is quoted: a gentile's unspecified intent is directed to idol worship.
Ami says the mishna teaches that gentile slaughter is a carcass, while a heretic's slaughter is for idolatry.
A baraita is cited teaching that a heretic's slaughter is for the sake of idol worship.
Baraita lists the heretic's items: bread like a Samaritan's, wine as libation wine, scrolls of sorcerers, and untithed produce.

13b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The heretic's sons are mamzerim, since he is indifferent to his wife's adultery.
Gemara explains why the first tanna omits this: in his view a heretic does not release his wife to adultery.
Mishna: slaughter performed by a gentile renders the animal an unslaughtered carcass.
Gemara challenges: perhaps the gentile slaughterer is a heretic, whose slaughter would be prohibited.
Rav Naḥman says in the name of Rabba bar Avuh that there are no heretics among the gentile nations.
Gemara objects: but we see that such heretics do exist.
Reply: the majority of gentiles are not heretics, and slaughter follows the majority.
Rabba bar Avuh holds like Ḥiyya bar Abba citing Yoḥanan: gentiles outside Eretz Yisrael follow their ancestors' custom, not true idolatry.
Rav Yosef bar Minyumi reports Rav Naḥman's ruling that gentile heretics do not have the status of heretics.
With respect to what matter is this ruling made, slaughter or the halakha of lowering into a pit? Both readings are challenged.
Rav Ukva bar Ḥama says the ruling concerns accepting offerings from gentiles.
A baraita on the verse Of you shows that offerings from gentiles are accepted and the verse excludes only Jewish transgressors.
Gemara asks: perhaps the verse means accept only from righteous Jews, and never accept gentiles' offerings?
Gemara rejects that reading: it should not enter one's mind, since the verse is not limited to Jews.
A baraita on the repeated word ish includes gentiles, who may vow and donate offerings like Jews.
Mishna: the carcass of a gentile-slaughtered animal imparts impurity through carrying.
Gemara asks: isn't this obvious, since it is a carcass and imparts impurity through carrying?
Rava: the tanna teaches that this animal imparts impurity by carrying, while an idolatrous offering imparts impurity even in a tent, following Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.
Alternative version of Rava: the mishna's animal is like the other only in carrying impurity, and this view does not follow Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira.
A baraita of Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira derives tent impurity of idolatrous offerings from Psalms 106:28, comparing them to a corpse.
Mishna: slaughter by one who slaughters at night, or by a blind person, is valid.
Gemara infers from the mishna's wording that such slaughter is valid after the fact but not ab initio.
Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita permits slaughter ab initio during the day and at night, on a rooftop or ship.
Rav Pappa: the baraita refers to a case where a torch is placed opposite the slaughterer, making it permitted ab initio.
Rav Ashi: the baraita's wording is precise, equating night slaughter with daytime slaughter, while the mishna equates it with a blind person's, so only after the fact.

14a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: slaughter performed on Shabbat or Yom Kippur is valid, even though the slaughterer incurs the death penalty.
Rav Huna reports Rav's teaching via Ḥiyya: such slaughter is valid but the meat is forbidden to eat that day, and the sages attribute this to Yehuda.
Which opinion of Rabbi Yehuda is this?
Rabbi Abba: it is Yehuda's view about preparation for Shabbat, that a non-prepared item is forbidden.
Mishna on cutting gourds and carcasses before animals and dogs on Shabbat; Yehuda forbids what was not prepared before Shabbat, so the same logic applies here.
Abaye objects: the cases are not comparable, since the animal was initially fit for human use and is now fit for dogs in one case but still fit for humans in the other.
Rabbi Abba rejects the distinction: an animal alive is designated for breeding, not for consumption.
Abaye asks: if so, how do we slaughter an animal on a Festival?
Rabbi Abba: an animal is designated both for consumption and for breeding, and slaughter retroactively clarifies which designation applied.
Doesn't Yehuda reject retroactive designation? If so, from where do we know this is his view?
A baraita on a buyer of wine from Samaritans: the Sages, including Yehuda, forbid drinking before separating tithes, so Yehuda rejects retroactive designation.

14b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara rejects the proof: there Yehuda's reason is the concern about a wineskin bursting, as the baraita's final clause shows.
The baraita's later clause: the Rabbis argue with Meir that the wineskin may burst before tithes are separated.
Ayo's baraita: Yehuda holds one may not stipulate joining of boundaries on two matters, which shows he rejects retroactive designation.
What is different about stipulating east or west versus here or there, if both lack retroactive designation?
Rabbi Yoḥanan: in the Ayo case the Sage has already arrived, so the stipulation is clarified without retroactive designation.
Rav Yosef: Rav's ruling that slaughtered meat is forbidden that day follows Yehuda's view about vessels.
Mishna on moving vessels and their shards on Shabbat, with the shard use limited to a similar labor.
Yehuda's gloss: shards may be moved only if suited to a labor similar to their original use.
Gemara infers that an item not prepared from yesterday for the new labor is prohibited, so the slaughtered animal is likewise prohibited.
Abaye objects: the cases differ, since the shard is a newly created item, while the slaughtered animal was food both before and after.
Mishna: one may not squeeze fruit on Shabbat, and liquid that seeps out is forbidden lest one come to squeeze.
Yehuda's view: food-designated fruit's seeping liquid is permitted, while liquid-designated fruit's liquid is forbidden.
Gemara rejects this reading: Yehuda conceded to the Rabbis that liquid from olives and grapes is forbidden.
Gemara explains the Rabbis' decree: since the item is designated for squeezing or slaughter, permitting its use invites doing that act on Shabbat.
Gemara challenges Abaye's reading: it holds only according to Rav, who said Yehuda disagreed with the Rabbis even on olives and grapes.
Rav Sheshet, son of Rav Idi: Rav's ruling follows Yehuda's view about lamps, which is not analogous to slaughter.
A baraita: Yehuda permits moving a new lamp but not an old one set aside for repugnance, for all of Shabbat.
Gemara rejects the analogy: one may have heard Yehuda forbid an item set aside for repugnance, but not one forbidden by prohibition.
Did you actually hear Yehuda say that about an item set aside due to a prohibition?
Yes: a baraita is cited where Yehuda rules on this case.

15a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Metal lamps may be moved on Shabbat, except one kindled that same Shabbat and burning when Shabbat began.
Gemara rejects the analogy: perhaps the burning lamp differs, since it was set aside by direct action, unlike an animal.
Rav Ashi: Rav's ruling that slaughtered meat is forbidden follows Yehuda's view about one who cooks on Shabbat.
A baraita on one who cooks on Shabbat: an unwitting cook may eat, an intentional cook may not, following Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda: an unwitting cook may eat at Shabbat's end, while an intentional cook may never eat from the dish.
Yoḥanan HaSandlar distinguishes permission for others but not for the cook, and reads the mishna as referring to unwitting slaughter per Rav.
Gemara suggests reading the mishna as intentional slaughter, in accordance with Rabbi Meir.
Gemara rejects that reading: the mishna juxtaposes Shabbat slaughter with Yom Kippur, where intent and inadvertence make no difference.
Can the mishna be read as unwitting slaughter per Yehuda, given that the mishna states the death penalty?
The mishna means: intentional slaughter incurs death, while unwitting slaughter is valid.
Gemara suggests reading the mishna per Yoḥanan HaSandlar, but the mishna's ruling on slaughter is unqualified and does not match his distinction.
A baraita taught before Rav permits an unwitting cook to eat, but Rav silenced the teacher.
Why did Rav silence the baraita's teacher if he holds Yehuda's view and the baraita follows Meir?
Rav Ḥanan bar Ami says Rav rules like Meir to students and like Yehuda in public, which challenges Rav holding Yehuda's view.
Is it true that everyone listens to the teacher of a baraita, rather than to the amora who repeats Rav's ruling?
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: the tanna taught the case of one who slaughters before Rav.
The baraita: one who slaughters on Shabbat unwittingly may eat the animal, while one who slaughters intentionally may not.
Rav's reply: Meir permits eating only a cooked dish that was fit to be chewed raw, not a slaughtered animal that was never fit to eat.
Isn't the mishna about slaughter, and didn't Rav Huna teach that the meat is prohibited per Yehuda, implying Meir permits it?
Yes: Meir permits slaughtered meat on Shabbat, as the answer shows.

15b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The tanna's silence is explained: the animal was designated for a patient who was ill before Shabbat, so it was not set aside.
If so, what is the reason for Rabbi Yehuda's prohibition on meat on Shabbat?
Yehuda's prohibition concerns a case where the patient was ill before Shabbat and then recovered.
Rav's ruling: slaughtering for an ill person makes the meat forbidden to the healthy, but cooking for one permits it.
What is the reason for this distinction?
Cooked food was fit to be chewed raw, so it was not set aside; the animal was not fit to eat before slaughter, so it was set aside.
Rav Pappa: slaughter for an ill person may be permitted or forbidden depending on whether the animal was designated before Shabbat.
Rav Dimi of Neharde'a rules that slaughter for an ill person is permitted for the healthy, because slaughter is done with the patient in mind; cooking is forbidden by rabbinic decree.
Mishna: slaughter with a hand sickle's smooth side, flint or split reed is valid; serrated tools are not, since they strangle.
Gemara: the mishna's phrasing shows such slaughter is valid after the fact but not ab initio.
Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita permitting slaughter with flint and reed ab initio.
The baraita refers to detached blades, while the mishna refers to blades attached to the ground, which Rabbi Ḥiyya permits only after the fact.
Which opinion does this reading follow, Rabbi Ḥiyya's view that such slaughter is valid after the fact?
A baraita permits slaughter with any cutting item, whether attached or detached, and whether the knife is above or below the neck.
Whose opinion does that baraita follow, given that it is neither Yehuda HaNasi's nor Ḥiyya's?
Rabbi Ḥiyya always permits slaughter with these blades, even ab initio, and the disagreement exposes Yehuda HaNasi's stringent view.
Whose opinion does the mishna here follow, given that it is neither Yehuda HaNasi's nor Ḥiyya's?
Rabbi Ḥiyya permits these blades even ab initio, so the mishna follows Yehuda HaNasi.
Gemara objects: Yehuda HaNasi appears to contradict himself, ruling both ways in different statements.
There is no contradiction: Yehuda HaNasi disqualifies a blade attached from the start, but accepts one detached and later reattached.
From where do we know there is a difference between a blade attached from the start and one detached and later reattached?
A baraita: slaughter with a blade on a wheel, embedded in a wall, or attached to the ground is valid; a flint or reed that emerges on its own is invalid.

16a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The two clauses of the baraita seem to contradict each other.
The Gemara concludes that a blade attached from the outset differs from one detached and later reattached.
The mishna: slaughter with a knife attached to a wheel's mechanism is valid.
A baraita rules that such slaughter is invalid, so the mishna appears to conflict with it.
Resolution: the baraita refers to a wheel driven by a potter's pedal, or by primary versus secondary force of the water.
Rav Pappa's case of a man who diverted water onto a bound person: liability depends on primary, not secondary, force.
Yehuda HaNasi, seated before Rabbi Ḥiyya, asks where slaughter with a detached blade is derived.
Yehuda HaNasi's proof: the verse that Abraham took the knife to slaughter, which shows it was a detached blade.
Rav asks Rabbi Ḥiyya what Yehuda means; Ḥiyya says the reasoning is faulty, like a vav written on bark.
But the verse is in fact saying something, so why dismiss the proof?
The verse teaches Abraham's diligence in preparing a knife, not a halakha of ritual slaughter.
Rava: an item detached and later reattached has the status of a detached item for idolatry, since bowing to one's house forbids it.
Deuteronomy 12:2: their gods are upon the mountains, so items attached to the ground are never rendered idolatrous.
The seed dispute: a mishna on a bowl placed on a wall in rain, which renders produce susceptible only if placed to rinse the bowl.
Gemara: this mishna is itself difficult, since the first clause and the second clause infer contradictory results.
The second clause of the mishna is cited: a bowl placed so the wall is rinsed renders produce susceptible, since a detached-built wall counts as detached.
Rabbi Elazar says the mishna is disjointed, while Rav Pappa says it is one tanna describing a cave wall and a built wall.
Rav Pappa restates the mishna as a single rule, with the wall of a cave versus the wall of a building.
Clarification: the rule applies to a cave wall attached from the outset, while a built wall rinsed by the bowl renders produce susceptible.
Rava raises a dilemma.

16b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What is the halakha for slaughter with a blade that was detached and later attached?
A baraita: a flint emerging from a wall or a reed growing on its own is invalid, since the wall was built from detached stones.
The baraita means a cave wall that was always attached, and the wording's parallel with a reed suggests that reading.
A baraita: slaughter with a knife embedded in a wall is valid, which suggests a detached then reattached blade works.
A knife is different, since it is not subsumed into the wall.
A baraita: slaughter with an item attached to the ground is valid, suggesting detached then attached items work.
Perhaps the later phrase explains the earlier case, so the knife is the item attached to the ground; a flint would be invalid.
The Master's baraita: slaughter with a knife embedded in a wall is valid.
Shmuel: this applies only when the knife is above and the neck below, since the reverse risks pressing the simanim.
But the baraita explicitly permits both knife-above and knife-below positions, with attached and detached blades?
Rav Zevid: the baraita is disjunctive, with detached blades in one position and attached in the other; Rav Pappa limits the permission to birds.
Rav Ḥisda: a baraita rules five things about a reed stalk: no slaughter with it, no circumcision, no meat cutting, no teeth picking, no wiping.
But another baraita permits slaughter with any sharp object, including a reed stalk.
Rav Pappa: the permitted reed is a specific marsh reed that dries into a smooth hard surface.
Rav Pappa and Rabba bar Rav Huna cut fish innards and bird meat with reed stalks, where splinters are visible or the meat is soft.
Derive the prohibition on wiping from the rule that flammable wiping loosens the teeth, which is the wiping's own reason.
Rav Pappa: the baraita speaks of wiping blood or dirt from a wound, not wiping after relieving oneself.
Mishna: all slaughter is permitted and one may always slaughter.
Gemara: the phrase all slaughter includes all animals, even birds, for slaughter.
Who is the tanna who taught that one may always slaughter?
Rabba: it is Rabbi Yishmael, as a baraita shows.
Deuteronomy 12:20: Rabbi Yishmael says the verse permits meat of desire to the Jewish people once they enter the land.
Explanation: meat of desire was forbidden in the wilderness near the Tabernacle and permitted after entering the land.
Rabba adds that after the exile one might think the prohibition returns, so the mishna teaches one may always slaughter.
Rav Yosef objects: the phrasing should be always slaughter and eat, since permission primarily concerns eating.
Furthermore, why was it initially forbidden in the wilderness near the Tabernacle, and why permitted once they were far from it?

17a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If stabbing was already forbidden in the wilderness, it is all the more so forbidden in exile, far from the Temple.
Rav Yosef identifies the tanna of the mishna as Rabbi Akiva, citing a baraita.
The verse in Deuteronomy about slaughtering from herd and flock when the place of God's name is far away.
Rabbi Akiva's reading: the verse only forbids stabbed meat after entry into the land, and it was permitted before.
Rav Yosef adds that exile must not restore stabbed meat, so the mishna teaches that slaughter is always required.
The Gemara asks what the underlying disagreement between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yishmael is.
Rabbi Akiva holds desire-meat was never forbidden; Rabbi Yishmael holds stabbed meat was never permitted.
On Rabbi Yishmael's view, the verse about slaughtering the bull explains the requirement of slaughter.
Leviticus 1:5 on slaughtering the young bull for the burnt offering.
How can Rabbi Akiva explain the word slaughter in that verse if stabbing was permitted?
Sacrificial animals differ, since slaughter is required for them.
On Rabbi Yishmael's view, the verse in Numbers about slaughtering flocks for the people in the wilderness is explained.
Numbers 11:22 on flocks and herds being slaughtered for them.
If Rabbi Akiva holds stabbing was allowed, why does the verse say slaughter rather than stab?
In the wilderness, their stabbing counted as their slaughter.
On Rabbi Yishmael's view, the cited mishna about covering blood is understood straightforwardly.
The mishna exempting one who stabs or rips the simanim from covering blood.
Why is the stabber exempt from covering blood on Rabbi Akiva's view, given that stabbed meat was permitted?
On Rabbi Akiva's view desire-meat was never forbidden, which explains the verse permitting gazelle and deer.
Deuteronomy 12:22 on eating gazelle and deer as the pure and impure may eat them.
On Rabbi Yishmael's view, were gazelle and deer themselves permitted in the wilderness, since they are not offerings?
The prohibition applied only to domesticated animals fit for sacrifice, not to wild animals.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks about the status of stabbed-meat limbs that Israel brought into the land, per Rabbi Akiva.
The Gemara asks when this dilemma applies: to the seven conquest years?
Suggested reading: during the conquest, non-kosher food was already permitted to them, so stabbed meat would be too.
Deuteronomy 6:10-11 on houses full of good things that the people would eat.
Rav Yirmeya bar Abba cites Rav that pork found in the houses was permitted to them.
Is it even necessary to ask whether stabbed kosher meat was permitted, given the pork ruling?
The dilemma concerns the period after the conquest instead.
Alternatively, the dilemma is about the conquest years, but only spoils from gentiles were permitted; the matter stays unresolved.
Rabba explains the mishna phrases all slaughter and always slaughter.
How should the phrase about slaughtering with any cutting item be explained?
Suggested reading: the phrase refers to what is slaughtered with flint, glass, or reed.
Objection: the phrase is taught parallel to the others, so it must refer to the same party as they do.
Rather, Rava says the entire mishna refers to those who slaughter.
Rava explains each phrase: hakkol includes Samaritans and Jewish transgressors, and the other phrases cover time, place, and tools.
The mishna's exception: except the serrated side of a harvest sickle and a saw.
Shmuel's father notched knives and sent them to Eretz Yisrael to learn which notch invalidates slaughter.
They replied that the invalidating notch is like a saw, as we learned in the mishna.
The Sages taught in a baraita:

17b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A knife with many notches is like a saw; with one notch, catching invalidates slaughter while entangling does not.
What is the practical difference between a catching notch and an entangling notch?
Rabbi Eliezer: a catching notch has a sharp edge on two sides, an entangling notch on one side.
Challenge: a one-sided notch also has a point that cuts the neck and an edge that rips the simanim, so the distinction fails.
The reference is to a notch at the top of the knife, where slaughter begins.
Objection: the knife cuts the neck going one way and rips the simanim coming back, so the notch works in both directions.
The case is one where the slaughterer drew the knife backward but did not draw it forward.
Rava teaches three kinds of notches and the halakha for slaughtering with each, both ab initio and after the fact.
Rav Huna son of Rav Nehemya challenges Rav Ashi: you cited Rava as ruling that an entangling notch invalidates slaughter.
Counter-citation: Rava also says an entangling notch gives valid slaughter, which seems to contradict the earlier ruling.
No contradiction: invalid when the knife went back and forth, valid when it was only drawn backward.
Rav Aha son of Rav Avya asks about a knife like a grain awn, smooth but without actual notches.
Rav Ashi replies dryly that someone should bring the meat of that animal so they can eat it.
Rav Hisda states a rule about examining knives.
From where in the Torah is the obligation to examine a knife derived?
First Samuel 14:34 about slaughtering with the knife and eating, implying the knife was checked first.
