Is the need to examine a knife not obvious, since a perforated gullet makes the animal a tereifa?
The point is establishing a source for showing the knife to a Torah scholar.
Objection from Rabbi Yohanan: showing the knife to a scholar is only rabbinic, done out of respect for the scholar.
The verse is merely a support text, not a source of the obligation.
Customs: in Eretz Yisrael knives were checked in sunlight, and in Neharde'a by placing them on water.
Rav Sheshet checked a knife with the tip of his tongue.
Rav Aha bar Ya'akov checked a knife by drawing a hair across the blade to catch on any notch.
In Sura they say the flesh should check the knife, since the knife consumes the flesh.
Rav Pappa says examination is needed on the flesh, the fingernail and the three sides of the blade.
Ravina reports to Rav Ashi that Rav Sama cited him in Rava's name for the flesh, nail and three-sides examination.
Rav Ashi clarifies that he said flesh and nail, and did not say the three sides.
Others report that Rav Ashi said all three checks, but did not attribute them to Rava.
Ravina and Rav Aha son of Rava sat before Rav Ashi when a knife was brought to him for examination.
Rav Ashi tells Rav Aha to examine the knife on the nail, the flesh and the three sides.
Rav Ashi approves, noting Rav Kahana also said this is the proper way to examine a knife.
Rav Kahana's view is cited as confirming the same method of examination.
Rav Yeimar holds that the nail and flesh checks are required but the three-sides check is not.
Rabbi Zeira cites Shmuel: a knife heated to white hot still gives valid slaughter if the sharp blade precedes the heat.
The blade's sharpness acts before the heat takes effect on the tissue.
Objection: the sides of the knife should burn the throat and make the animal a tereifa.
The slaughter area separates quickly, so notches on the sides never touch the simanim, just as with the white-hot knife.
Rav Huna bar Rav Ketina cites Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish on three deficiencies that disqualify sacrifices in the same way.
Rav Hisda adds that a deficiency in a knife is also disqualifying.
Why does Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish not include the knife among the deficiencies?
He addresses only sacred animals, not non-sacred ones.
All these deficiencies have the same measure as the deficiency that disqualifies the altar.

18a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What measure of altar deficiency is enough to catch a fingernail?
Objection from a baraita giving conflicting measures: a handbreadth according to one tanna, an olive-bulk according to another.
The measures refer to different materials: a limestone coating versus the stone itself.
Rav Huna says a slaughterer who does not show his knife to a scholar is ostracized, and Rava says his meat is declared tereifa.
The two rulings do not conflict: they apply depending on whether the knife was found intact.
Ravina says if the knife was found damaged, the meat is smeared with excrement so even a gentile will not buy it.
A story: Rava bar Hinnana ostracized a slaughterer who did not present his knife and declared his meat tereifa.
Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi visit Rava bar Hinnana, who asks that the matter of the slaughterer be examined by the Sages.
Rav Ashi examines the knife, finds it intact and declares the meat fit.
Mar Zutra objects that Rav Ashi should have shown respect to the elder who had removed the slaughterer.
Rav Ashi replies that he is carrying out the elder's own request to examine the matter.
Rabba bar Huna holds that a detached tooth or detached fingernail may be used for ab initio slaughter.
Objection: a mishna lists teeth and fingernails as invalid because they strangle the animal.
Reconciled: one tooth is fine but two teeth rip the simanim; a detached nail is fine, an attached one is not.
Mishna: a sickle with serrations that do not tear the flesh is treated like a knife if its serrations are smoothed.
Rabbi Yohanan says Beit Hillel validated such slaughter only for purity from carcass impurity, not for permitting consumption.
Rav Ashi argues the mishna's wording is precise, since it says invalid and valid rather than prohibited and permitted.
Objection: by that logic the mishna should have spoken of impurity and purity, so the wording proves nothing.
The terms invalid, valid, prohibited and permitted all mean the same thing, so no inference follows.
Mishna: slaughter from within a complete ring of the cricoid is valid if a thread's breadth remains; Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda disagrees.
Rav and Shmuel rule like Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda, but only for the large complete upper ring, not the incomplete rings.
Objection: a baraita states Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda's view without that limitation.

18b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A slaughter from the other rings is valid if they encircle most of the windpipe; Rabbi Hanina ben Antigonus testifies to a similar case.
Rav Yosef says Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda makes two claims, and Rav and Shmuel accept only one of them.
Objection: Rav and Shmuel's statement should be read as applying only to the large ring, not to the other rings.
Rabbi Zeira ate meat from a slaughter that Rav and Shmuel had invalidated, after moving up to Eretz Yisrael.
The Eretz Yisrael scholars object that Zeira comes from Babylonia and should follow Rav and Shmuel.
Zeira replies that the ruling came from Yosef bar Hiyya, who learns from everyone, including misquoters.
Rav Yosef is angered and insists he learned from Rav Yehuda, who cited even uncertain attributions carefully.
Rav Yehuda cites Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba on a tribunal of three permitting a blemished firstborn where no expert is available.
Does Rabbi Zeira not accept that a traveler takes on the stringencies of both his origin and his destination?
Abaye: that principle applies within Babylonia or from Eretz Yisrael to Babylonia, but not when ascending to Eretz Yisrael.
Rav Ashi: even moving from Babylonia applies only if one intends to return, and Zeira did not intend to return.
Abaye objects: scholars from Mehoza report Rabbi Zeira in the name of Rav Nahman that such slaughter is valid.
Rav Yosef replies that each place follows its own custom, and Mehoza did not follow Rav and Shmuel.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish validates cutting at the tip of the thyroid cartilage, and Rabbi Yohanan criticizes him for exaggerating.
Rav Pappi cites Rava: encountering the arytenoid cartilage outside the area of slaughter makes the animal a tereifa.
A dilemma: does encountered mean actually touched?
First Kings 2:25 uses the word encountered for a blow that caused death.
Or does encountered mean reached without touching?
Genesis 32:2 uses encountered for angels who met Jacob without touching him.
Rav Pappa cites Rava: if part of the arytenoid cartilage is left, the slaughter is valid.
Rav Ameimar bar Mar Yenuka reports Rabbi Hiyya bar Avya ruling that leaving part of the arytenoid cartilage is valid.
Ravina reports Rav Shemen citing Mar Zutra, who taught the same ruling that leaving part of the arytenoid is valid.
Mar bar Rav Ashi rules: encountering the arytenoid is valid, but leaving part of it makes the animal a tereifa.

19a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The halakha: slaughter from the incline of the thyroid cartilage downward is valid, matching the view about the arytenoid cartilage.
Rav Hanan bar Rav Ketina asks Rav Nahman whose opinion his ruling follows, since it fits neither the Rabbis nor Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Nahman replies that he knows neither Hillek nor Billek, but he knows the halakha itself.
A chain of transmitters traces the ruling that slaughter from the incline of the thyroid cartilage downward is valid.
Analysis of the baraita: Rabbi Hanina ben Antigonus agrees with the view that slaughter is valid when the knife diverts above the ring.
Objection: that conclusion is obvious; the reading must be checked against the possibility that Ben Antigonus agrees with the Rabbis.
Objection: if Ben Antigonus agreed with Rabbi Yosei, the baraita should have introduced him with the word testified.
The halakha follows Rabbi Hanina ben Antigonus, as Rav Nahman also rules.
Rav Asi's dispute: the Rabbis require the whole slaughter within the ring, while Rabbi Yosei treats most of the windpipe as its whole.
If one-third is cut outside the ring and two-thirds inside, all agree the slaughter is invalid, since the animal's life must leave validly.
Rav Hisda counters: the dispute should be reversed, applying to the case where one-third is cut outside and then two-thirds inside.
In that reversed case, Rabbi Yosei treats the slaughter like a windpipe with a deficiency in half of it.
The Rabbis distinguish: that deficiency was in the proper place, while here the cut was made outside the proper place, so it is valid only if the second part was ritually cut.
The mishna teaches that the majority of one siman is treated as all of it.
Rav Yosef asks who will tell us the mishna's majority principle was taught by the Rabbis rather than by Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda.
Abaye objects: does that mean Rabbi Yosei taught every majority principle in general?
Rav Yosef replies that he is speaking only of majorities in slaughter, since the Rabbis are known to disagree there.
An alternative version of the same discussion, in Rav Huna's and Rav Asi's name, presented with the same conclusions.
Restating the case: cutting two-thirds in the ring and then the rest outside is valid by agreement.
The mishna again cited: the majority of one siman is like the whole siman.
Rav Hisda objects, repeating Rav Yosef's challenge about whether Rabbi Yosei taught the majority principle.
Rav Yosef repeats the objection that Rabbi Yosei cannot be credited with every majority principle.
Rav Hisda replies that he speaks only of majority in slaughter, as the Rabbis are known to disagree there.
The case is set out: one-third cut, one-third cut properly, then the final third cut after diversion.
Rav Yehuda and Rav Huna give opposing rulings on that case, each attributed to Rav, based on whether the majority was validly cut.
Rav Yehuda says in Rav's name that a case of one-third, diversion, and one-third properly cut is valid.
The Sages come to Rav Huna, who rules that the animal is a tereifa.
Rav Yehuda is angry, complaining that he calls it a tereifa while Rav Huna calls it valid.
Rav Huna says Rav Yehuda's anger is proper, since he heard the ruling from Rav directly and the majority of the siman was validly cut.
Rav Hisda tells Rav Huna not to retract his ruling.

19b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Retracting the earlier ruling would undermine its reasoning, since the second third was validly cut and life left in the course of valid slaughter.
Rav Nahman is asked about slaughtering one-third, diverting, then cutting one-third, then the final third properly.
Rav Nahman cites Rabbi Elazar bar Minyumi: slaughter jagged like a comb's teeth is valid.
Objection: perhaps that ruling applies only when the slaughter wanders within the proper place.
Lest one think a slaughter must be straight and unbroken, the ruling teaches that a jagged one is still valid.
The Gemara sets up a mnemonic for the Sages and seating order: Rabbi Abba, Rav Kahana and Rav Yehuda, with the questions passed between them.
Rav Kahana asks Rav Yehuda about the case of one-third, diversion, one-third, and then the final third.
Rav Yehuda says the slaughter is valid.
Rav Kahana asks about cutting one-third, then diverting, cutting one-third properly, and then diverting for the final third.
Rav Yehuda says that slaughter is invalid.
Rav Kahana asks about cutting where a perforation already exists in the front of the windpipe and continuing.
Rav Yehuda says that slaughter is valid.
Rav Kahana asks about encountering a perforation after half the windpipe has been cut.
Rav Yehuda says that slaughter is invalid.
Rabbi Abba brings these rulings to Eretz Yisrael, where Rabbi Elazar repeats them to Rabbi Yohanan.
Rabbi Yohanan asks what distinguishes cutting at a perforation from encountering one mid-slaughter.
Rabbi Elazar: cutting at a perforation is like a gentile starting and a Jew finishing, which is valid; encountering one is like the reverse, which is invalid.
Rava says Rabbi Yohanan rightly mocked the distinction, repeating the gentile label.
Rava explains: in the gentile-starts case, life left by a gentile's hand; here the Jew slaughtered the whole animal.
Rava's objection: why should it matter whether the perforation was at the start or was encountered mid-slaughter?
Mishna: slaughter from the sides or nape of the throat is valid or not, while pinching a bird from the nape is valid, and the two rules are not interchangeable.
What does oref mean in the mishna, the actual occipital bone or the nape?
Leviticus 5:8 says to pinch the head adjacent to its oref, not the oref itself.
The verse thus means adjacent to the nape rather than the bone itself.
The oref in the mishna is the nape below the occipital bone, as the mishna's latter clause says the entire nape is valid for pinching.
From where are these matters derived?
A baraita reads adjacent as seeing the oref, citing Numbers 22:5 and Jeremiah 2:27.
Jeremiah 2:27 is cited: they turned their oref to Me and not their face.
What does the latter proof add to the earlier one?
If the oref itself is unknown, how would we know where to find the adjacent point?
Come and hear Jeremiah 2:27: the oref is opposite the face, at the back of the head, so it can be located.
The sons of Rabbi Hiyya describe the mitzva of pinching: move the simanim behind the nape, with some saying it is required and others saying it is preferred.
The Gemara states it is reasonable to follow the view that one may move the simanim behind the nape.
The mishna shows this: slaughter from the nape is invalid, while pinching from the nape is valid.

20a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If pinching requires moving the simanim behind the nape, why does the mishna say pinching is valid? Slaughter from there would also be valid, so the mishna must mean the simanim were not moved.
Rabbi Yannai rejects the sons of Rabbi Hiyya's reading: the exclusion must be of moving the simanim behind the nape, which is valid for slaughter but not pinching.
Rabba bar bar Hana proposes the exclusion may cover a tooth or fingernail that is not detached.
Objection: the mishna already states tooth and fingernail explicitly, so the exclusion cannot be for them.
Rabbi Yirmeya proposes the exclusion is for drawing the fingernail back and forth during pinching.
If drawing back and forth is valid according to some, what is the point of the exclusion?
The sons of Rabbi Hiyya follow the view that drawing back and forth in pinching is invalid.
Rav Kahana: the mitzva of pinching is to cut with the fingernail from the nape and continue downward.
Rabbi Avin objects that drawing back and forth should be excluded.
Rabbi Yirmeya replies that drawing back and forth is all the more so valid in pinching.
What does that is its mitzva mean, implying a restriction to that method?
It can be read as saying that this too is a valid method.
Shmuel: any place valid for slaughter on the throat corresponds to a valid place for pinching on the nape.
What does that rule exclude?
Objection: if it excludes ripping the simanim, that conflicts with Rami bar Yehezkel's ruling that ripping is not disqualifying for birds.
Rav Pappa: it excludes pinching at the back of the head, which is not the place of slaughter.
Leviticus 5:8 says adjacent to its nape, not at its head, so the exclusion is needed.
The head that is excluded is the incline of the head, where cutting begins incorrectly and then continues down to the simanim.
This matches Rav Huna's citation of Rav Asi: if the knife diverted and cut one-third before two-thirds within the ring, the slaughter is invalid.
Rav Aha son of Rava asks Rav Ashi about Rami bar Yehezkel's teaching on bird ripping.
Rav Aha explains that Rami's ruling holds only according to the view that there is no Torah-based slaughter for birds.

20b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: On the view that birds have a Torah-based slaughter, ripping the simanim also disqualifies a bird.
Rav Ashi argues the reverse is more reasonable: even if birds have Torah slaughter, the no-ripping rule may have been revealed to Moses orally.
On the view that bird slaughter is only rabbinic, its rules are learned from animal slaughter, so birds are treated like animals entirely.
Ravina cites Ravin bar Kisi: no-ripping applies only to pinching, while for slaughter ripping does disqualify a bird.
Objection: Shmuel's principle that pinching follows slaughter contradicts that reading, so it must disagree with Shmuel.
Ze'eiri holds that if the neck bone breaks and most surrounding flesh is cut, the bird is an unslaughtered carcass.
Rav Hisda cites a mishna: a bird pinched with a knife rather than a nail makes garments impure, showing it is a carcass.
The Sages explain that pinching with a knife does not count as slaughter at all; Rav Huna says from concealing the knife, Rava says from pressing it.
If Rav Huna's reason is concealing the knife, why not say pressing?
Rav Huna holds that drawing back and forth in pinching is valid, so pressing is not the issue.
If Rava's reason is pressing, why not say concealing the knife?
Concealing means the knife is hidden like a rat in house foundations, but when pinching from the nape the knife is exposed.
Rava objects that Ze'eiri's broken-neck rule is difficult: how can a bird be prepared for sacrifice if it is already dead when pinched?
Abaye counters that a burnt bird offering needs two simanim, so the same problem arises even without Ze'eiri's rule.
Rava replies that the pinching continues to fulfill the mitzva of separating head from body in a bird burnt offering.
If so, should the skin also need cutting to fulfill the separation mitzva?
Abaye: anything that invalidates slaughter invalidates separation, and anything that does not invalidate slaughter does not invalidate separation.
Objection: according to the Rabbis a minority of the simanim does not invalidate slaughter yet invalidates separation, breaking the principle.
Revised principle: whatever is required for slaughter is required for separation, and whatever is not required for slaughter is not required for separation.

21a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava objects that Ze'eiri's halakha is hard to accept as stated.
Rava offers a reinterpretation: the pinching means cutting the spine and neck bone without most of the flesh.
Rabbi Zeira arrives in Eretz Yisrael and finds Rabbi Ami teaching Ze'eiri's ruling.
Rabbi Zeira asks whether one can pinch a dead bird while standing, citing a verse from Daniel.
Rabbi Ami is briefly astonished by the challenge and then reconsiders.
Rabbi Ami restates the ruling as cutting the spine and neck without most of the flesh.
A baraita describes pinching a bird sin offering and specifies one siman or two for a burnt offering.
Which tanna is the baraita following, since the Rabbis and Rabbi Elazar ben Shimon seem to conflict with its wording?
Two simanim follows the Rabbis and a majority of two follows Rabbi Elazar ben Shimon, or both follow him with a different reading.
Shmuel holds that a person whose neck was broken with most of the flesh cut imparts impurity in a tent.
The incident of Eli, whose neck broke without the flesh being cut, seems to contradict Shmuel's ruling.
Old age is different, so Eli's death does not contradict the ruling.
The verse about Eli's fall and broken neck is cited to support the explanation of old age.
Rabbi Yochanan holds that a person ripped lengthwise like a fish is a corpse, and Shmuel bar Yitzchak limits this to ripping from the back.
Shmuel holds that an animal cut into two pieces widthwise is an unslaughtered carcass even while convulsing.
Rabbi Elazar holds that an animal whose thigh is removed and whose hollow is visible is an unslaughtered carcass.
What is meant by the hollow being visible?
Rava explains that it means an animal that is collapsed while its hind leg is visibly missing.
A mishnah on creeping animals says a severed head leaves the body impure even while convulsing, like a lizard tail.
What does the word severed in the mishnah mean?
Reish Lakish explains that severed means actually cut off.
Rabbi Asi, citing Rabbi Mani, compares this to separating the head of a burnt bird offering.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether Rabbi Asi means the Rabbis' method of separating the head, which would leave no dispute with Reish Lakish.
Or perhaps Rabbi Asi means Rabbi Elazar ben Shimon's method, in which case he disputes with Reish Lakish.
Rabbi Asi clarifies that he means Rabbi Elazar ben Shimon's method, and that they indeed disagree.
Some report that Reish Lakish held the severing was actual removal.
Rabbi Asi, citing Rabbi Mani, applies the burnt bird comparison to Rabbi Elazar ben Shimon's majority-of-two view.
What exactly are the positions of the Rabbis and of Rabbi Elazar ben Shimon?
A baraita on the sliding-scale bird offering cites the verse about preparing the second bird as a burnt offering according to the ordinance.
How can the phrase according to the ordinance be read, when it appears twice?
The second phrase teaches that it follows the rules of an animal sin offering, which does not come on the altar in the same way.

21b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita teaches that a bird burnt offering comes only from non-sacred animals, only by day, and with the priest's right hand.
If so, perhaps just as the animal sin offering uses two simanim, the bird burnt offering also cuts a majority of two simanim?
The verse on pinching and burning the head and body separately shows that each part is treated on its own.
Rabbi Yishmael holds that according to the ordinance refers to the bird sin offering's ordinance.
The bird sin offering is pinched near the nape, so the bird burnt offering is pinched there too.
If so, perhaps the burnt offering is also not separated and leaves one siman uncut, as with the sin offering?
The verse about the priest bringing it teaches that the burnt offering is sacrificed uniquely, unlike the sin offering.
Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon holds that according to the ordinance refers to the bird sin offering's ordinance.
The verse on the second bird as a burnt offering according to the ordinance is read as pointing to the bird sin offering rule.

22a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: After pinching, the priest holds the head and body of the bird together and sprinkles its blood, the same as with the burnt offering here.
What is the baraita actually saying, since a sin offering bird does not require holding both parts?
When the head is still attached to the body, the blood is sprinkled, and the burnt offering rule matches this; the two-simanim point was cited earlier.
If so, perhaps the burnt offering is pinched by cutting only one siman, just as the sin offering is.
The verse says the priest shall bring it, showing the burnt offering differs and cuts two simanim.
Why is the phrase the priest shall bring needed, if the pinching and burning already establish cutting both simanim?
Without that phrase one might read according to the ordinance as making the burnt offering cut only one siman like the sin offering.
Alternatively, the verse on burning might instead teach that pinching is done on top of the altar, as burning is.
Since the verse says the priest shall bring it, it marks the distinction, and the full separation of head and body is derived from the pinching verse.
How do we know that an animal sin offering comes only from non-sacred animals?
Rav Chisda cites the verse on Aaron sacrificing the bull of his own sin offering to show it must be from his own cattle, not communal or tithe property.
The day requirement for the bird offering cannot come from the animal sin offering, since the verse about the day of its commanding is the source.
The day rule was cited in that list only incidentally, not as a derivation.
The right-hand rule for the bird offering seems to be derived from Rabba bar bar Chana's teaching, so the analogy is unnecessary.
Reish Lakish's principle: wherever finger or priesthood is mentioned for offerings, the rite is done only with the right hand.
The first tanna could not rely on that principle, because it needs both priesthood and finger, and the bird offering mentions only priesthood.
How do the first tanna and Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon derive that the bird burnt offering is pinched at the nape?
They derive the burnt offering's pinching from the sin offering's pinching, by a verbal analogy.
Mishnah: doves and pigeons are fit or unfit depending on age, and a bird in the intermediate yellowing stage is unfit for either.
A baraita explains the mishnah: the age that is fit for doves is unfit for pigeons, and the reverse.
A baraita derives from the verse on doves and young pigeons that doves must be mature, and raises an a fortiori argument.

22b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: An a fortiori argument: if pigeons, fit when young, are fit when old, then doves, fit when old, should be fit when young.
The verse says doves are older and not younger, which blocks the a fortiori inference.
Young pigeons must be younger and not older, by the same kind of a fortiori reasoning.
The mirror a fortiori argument: doves, unfit when young, are fit when old, so pigeons, fit when young, should be fit when old.
The verse says young pigeons, meaning younger and not older, which blocks that inference.
What is the biblical derivation for these rules?
Rava says the verse never mixes the wording, so doves are older and pigeons are younger.
Rava's derivation fails: the verse's young can apply to pigeons alone, so doves might be brought either older or younger.
Doves and pigeons are always juxtaposed in the Torah, so the rule for doves is the reverse of the rule for pigeons.
A baraita: one might think all doves and all pigeons are fit, so the verse limits the rule.
The verse says of doves and not all doves, and of young pigeons and not all young pigeons, to limit the rule.
The verse excludes birds at the start of yellowing, which are unfit for either category.
Doves are fit from when their feathers turn golden, and pigeons are unfit from when their feathers yellow.
Ya'akov Korcha's baraita says pigeons are fit from when their feathers become ruffled.
He teaches the baraita and gives its explanation.
Job 39:30 describes the fledglings sucking up blood, which supports the explanation.
Abaye says the stage is when a feather is plucked and blood emerges.
Rabbi Zeira asks: if someone vows a burnt offering of doves or pigeons and brings a bird at the start of yellowing, does he fulfill his vow?
Rava brings a proof from the baraita that the verse excludes birds at the start of yellowing as unfit.
If the bird at that stage were in doubt, the verse would not need to exclude it, which means it is a fixed category rather than a doubt.

23a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The verse's exclusion of bestiality and idolatry, not uncertainty, is what the phrase was needed for.
One might think the verse on corruption and blemish means that a corrupt animal is disqualified only by blemish.
The verse distinguishes corruption from blemish as two separate kinds of disqualification.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that corruption refers only to licentiousness and idolatry.
Scriptural verses show that corruption refers to sexual licentiousness and to idolatry.
Any offering disqualified by blemish is also disqualified by licentiousness or idolatry, and those not disqualified by blemish are not disqualified by them either.
Since blemish does not disqualify birds, licentiousness and idolatry should not disqualify them either.
The verse teaches that bestiality and idolatry do disqualify these birds, despite the lack of a blemish rule.
Rabbi Zeira asks: if someone vows a burnt offering from a ram or lamb and brings a palges, which is between them in age, is it fit?
According to Rabbi Yochanan there is no dilemma, because a palges is an entity in itself.
The mishnah and a verse on the meal offering of a ram show that a palges is included with the ram's offering rules.
The dilemma only arises according to bar Padda, who holds that the palges is a case of uncertainty.

23b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: One who sacrifices a palges brings the ram's meal offering and libation and stipulates how the remainder is to be treated.
Does the stipulation cover only a ram or lamb, or also the possibility that the palges is in itself a separate entity? The question is then applied to Rabbi Zeira's siur dilemma.
Analysis of the siur cases under each of Rabbi Meir's and Rabbi Yehuda's views, and whether the siur's status is doubtful or unique.
Rav Huna says the vow requires a full thanks offering and all its loaves, so doubt about the siur cannot satisfy the vow.
The dilemma is needed only when the vower is exempting another person's thanks offering, so he never took on the full obligation.
Under the other man's contribution, the thanks-offering bringer would still need both matza and leavened loaves, so the siur would not exempt him.
The dilemma applies only when the vower did not say he was exempting the other's offering; it stays unresolved.
Mishnah and baraita: a red heifer is fit by slaughter and unfit by neck-breaking, and a heifer with broken neck is the reverse.
Can the red heifer be derived by an a fortiori argument to be fit by neck-breaking, since a heifer with broken neck is fit that way?

24a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The verse on the red heifer's slaughter and its statute shows that slaughter, not neck-breaking, renders it fit.
Is an a fortiori inference barred wherever statute is written, given the Yom Kippur lot rule?
A baraita: the lot makes the goat a sin offering, but a verbal designation does not.
One might argue a fortiori that a verbal designation should sanctify the goat, since the lot sanctifies it.
The verse says and render it a sin offering to block that inference; the heifer's neck-breaking is restricted by its own verse.
If neck-breaking makes the heifer fit, slaughter should make the broken-neck heifer fit by a fortiori argument.
The verse says the heifer shall have its neck broken, not slaughtered, which blocks the a fortiori argument.
Mishnah and baraita: priests and Levites differ in which blemishes and which ages disqualify them.
From where are these rules about Levites and the passage of years derived?
Numbers verses show that the passage of years disqualifies Levites.
One might think blemishes also disqualify Levites, by a fortiori argument.
The word this teaches that only the passage of years disqualifies Levites.
One might think years disqualify priests, by a fortiori argument from the Levite rule.
The word which pertains to the Levites excludes priests.
One might think Levites are disqualified by years even in Shiloh and the eternal Temple.
The verse on service and carrying burdens limits the rule to the time of carrying on shoulders.
Two verses give different ages for Levite service, twenty-five and thirty.
Twenty-five is the apprenticeship age and thirty the service age, reconciling the two verses.
A student without a good sign after five years will not see one later; Rabbi Yosei says the period is three years.
Daniel's verses on three years of study support Rabbi Yosei's view.
The other tanna distinguishes the easy Chaldean language from the difficult Temple service rules.
Baraita: a priest is fit from pubic hair growth until old age, and a Levite from thirty to fifty; Shiloh and the eternal Temple differ.
Rabbi Yosei asks which verse this halakha is derived from.

24b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A verse from Chronicles shows that Levites must sing in one unified voice to be fit for service.
Until what age does a priest remain fit for service?
Rabbi Ela, citing Rabbi Chanina, says aging means when the hands begin to tremble.
A mishnah on seminal emission and urination, with Rabbi Yosei's view, shows how residue determines impurity by age and health.
Until when is a person considered young?
Rabbi Ela, citing Rabbi Chanina, says a person is young while he can stand on one leg and remove and put on a shoe.
Anecdotes about Rabbi Chanina's vigor, and a baraita on when a priest is fit to serve and to lead prayer, with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view of age twenty.
Rav Chisda explains Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's view by citing a verse about appointing Levites from age twenty to oversee the Temple work.
The other tanna holds that oversight is a different task and requires an older priest.
How can that verse prove the rule for priests, when it is written about Levites?
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds that the Bible calls priests Levites in twenty-four places, so the verse can apply to priests.
A verse on a blemished descendant of Aaron is used to derive the rule that a minor priest is unfit.
Rabbi Elazar's rule that a minor priest is unfit, the dispute about rabbinic disqualification, and the Mishnah and baraita on earthenware vessels.
From where are the baraita's rules on earthenware vessels derived, and whether tokho requires contact with the impure item?
Rabbi Yonatan ben Avtolemos uses two uses of the word tokho in the verse to show that contact is not required.
From where do we derive that food becomes impure in its airspace without contact?
The Torah testified about the earthenware vessel, so the rule for other cases is derived from that testimony.

25a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A vessel makes its contents impure even when filled with mustard seeds that do not touch its walls.
Rav Adda bar Ahava challenges by a fortiori: earthenware should become impure from outside contact like other vessels.
Cites the Numbers verse about an open vessel that lacks a sealed cover.
Asks which vessel's impurity takes effect as soon as an impure item enters its opening.
Identifies earthenware as that vessel; a sealed one stays pure, so impurity depends on its opening.
Reverses the argument: if earthenware is impure through its airspace, other vessels should be too.
The verse's word tokho shows that only the airspace of an earthenware vessel renders it impure.
Objects that the Sages already used this tokho wording to derive a different halakha.
Explains the four occurrences of tokho in the verse and the separate teaching each one supports.
Asks whether other vessels should become impure only from their insides, by a fortiori reasoning.
Cites the Numbers verse about an open vessel that lacks a sealed cover.
Explains the verse: earthenware without a sealed cover is impure and sealed is pure; other vessels are impure either way.
The Mishna: what is pure in wooden vessels is impure in metal vessels, and the reverse.
Baraita explaining the Mishna: unfinished wooden receptacles are susceptible to impurity, flat ones are not, and metal is reversed.
Lists unfinished wooden vessels still awaiting smoothing, decoration or missing parts, which remain susceptible to impurity.
Asks whether it is obvious that a vessel lacking hollowing is not susceptible to impurity.
The ruling is needed for a three-log hollow inside a receptacle meant to hold one kav.
Begins the list of unfinished metal vessels, which are those still planned for later finishing work.

25b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continues the baraita: unfinished wooden vessels lacking a base, rim or handle are not susceptible, but lacking a cover is.
Asks what distinguishes unfinished wooden vessels, which are susceptible, from unfinished metal vessels, which are not until completed.
Rabbi Yochanan says metal vessels are made for honor, so unfinished they are not vessels; Rav Nachman cites their high cost.
Asks what practical difference follows from these two explanations.
The difference concerns bone vessels from horns: costly but not made for honor, so Rav Nachman treats them like metal.
Asks whether this implies that bone vessels are susceptible to impurity.
Yes: a baraita derives from the word goats that horn and hoof vessels are susceptible, and excludes vessels made of bird bones.
Mishna: the stage obligating tithes for bitter almonds exempts sweet almonds, and the stage obligating sweet almonds exempts bitter ones.
Baraita: small bitter almonds are obligated and large ones exempt; large sweet almonds are obligated and small ones exempt.
Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei, citing his father, exempts both small and large bitter almonds; others obligate both.
Rabbi Ela reports that Rabbi Chanina ruled in Tzippori following the view that exempts both almonds.
Asks why large bitter almonds are useful according to the view that obligates both.
Rabbi Yochanan replies that roasting them over fire sweetens them, making them fit for consumption.
Mishna on temed: unfermented temed is not bought with second tithe and invalidates a ritual bath; fermented temed is wine and does neither.
Asks whose opinion the Mishna follows, since it seems to be neither Rabbi Yehuda nor the Rabbis.
Cites a baraita: the Rabbis exempt temed matching the water measure; Rabbi Yehuda obligates it because taste indicates wine.
Analyzes the Mishna: if it follows the Rabbis, it exempts even fermented temed; if Rabbi Yehuda, it obligates even unfermented.
Begins Rav Nachman's report of a teaching attributed to Rabba bar Avuh.

26a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Clarifies that the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis concerns only temed that has fermented, as Rabbi Yosei ben Chanina also taught.
Introduces Rav Nachman's report of Rabba bar Avuh's teaching on temed purchased with second tithe money.
Holds that temed bought with second tithe money that later ferments takes on second tithe sanctity, and the money becomes unsanctified.
Gives the reason: the matter was revealed retroactively, so the temed was always produce when it was purchased.
Asks why the Mishna states flatly that unfermented temed cannot be bought, since it might ferment if left longer.
Rabba answers that the Mishna refers to temed left in a cup that did not ferment, showing it was never produce.
Rava rejects that reading and asks whose opinion this Mishna represents.
Answers that it is the view of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri.
Cites a Mishna: a small amount of wine or milk added to water, making the mixture look like wine or water, does not invalidate a ritual bath.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds that the appearance of the liquid determines its halakhic status throughout.
Rava argues that ben Nuri's appearance principle applies here too, so the temed case should follow appearance.
Concludes that the taste and appearance of the temed liquid are those of water, so it remains water until it ferments.
Challenges Rav Nachman: Rabbi Elazar holds that everyone agrees one cannot separate tithe from other temed unless it fermented.
Explains Rabbi Elazar's view: the dispute concerns unfermented temed, and tithe may not be separated from other temed to avoid mixing obligation and exemption.
Begins a baraita on unfermented temed, addressing its ritual impurity.

26b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava limits the rule: a ritual bath purifies temed only if its water was pure and later became impure.
Rav Geviha brings this ruling before Rav Ashi and raises a question about it.
Asks why temed impure from the start is not purified, since floating residue would block bath water, which should also apply to pure-then-impure temed.
Answers that the residue is mixed in, so bath contact works here as well.
Mishna: where a daughter may be sold as a maidservant, no fine is paid to her father for seduction or rape, and where a fine applies, no sale occurs.
Rav Yehuda reports Rav's view that this sale-fine principle is Rabbi Meir's, while the Rabbis allow both sale and a fine.
Cites a baraita on a girl's stages of sale and fines, stated by Rabbi Meir with his principle that sale and fine never coexist.
The Rabbis hold that a girl from age three years and a day until adulthood is entitled to a fine.
Asks whether she is entitled to a fine but not subject to sale, since her father may sell her during most of that period.
Answers that the Rabbis hold she is entitled to a fine even while she is subject to sale.
Mishna: where a minor has a right of refusal, there is no halitza; where halitza applies, there is no refusal.
Rav Yehuda reports Rav's view: refusal is Rabbi Meir's position, while the Rabbis hold that refusal applies where halitza does.
Cites a baraita on when a girl may refuse: Rabbi Meir says two pubic hairs, and Rabbi Yehuda says when black hair overtakes white.
Mishna: where a shofar is sounded before a festival on Shabbat eve, havdala is not recited; where havdala is recited, no shofar is sounded.
Explains: on a festival on Shabbat eve, shofar but no havdala; on a festival ending Shabbat, havdala but no shofar; Rabbi Dosa's formula differs.
Asks how a tekia is sounded on a festival falling on Shabbat eve, since the sanctity difference is less pronounced.
Rav Yehuda says to sound a tekia and a terua from its midst; Rav Asi says to sound both in one breath.
Notes that Rav Asi instituted his practice in the city of Huzal according to his own ruling.
Objects with a baraita saying only tekia is sounded on such a festival, which seems to exclude terua entirely.
Resolves the baraita: each amora reads it through his own view, one denying a separate terua and the other requiring a single breath.
Cites the Mishna's case of a festival ending Shabbat in abbreviated form.
Asks where in the blessing the special festival formula should be recited.
Rav Yehuda and Rav Nachman both say the formula is recited at the end of the blessing.
Rav Sheshet holds it may also be recited at the beginning of the blessing, but the halakha is not like him.
Cites Rabbi Dosa's formula of greater and lesser sanctity, but the halakha is not like him.
Rabbi Zeira rules that a midweek festival's end uses the full list of distinctions, including sacred from profane and light from darkness.
Asks the reason; answers that the formula enumerates the distinctions the Sages instituted, not only the one unique to that day.
Chapter-closing formula that names the first words of the next chapter.

Genesis verse: formed from the ground every bird of the air, suggesting birds came from land

Narration: his students look at each other, and he remarks on it
He dismissed the enemy with a flimsy pretext; birds came from water, brought to Adam to name
Some say he told the official the other formulation, from water, in a different language
He told his students the mud version because of the verse about formed from the ground
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak ben Pineḥas: slaughter of a bird is not required by Torah law
Verse: he shall spill its blood, indicating that mere spilling suffices

But the verse says he shall spill its blood, which answers the objection

Verse on eating the deer and gazelle, quoted as a source
What does the verse teach us about deer and gazelle if not that they are included
Deer and gazelle are juxtaposed to consecrated animals, so birds need slaughter only by rabbinic law
Who is the tanna who disagrees with Rabbi Elazar HaKappar
Baraita of Rabbi Yehuda: Moses was told to cut the gullet and windpipe, or one siman in birds
Rav Naḥman says the bird may be cut by either gullet or windpipe
Rav Adda bar Ahava says the gullet alone is required
Rav Naḥman restates that the mishna teaches either gullet or windpipe, one of them
Rav Adda bar Ahava restates that the gullet alone suffices and not the windpipe
What does the word one mean, a specific one?
Mnemonic for the proofs: slaughter, halves, windpipe, deficiency, sin-offering of bird
Objection from a baraita: if the windpipe slips after slaughter the slaughter is valid, implying it is not required
Baraita: cutting two halves of simanim in a bird is invalid, and Rabbi Yehuda requires gullet and veins
Baraita: one who cut half of the windpipe and paused long enough for another cut, slaughter valid
Is this not about birds, and what does it teach for the gullet and whole slaughter
Baraita: if half the windpipe was defective and one added a bit more, slaughter is valid
Is this not about birds, and what does that teach for the windpipe and gullet
Baraita on plucking a bird sin-offering: cut the vertebra, and one siman with meat suffices
This baraita refutes Rav Adda bar Ahava
What is the status of this refutation, as you say, so is it not refuted
Perhaps there it is different, since the vertebra is severed, so the refutation fails
Story of a goose whose blood was crushed in Rava's house, offered as a case
Rava asks: how shall we act in such a case

ranges.en: Should one check the animal before or after slaughter, as a possible perforation at the spot
Rabbah: the gullet cannot be examined from outside, only from inside
Rav Yosef: examine the windpipe, slaughter it, then check and pierce the gullet
Rava praises Yosef: his view matches Rabbi Yoḥanan regarding a tereifah
Rabbi Yehuda says one must cut through until the slaughter is complete
Rav Ḥisda: Rabbi Yehuda speaks only of birds, since they are roasted whole, not animals
Does this mean Rabbi Yehuda's reason is that the veins carry blood
Objection from a mishna: Rabbi Yehuda requires cutting the veins, so emend to piercing
What is the difference between until he slaughters and until he pierces at slaughter
Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda requires the veins to be pierced at the time of slaughter
Baraita argument: the veins are mentioned only to drain blood, so Rabbi Yehuda must hold they are in slaughter
Rabbi Yehuda holds life-blood comes out during slaughter, not otherwise, so piercing must be at slaughter
Rabbi Yirmiyah asks: for Rabbi Yehuda, what if one paused in the veins or trampled them
An elder replies that Rabbi Elazar said it
Rabbi Yoḥanan: one who pierces with a thorn, the animal remains valid
A baraita agreeing with Rav Ḥisda: cutting two halves of simanim in a bird is invalid
Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda says in a bird one must cut the gullet and veins, one half siman suffices otherwise
Rav: half on half counts as a majority
Rav Kahana: half on half does not count as a majority
Rav again: half on half counts as a majority
God told Moses not to leave the majority, which supports Rav
Rav Kahana restates that half on half is not a majority
God told Moses to slaughter the majority, supporting Rav Kahana
Mnemonic for the proofs: half the small windpipe, defect
Mishna: one and a half simanim in an animal makes slaughter invalid
If half on half is a majority, why is it invalid, since he did achieve a majority by rabbinic rule
Reply: perhaps he will not make the halves, and Rav Katina said so

Why are they pure if exact division is possible
Go: here there is a majority, so the halves are not equal

Baraita: one who cut half of the windpipe and paused in it

If half on half is a majority, why is the animal treated as a tereifah, or is the bird meant
Baraita: a half-windpipe defective, with a little added, makes the slaughter valid
If half on half is a majority, the animal would be a tereifah, which is absurd
Rava: the case differs for tereifah, which requires a majority visible to the eyes
Abaye objects: a fortiori, slaughter should also require a majority visible to the eyes
Abaye concludes that all agree half on half is not a majority
Rav and Rav Kahana dispute, in the Passover context, whether half on half is a majority
Rav's reason: the verse on a man who is impure and cannot be included, so the community is excluded
Mishna: the majority of one siman in a bird
We learned once that the majority of one is like the whole, as support
Rav Hoshaya: taught twice, once for non-sacred and once for sacred, and both needed
Explanation: non-sacred needs a majority only, but sacred requires the whole for the blood
Which clause concerns non-sacred and which sacred animals
Rav Kahana: the first clause concerns non-sacred and the last sacred, from the wording
Objection: if the first clause were sacred, the tanna would say plucking, not slaughter
Reply: no difficulty, since the tanna moved from birds to animals and says slaughter valid
Objection: the first clause refers to a bird, and if sacred it would say plucking
Rav Shimi bar Ashi: the first clause concerns non-sacred, from the one in a bird
Objection: if sacred, a bird olah requires two simanim, so the last clause would be questioned
Objection continues: the majority of one in a bird conflicts with the bird olah requiring two simanim
Resolution: the tanna should have taught majority for each, but a sin-offering is covered by one siman
Rav Pappa: the first clause concerns non-sacred, from the teaching of Rabbi Yehuda
Rabbi Yehuda requires cutting the veins, and the Sages disagree with him
If the dispute concerns sacred animals, why would the Sages disagree, since he requires blood
Rav Ashi: the last clause concerns sacred animals, from the teaching of one who cuts two heads
Mishna: one who slaughters two heads at once, his slaughter is valid
If the last clause concerns sacred animals, ab initio should be invalid, which is objectionable
That is why ab initio is disallowed for sacred animals, as Rav Yosef taught
Verse: one slaughters, not two slaughter one sacrifice, and Rav Kahana says the verse is written

Resh Lakish holds the first clause is non-sacred and the last sacred

Because the mishna teaches that the rule applies to a bird and to an animal
Tamid story: they brought the tamid, cut it, and someone else cleansed it after the slaughter

ranges.en: Gemara objects that if completing the slaughter were valid, it would be a service performed by another priest.
A baraita teaches that all Yom Kippur service is valid only when performed by the High Priest himself.
Gemara explains the objection: one might think rabbinic invalidity applies, which is why the mishna is cited.
The mishna rule: a majority of one siman in a bird, and a majority of two simanim in an animal.
Why is the other priest needed to finish the cutting if not even rabbinic invalidity results?
Completing the slaughter ab initio is a mitzva, so that the blood flows freely.
Resh Lakish, in the name of Levi the Elder: slaughter takes effect only at its conclusion.
Rabbi Yochanan holds that slaughter is effective throughout, from the beginning to the end of the act.
Rava: everyone agrees that if a gentile cut one siman and a Jew cut the other, the animal is invalid.
The same applies to a bird burnt offering pinched partly below the red line and partly above it.
They disagree only if one cut a siman outside the Temple courtyard and one inside; liability follows each view.
Rabba bar Shimi tells Rava that the Master did not say this; the real view is Rav Yosef's.
Rav Yosef holds that cutting one siman outside and one inside is invalid in all views, and incurs liability.
They disagree only when the minimum of each siman is cut outside and completed inside; liability follows each view.
Rabbi Zeira objects from a mishna on the red heifer rite, whose participants are engaged from beginning to end.
The cited mishna: if the heifer became disqualified during slaughter, earlier handlers' garments are impure, later ones not.
Rabbi Zeira elaborates: if slaughter spans beginning to end, the mishna should distinguish timing within the slaughter.
Rava replies that the slaughter was invalid from the start, so the heifer conveys no impurity at all.
Rava: the difficulty for the view that slaughter counts only at the end is a case of two men slaughtering the heifer.
Rav Yosef rejects that case, noting a baraita already excludes two men slaughtering one offering.
Baraita: the word tizbahuhu is read two ways, excluding two slaughterers on one offering and one slaughterer on two.
Rav Kahana reads the spelling without a vav as singular, again excluding two slaughterers together.
Abaye asks whether this halakha was not already stated in another transmission.
Rabba bar bar Hana, citing Rabbi Yochanan, attributes this teaching to Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon.

30a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Unattributed opinion: the Sages hold that two people may slaughter one offering.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Shimon's view challenges the mishna with a two-cloths case, so the tanna must address only a disqualified heifer.
Rav Idi bar Avin objects from a Pesachim mishna on leaven liability, against the view that slaughter is valid only at its conclusion.
The Gemara explains the mishna: intent for the Paschal offering creates liability, while unspecified intent is exempt.
Why is he exempt for unspecified intent, if such an animal would become a peace offering and be forbidden with leaven?
Rabbi Hiyya bar Gamda: the case is owners made impure on Nisan 14, so the offering is deferred and needs explicit revocation.
If slaughter counts only at its end, cutting a bit first rejects the animal as a Paschal offering, so the rest is a peace offering.
Abaye objects that redemption may remain possible until slaughter is complete, so the slaughter is still for a Paschal offering.
Mishna: once two simanim are cut and the animal still convulses, it is treated like a living animal in all respects.
Rav rules that slaughter cut in two or three places on the neck, together making the measure, is valid.
Shmuel objects that slaughter must be clear and obvious, and cuts in several places do not meet that standard.
Resh Lakish also holds that slaughter must be clear and obvious.
Resh Lakish derives clear slaughter from the verse calling the tongue a sharpened arrow, which strikes plainly.
Rabbi Elazar objects from the mishna: two people holding one knife, each cutting at different points, are valid, contrary to the clear-slaughter rule.
Rabbi Yirmeya: the mishna means one knife held by two people, making a single diagonal cut.
Rabbi Abba asks what the baraita's teaching not to worry about each making the animal a tereifa means on that reading.
Rabbi Abba: with two knives and two people it works, since each might otherwise rely on the other, so no concern is needed.
Rabbi Abba objects: on the one-knife reading the baraita should have warned about pulling in opposite directions and pressing the knife.
Rabbi Avin replies by reading the baraita as it stands, so that no concern about the knife arises.

30b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continuation of the baraita's teaching: one need not worry that each will cause the other to press the knife.
Rabbi Avin objects from a baraita allowing cuts of the gullet and windpipe in reversed order, asking why that slaughter is valid.
Rabbi Avin resolves his own objection: the baraita describes a diagonal cut, not cuts at two places on the neck.
Story of a bull slaughtered in several places; Rav Yitzchak bar Marta's meat sale shows validity, and Rabbi Zeira infers two knives are meant.
Rav: if the knife is hidden between the gullet and windpipe, slaughter is invalid; if hidden beneath the hide and both simanim are cut, it is valid.
What is Rav teaching, since a mishna already states that a hidden knife in cutting the second siman makes an animal invalid?
The mishna could be read as limited to cutting upward from the nape, so Rav teaches that any hidden knife invalidates the slaughter.
The school of Rav reports that Rav was unsure whether hiding the knife beneath the hide and cutting both simanim is valid.
Dilemmas raised before the school of Rav: hidden knife beneath a neck cloth, or beneath tangled wool; both remain unresolved.
Rav Pappa's dilemma: a hidden knife while cutting the minority of simanim, then the majority cut properly; unresolved.
Mishna: slaughtering two heads at once is valid, and two people holding one knife, each cutting at a different point, is also valid.
Mishna: decapitating in one motion without drawing the knife back and forth is invalid; with a knife long enough for the neck it is valid.
Mishna: the same rule applies to decapitating two heads in one motion, depending on knife length.
Mishna: the length concern applies only when the knife is drawn back without forth, or forth without back; drawing both ways makes it valid.
Gemara asks from where the rule that one-motion decapitation is invalid is derived.
Shmuel derives it from the verse about the tongue as a sharpened arrow: slaughter must be drawn across, not pressed or struck.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives the same from the words for slaughter and drawn gold and arrow.
What is the purpose of citing the additional verse introduced with the term and the verse states?
If drawn gold means spun thread, that would undermine the derivation from drawn gold.
Come and hear: the verse about the tongue as a sharpened arrow shows shaḥut means drawn, not thread.
Rava tested an arrow for Rabbi Yona bar Tachlifa and used it to slaughter a bird in flight.
Perhaps the arrow performed an inverted slaughter, concealed in the neck and cutting the simanim from back to front.

31a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concluding the prior point: the arrow unraveled the feathers at the front of the neck, showing slaughter from the front.
The blood of a bird requires covering with earth, so how could an arrow-slaughtered bird's blood be covered, citing Rav.
Rav's teaching from the verse: the slaughterer must place earth beneath and above the blood, so it lies within the earth.
Rabbi Yona bar Tachlifa designates the earth of the whole valley beforehand as the lower layer, then covers with another.
Mishna on one-motion decapitation: the knife must match the neck's breadth, and Rabbi Zeira adds that it must extend beyond it.
Dilemma: does Rabbi Zeira require a knife extending beyond the neck by the breadth of the entire neck, or by any amount?
Come and hear from the mishna on two heads; the phrase one entire neck must mean the knife extends beyond by a full neck.
Learn from the mishna that this was indeed Rabbi Zeira's intent: a knife matching the neck and extending beyond it.
Mishna continues: the rule applies when the knife is drawn back without forth, or forth without back.
Rav Menashe: the rule about any length of knife applies to a scalpel with no protrusions, since protrusions could perforate the simanim.
Rav Aha asks Rav Menashe about slaughter with a needle.
Rav Menashe: a needle pierces the simanim, perforating rather than cutting them.
Rav Aha asks about slaughter with a cobbler's needle, which is flat and sharp-sided.
Rav Menashe cites the mishna: even a knife of any length is valid.
Gemara asks whether the mishna's any-length knife refers to a cobbler's needle rather than a scalpel.
The mishna explicitly names the scalpel, so the any-length phrase must refer to a scalpel, explained by that example.
Teaching both cases is necessary, since one might otherwise decree against scalpels, but the mishna rejects that decree.
Mishna: if a knife fell and slaughtered an animal, the slaughter is invalid, since the verse permits only what you slaughter.
Gemara: the invalidity is because the knife fell; by inference, a dropped knife is valid even without intent.
Gemara asks which tanna holds that slaughter does not require intent.
Rava: it is Rabbi Natan, and Oshaya taught a baraita on a knife thrown at a wall that slaughtered an animal.
The baraita: Rabbi Natan deems such slaughter valid, while the Sages deem it invalid.
Oshaya ruled that the halakha follows Rabbi Natan: slaughter needs no intent.
Did Rava not already say this once, citing the mishna on deaf-mutes, imbeciles and minors whose slaughter is supervised?
Rava had said Rabbi Natan's view is the tanna who does not require intent for slaughter.
Both statements are needed: the deaf-mute case alone would suggest intent to cut in general, while the knife case alone suggests a competent person's act.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: a menstruant immersed under compulsion is pure for her husband but forbidden terumah; Rabbi Yochanan says not even for him.
Rava objects to Rav: a prohibition of karet was lifted by compelled immersion, so why would terumah remain forbidden?
Rav Naḥman: her husband is non-sacred, and non-sacred matters require no intent for purification.
Mishna on a wave of forty seah that falls on a person or vessels: they are pure, so a person, like a vessel, needs no intent.
Perhaps the case is one who sits by the water waiting for the wave, which amounts to intent to immerse.

31b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Vessels are like persons: just as a person's intent is required for purification, so vessels are purified only when a person intends it.
If the mishna means one who sits and waits for the wave, why state the halakha at all, since it is obvious?
The halakha is novel: one might decree against purification by rainwater cascades or by pushing vessels into airborne wave arcs, but the tanna rejects both decrees.
A baraita: one may immerse in the edges of waves but not in their arcs, since one may not immerse in air.
From where do we know that non-sacred matters require no intent for purification?
Mishna in Makhshirin: produce that falls into a stream and is handled by a man with impure hands shows that intent is not needed for his hands to be purified.
Rava objects to Rav Naḥman from a Ḥagiga mishna: immersion without assuming purity status prohibits second tithe, implying intent is required.
Rav Naḥman rejects the proof: no intent is needed for non-sacred food, and the mishna means second tithe remains forbidden.
Rava objects again from the same mishna: immersion without intent is as though he did not immerse at all.
Rav Naḥman rejects this as well; Rava checks and finds a baraita supporting Rav Naḥman's reading.
Abaye suggests the baraita refutes Rabbi Yochanan, who holds that a menstruant's immersion without intent is ineffective for her husband.
Rav Yosef: the baraita contradicts Rabbi Yochanan's view, but he is following Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef's opinion.
Baraita on the leprous garment: Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef derives from the word second that the immersion requires intent, like the laundering.
The same juxtaposition could yield a priest's intent requirement, but the verse says pure, showing intent alone suffices.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi objects: does Rabbi Yochanan really require intent for non-sacred immersion, when he rules by an unattributed mishna?
Mishna: if a knife fell and slaughtered an animal, the slaughter is invalid, although the knife cut in the standard way.
The Gemara asks which tanna holds that slaughter requires no intent.
Rava: it is Rabbi Natan, so Rabbi Yochanan should follow the unattributed mishna's view of Rabbi Natan.
Even Rabbi Yonatan ben Yosef concedes slaughter needs no intent, since the verse you shall slaughter to your will disqualifies only deliberate acts.
The Rabbis hold that although slaughter needs no intent, the cutting itself requires intent.
Rava: does the verse say you shall cut as well as slaughter? If intent is needed for cutting, it should be needed for slaughter too.
What is the case of a menstruant compelled and immersed by another?
If another woman compelled her, that is full-fledged intent, so immersion is valid even according to Rabbi Yochanan.
Mishna in Nidda: a competent friend examines and immerses an incompetent woman, enabling her to eat terumah, showing another's intent suffices.
Rav Pappa explains the cases: Rabbi Natan's case is a woman falling from a bridge, and the Rabbis' case is one entering water to cool off.
Rava: if one slaughtered a red heifer together with another animal in the same action, all agree the heifer is disqualified.

32a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If another animal was slaughtered with the red heifer, Rabbi Natan disqualifies the heifer while the Rabbis do not; the other animal is valid only per Rabbi Natan.
The Gemara asks: why does Rava need to state this, since it is obvious?
Rava teaches it lest one read the verse as allowing only the heifer alone, so that slaughtering another animal together with it would not disqualify it.
Rava adds: cutting a gourd together with the heifer disqualifies it, but an accidental gourd cut in the same action does not.
Mishna: an interruption of a slaughter-length interval, after the knife or garments fell or the slaughterer tired, invalidates it; Rabbi Shimon uses examination length.
What is the meaning of an interval equivalent to the duration of an act of slaughter?
Rav: it means the duration of slaughtering another animal, not the time to finish the interrupted slaughter.
Rav Kahana and Rav Asi ask whether a bird's slaughter is measured by an animal's slaughter time, or by a bird's, and the reverse.
Rav replies that he was not close enough to his uncle Rabbi Hiyya to ask, so the dilemma remains unresolved.
Amoraic dispute: Rav holds like-for-like durations; Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan hold an animal's duration applies even to birds.
Rabbi Hananya: the interval is the time needed to bring another animal and slaughter it.
Does that mean the time to bring an animal even from elsewhere, which would give an overly long measure?
Rav Pappa's dilemma and the western tradition in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Ḥanina: the time to lift, throw down and slaughter the animal.
Rava: slaughter with a bad knife is valid even if it takes the whole day.
Rava asks whether intervals of delay combine, so that the cut continues from where it was.
Rav Huna bar Rav Natan asks about a delay while cutting the minority of simanim; the dilemma remains unresolved.
Rabbi Shimon: an interval equivalent to the time of an examination invalidates the slaughter.
What is the duration of an examination?
Rabbi Yochanan: the examination time of a sage, so the measure is the time a skilled slaughterer needs to examine.
Mishna: a slaughterer who cuts the windpipe and then the gullet, or stops midway, makes the animal a nevela or tereifa per Rabbi Yishbav and Rabbi Akiva.
The mishna's continuation: Rabbi Akiva concedes in the case of the windpipe cut with interruption.
A contradictory baraita lists these as tereifot in animals, challenging the mishna's ruling.

32b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna case: an animal with a perforated gullet, or with a severed windpipe, is a tereifa rather than an unslaughtered carcass.
Rava: the cases differ by order. Cutting the gullet then severing the windpipe makes a carcass, while the reverse makes a tereifa due to another cause.
Rav Aha bar Huna objects from a baraita that the order is irrelevant, so severing the windpipe first also yields a carcass.
Rava: the baraita's latter case means the gullet was already cut at the outset, so there is no contradiction.
Rav Aha bar Huna replies that this makes the case identical to the first, and the baraita explicitly states the reverse order as a carcass.
Rava's alternative: the term tereifot in the next mishna is general, and includes both carcasses such as a severed windpipe and tereifot.
Gemara objects: the mishna should also list the cases of Ḥizkiyya and Rabbi Elazar, which make an animal a carcass.
Those cases are of an animal that becomes a carcass but cannot impart impurity while alive, which the mishna does not teach.
Resh Lakish reconciles the two mishnayot: same-place gullet cut makes a carcass, different-place cut makes a tereifa.
Gemara asks whether Resh Lakish really holds that slaughter prevents impurity after the windpipe is severed, given his lung ruling.
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan: the views concern before and after a retraction, and a mishna stays in place after the retraction.
Resh Lakish: if the windpipe was cut and the lung perforated before the gullet, the animal is fit.
Rava: this applies only to the lung, whose function depends on the windpipe; innards perforated after the windpipe cut make a tereifa.
Rabbi Zeira objects: if signs developed after slaughter began were disregarded for the lung, why distinguish the innards?
Rabbi Zeira retracts and asks: if the innards were perforated between the two simanim, does the first siman join the second for purity?
Ilfa's similar dilemma: a fetus's foreleg outside the womb between the two simanim, what is the halakha?

33a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Dilemma restated: does the first siman join the second to purify the animal from carcass impurity, or do they serve different purposes?
The dilemma concerns only impurity of the foreleg; for eating, all agree the animal is forbidden as a tereifa.
Rav Aha bar Rav suggests Rabbi Zeira never retracted, since he always held that a perforation of either lung or innards makes a tereifa.
Rav Aha bar Yaakov: from Resh Lakish one may invite Jews, but not gentiles, to eat the innards of a slaughtered animal.
Reason: for Jews the meat's fitness depends on valid slaughter, while for gentiles it depends on death, so convulsing innards are forbidden to them.
Rav Pappa recounts sitting before Rav Aha bar Yaakov, deciding not to challenge his reasoning, since he gave a reason.
A baraita that disagrees with Rav Aha bar Yaakov: a gentile and a Jew may both eat the salted olive-bulk before the soul departs.
The baraita supports Rav Idi bar Avin's ruling in the name of Rav Yitzchak bar Ashyan on the same permission for both.
Mishna: slaughtering a domesticated, wild, or bird animal, with no blood emerging, is valid; Rabbi Shimon says the slaughter itself consecrates it.
Reason: the blood-free animal is not eaten by hands made impure, since second hands cannot make a third in non-sacred food.
How do we know the case concerns non-sacred animals, given the mishna's wording about animals?
If the case is sacred animals, then the blood of sacrifices is needed for offering, so the mishna's point is unclear.
Rabbi Yochanan: the verse pour it like water shows sacred blood does not render food susceptible to impurity.
If the case is sacred, is the meat still rendered susceptible by regard for sanctity without any liquid?
Rav Naḥman citing Rabba bar Avuh: the case is non-sacred food bought with second-tithe money, not following Rabbi Meir's mishna.

33b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: items requiring immersion are second-degree impure; Rabbi Meir permits contact with second tithe, while the Rabbis forbid it.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi objects that the Rabbis may disagree only about a person eating second tithe, and the mishna's wording suggests feeding, not contact.
Rav Pappa: the mishna concerns hands with first-degree impurity, which make even non-sacred food impure.
Baraita in the name of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: first-degree hands render non-sacred food impure, second-degree hands invalidate teruma.
The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar distinguishes teruma from non-sacred food, and whether hands ever have first-degree impurity.
Mishna: one who inserts his hands into a leprous house has first-degree hands per Rabbi Akiva, second-degree per the Rabbis.
Entering with the hands alone is not entry by Torah law; the dispute concerns a rabbinic decree, and the Gemara reads the Rabbis against Rabbi Akiva.
Perhaps Rabbi Akiva's first-degree rule applies only to teruma and sacrifices, while for non-sacred food the hands are second-degree.
Rabbi Akiva's view that a second-degree item makes a third-degree item in non-sacred food, derived from the verse about earthen vessels.
Perhaps the rule applies only to Torah impurity, and not to rabbinic impurity.

Here too the case is a miracle, which is different
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef cites Rabbi Yochanan that the halakha follows the view of an olive's size
Did Rabbi Yochanan really say this
But Rabbah bar bar Chana cites Rabbi Yochanan that the halakha follows the anonymous mishna
Mishna: if the liver was removed and nothing remained, the animal is a tereifah
If something remained it is kosher, though it is not an olive's size; these are Amoraim, following Rabbi Yochanan
Rabbi Yochanan's rulings on a gall perforated and a liver covering it, and on a gizzard and sack
If the sack was perforated but the gizzard is intact, what is the ruling
Come hear: Rav Nachman says if one perforated and the other not, it is kosher
Rava says the gullet has two layers, an outer red and an inner white, and one perforated but not the other is kosher
Why do I need to say the outer red and inner white
If they were switched, it would be a tereifah
What if both were perforated, not opposite each other
Mar Zutra cites Rav Pappa: the gullet is kosher, but the gizzard is invalid
Rav Ashi objects: on the contrary, the gullet that one ate through and widened is a case of a perforated wound
Sometimes the two are pinched together, and the gizzard placed stays as it was
Rav Acha son of Rav Yosef tells Rav Ashi that Mar Zutra cites Rav Pappa, agreeing with him
Rabbah says a membrane that rose from a wound in the gullet is not a membrane
Rabbah says the gullet has no examination from outside, only inside
What is the practical difference

43b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A case of doubtful mauling came before Rabbah, who examined the animal
Rabbah examined the gullet from outside, and Abaye responded to him
Abaye objects: you yourself said the gullet is examined only from inside
Rabbah turned the animal over, examined it, found two drops of blood, and ruled it a tereifah
Rabbah did it only to sharpen Abaye, who wanted to test him
Ulla rules that a thorn lodged in the gullet need not be worried about, lest the animal be healthy
For Ulla, what is the difference from doubt of mauling
Ulla holds one does not worry about doubt of mauling
What is the difference from two pieces, one of fat and one of suet
There the prohibition was already established
What is the difference from one who slaughters with a knife and finds it defective
There a defect arose in the knife itself
What is the difference from doubt of ritual impurity in a private domain, which is impure, versus a public domain, which is pure
There the ruling was learned from the case of the wife suspected of adultery
A sage sat before Rav Kahana and said found was taught but sat means we are concerned
Rav Kahana tells them not to heed the sitting case
The taught found case was needed for Ulla
All these are included in the baraita about thorns that were eaten
Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on the gullet's tarvetz: by a minimal amount or by its majority, and whether it is a place of slaughter
Which one is the tarvetz of the gullet
Mar bar Mar Ukva cites Shmuel: whatever one cuts and widens is the tarvetz, and what one cuts and it stays in place is the gullet itself
Rav Pappi says did the master not say so
Who said so: Rav Bibi bar Abaye
Rather, whatever one cuts and it stays in its place is the tarvetz
What is the gullet itself, if whatever one cuts contracts
Zeira says the measure is through the throat; Rav Avya says less than a barley grain, which is more than wheat
A case of an ox belonging to the children of Rav Ukva where slaughter began in the tarvetz and finished in the gullet
Rava says he combines the stringencies of Rav and Shmuel and treats the ox as a tereifah
Rav himself said the tarvetz is a place of slaughter, as Shmuel says, so Rav and Shmuel are inconsistent
Rabbi Abba rules the ox permitted according to both Rav and Shmuel
Tell the son of Rav Yosef bar Chama that the ox was permitted for its owner
Mar son of Ravina raises an objection to Rava's opponents, and the halakha is always like Beit Hillel
Whoever follows Beit Shammai, or Beit Hillel, or the lenient rulings of either is called wicked

44a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The stringencies of Beit Shammai and the leniencies of Beit Hillel are both in view
Ecclesiastes 2:14 on the fool walking in darkness is cited as the support
Rather, should one act like Beit Shammai in both leniencies and stringencies, or like Beit Hillel
This itself is difficult: you said the halakha always follows Beit Hillel
A baraita teaches that whoever wishes to act like Beit Shammai may do so
Resolved: one ruling is before a heavenly voice and one after, or Rabbi Yehoshua does not heed a heavenly voice
Rav rules that the whole matter follows Rav Abba, who came and said do not heed these rules
Rav said the sages set a measure for the gullet, implying the tarvetz is not a place of slaughter
He said by a minimal amount, how far up
Rav Nachman: as far as the grip of a hand
How far down
Rav Nachman said Rabbah bar Avuh: until it bleeds
Objection: Rabina cites Gnaiva citing Rav that a handbreadth of gullet next to the stomach is the inner stomach
Why, when one slaughters in the stomach
Say instead: a handbreadth in the stomach next to the gullet is the inner stomach
Alternatively, Rav spoke of an ox that is more prone to sinking
Rav Nachman cites Shmuel: if the whole tarvetz of the gullet was removed, the animal is kosher
Baraita: if the lower jaw was removed, the animal is kosher
Rav Pappa objects that there is a case of cutting the sinews and the marks, and for Rav Pappa the mishna is difficult
For Rav Pappa the mishna is not difficult: one case is where it was uprooted, another where it was removed
For Shmuel it is difficult: say most, not all, since Rabbah bar bar Chana cites Shmuel on teeth loosened in their majority
Rav Shisha son of Rav Idi says the one case folds and the other is a separate matter
A teaching on the windpipe: how much of the windpipe is cut, and how much of it constitutes its majority, as Rav says

44b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A windpipe case that came before Rav, who examined it by the majority of its thickness
Students report the teaching by majority of hollowness, and Rabbah bar bar Chana examined and sold the meat
The sellers hid the meat and spread it out
How could he do such a thing
But it was taught that one sage declaring impure cannot be overruled by another, except here where Rav did not forbid
If a sage permitted it, how could he eat from it
Ezekiel 4:14 is cited: I have never eaten anything torn or unclean
Teaching in the name of Rabbi Natan on the animal whose gifts were not separated
These matters rest on reasoning; Rabbah bar bar Chana taught them, and one could derive it from suspicion
Baraita on judges who declare innocent or guilty and the witnesses who may buy
Sages said to keep far from the repulsive and from anything similar
That applies to items sold with a blemish; here the defect is clearly visible
