Like Rabbah who permitted a torn animal and sold its meat, and the daughter of Rav Chisda objected
That applies to a blemished ox, and here the defect is clearly visible
What is the concern about the best marrow, sold to me each day, said Rav Chisda
Rav Chisda: who is a sage, one who sees a tereifah for himself
Rav Chisda cites Proverbs 15:27 on one who hates gifts, who lives
Mar Zutra cites Rav Chisda: whoever reads and studies and sees a tereifah for himself and serves sages
Psalms 128:2 is cited: you shall eat the labor of your hands, you are happy and it is good for you
Rav Zevid says one merits two worlds, this world and the world to come
Happy are you in this world and good for you in the world to come
Rabbi Elazar's story: when the Nasi sent him gifts he did not take them, and when invited he did not go
He replied that the master does not want to live, since it is written that he who hates gifts shall live
Rabbi Zeira's parallel story: he did not take gifts, and when invited he went

45a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Yehuda cites Rav: a perforated wing combines with the rest to reach a majority
Rav Yirmeya objects from a skull with holes: they combine to fill a drill, so one should also combine by coin size
Rav's rule via Chama bar Goria: holes with a defect combine to a coin's size, those without to a majority
Rabbah bar bar Chana cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: a strip removed combines to a coin's size
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi about a perforated wing
He replies that the sages already said holes with a defect combine to a coin, without a defect to a majority
What about a bird
Rabbi Elazar's explanation: fold it over the windpipe; if it covers most of the windpipe it is a tereifah
Rav Pappa's marker: a swelling that caved in like a door; Rav Nachman: a width a coin can enter
Rav: even if only one vertebra remains above and one below, the animal is kosher
Rabbi Yochanan objects: say instead even a little above and a little below
Rabbi Yonatan's report: Babylonian scholars know how to explain such reasoning
Rabbi Chiya bar Yosef taught before Rabbi Yochanan: the whole neck is fit for slaughter up to the large ring
The lower limit of slaughter: the lower lung wings
Rava says whatever stretches out its neck and grazes, provided it was not coerced
If it coerced itself, what is the ruling
Left undecided; Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish settle that coerced marks with slaughter are invalid
A windpipe perforated below the chest is judged like a lung
The Sages define the chest: from the ground up to the neck and up to the stomach, cutting two ribs from each side
Topic: a perforated membrane of the brain
Rav and Shmuel both say the upper membrane counts even if the lower is not perforated
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani's marker: a creature whose brain is held in place
Rabbah bar bar Chana cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: the brain is recognized by the eggs in the opposite part
The brain in a pot is judged as brain; once it begins to extend it is judged as the spinal cord
From where does the brain begin to extend
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani explains from Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: it is like a second kind

45b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Beans at the skull opening: inner side treated as brain, outer as spinal cord; the beans themselves are uncertain.
Rabbi Yirmeya reports finding two bean-like protrusions on the skull opening of a bird.
Mishna: a perforated heart chamber makes the animal a tereifa.
Rabbi Zeira asks whether the mishna means the small chamber or the large one.
Abaye challenges the dilemma by pointing to a mishna that already settles it.
Rabbi Shimon's mishna about the lung, which Abaye cites as a source.
Rav's reading of Rabbi Shimon: perforation must reach the large bronchus.
The lung mishna speaks of plural bronchi, while the heart mishna says only chamber, so they are not comparable.
Rav holds any perforation of the aorta is fatal; Shmuel requires a perforation of its majority.
Which blood vessel is the aorta?
Rav identifies the aorta as the fat-covered artery on the sides.
Objection: the sides of the animal are not adjacent to the heart, so that identification fails.
The artery is instead the one in fat that runs along the lung walls.
Ameimar in Rav Nachman's name: three adjacent ducts, lung and heart ducts treated as Rav and Shmuel dispute.
Mar bar Chiyya teaches the reverse assignment for the lung and liver ducts.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef brings Rav's ruling on the aorta before Shmuel.
Shmuel rejects the ruling: if Rav said it, he knows nothing about tereifot.
Mishna: a broken spinal column with the cord cut makes the animal a tereifa.
Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi requires a majority cut, while Rabbi Yaakov says even a perforation suffices.
Rabbi ruled like Rabbi Yaakov; Rav Huna rules that the halakha does not follow Rabbi Yaakov.
How much of the spinal cord must be cut to make the animal a tereifa?
Rav: a majority of the surrounding membrane; others say a majority of the nerve tissue itself.
If a majority of the nerve tissue suffices, a majority of the membrane clearly does too.
If only membrane counts, what is the rule when the nerve tissue alone is mostly cut?
Rav Huna's ruling: the majority that matters is of the membrane, and the nerve tissue makes no difference.
Rav Natan bar Avin checks the membrane and then the nerve tissue in Rav's presence.
Rav replies that if the membrane is intact, the nerve tissue makes no difference.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: liquefied or softened spinal cord makes the animal unfit.
What exactly are liquefaction and softening?
Liquefaction means the tissue pours out like water; softening means it cannot stand upright.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks about a cord that is heavy and cannot stand but is not softened; left unresolved.
Rav's school: softening from disease is fatal, but partial emptying from the cord leaves the animal kosher.
A baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar calls an emptied cord a tereifa, contradicting that position.
The baraita should read softened, not emptied, so the attacked view stands.
Challenge: Levi ruled a man with softened brain tissue was fatally injured, which supports the view.
Abaye explains Levi meant the man could not reproduce, not that he would die.
Where does the spinal cord extend downward such that cutting above it is fatal?
Shmuel's teaching: the point between the branches of the cord behind the thighs.
Rav Dimi asks Rabbi Yehuda to show him the exact point between the branches.
Rabbi Yehuda tries kids of differing fat and bone, but the spot cannot be seen directly.
Rabbi Yehuda teaches Shmuel's rule by tradition: cut before the first gap is fatal, after the third is kosher, the middle unknown.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua raises a dilemma.

46a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Does Shmuel's cut-to-the-first-gap rule include the gap itself or stop before it?
Rav Pappa asks about a cut exactly at the mouth of the first branch.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks about the status of the first branch itself when it is cut.
A baraita about a cut branch of the spine: only the third branch fails to render the animal a tereifa.
Rabbi Yannai and Reish Lakish disagree on the lower boundary of the spinal cord in birds.
Ulla reports watching Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi check an injured bird up to the point between the wings.
Ulla does not know why the inspection stopped: no need to check further, or honor for the Nasi.
Mishna: if the liver was removed entirely, the animal is a tereifa.
The Gemara infers that any remainder of the liver keeps the animal kosher, even less than an olive-bulk.
This inference is contradicted by a mishna requiring an olive-bulk of the liver to remain.
Rav Yosef resolves it: the two mishnayot follow different Sages, Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon ben Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, illustrated by an anecdote.
A royal army forces Rabba and Rav Yosef to flee; Rabbi Zeira then teaches the liver olive-bulk rule, and Rav Adda bar Ahava gives a different location.
Rav Pappa reconciles both views: the olive-bulk is required in both places.
Dilemmas about whether scattered pieces, a strip, or a flat remnant of the liver can count as an olive-bulk, and about a detached liver.
Rabbi Ami says the detachment makes no difference, since the case is covered by either view.
Rav, Shmuel and Rav Asi hold that a perforated lung means the outer membrane, others say the inner; Rav Nachman's mnemonic settles it for the inner.
If only the outer membrane is perforated, the inner membrane protects the lung, as Rabba says.

46b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A lung whose outer membrane is removed, looking like a red date, is kosher.
If only the inner membrane is perforated, does the intact outer membrane still protect the lung?
Rav Aha and Ravina disagree on this; the ruling is that the outer membrane protects the lung.
Rav Yosef's test: inflate the lung and see whether bubbles appear, to show the perforation goes through both membranes.
Method details: use tepid water, not hot or cold, and a tereifa results only if bubbles appear.
If the sound comes from between the membranes, only the inner one is perforated, so the animal is kosher.
A mnemonic listing the terms of Rava's lung rulings.
Rava: a lung whose outer membrane was removed and looks like a red date is kosher.
Rava: if only part of the outer membrane reddened from bleeding the animal is kosher; if all of it reddened, it is a tereifa.
Ravina asks why partial reddening is kosher, since the animal may recover from either case.
A baraita on wounded creeping creatures suggests a full-red lung would also heal, which contradicts Rava's ruling.
A baraita on blood gathered under the skin of creeping creatures is offered as a basis for comparing the lung.
If the comparison held, partial reddening would also be fatal, so no distinction is possible.
Rava: a partly dried lung is a tereifa, and dryness means it can be crumbled with a fingernail, per Rav Pappi.
Whose opinion is this measure of dryness: Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam's?
A mishna on the dried ear of a firstborn, where Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam gives the same fingernail test.
The Rabbis may agree: an exposed ear differs from a lung, and a lung with scabs or sores is still kosher per Rava.
Ameimar, citing Rava: cysts on the lung cannot be compared, since one cannot tell when a cyst was perforated.
Rava: adhering lobes of the lung need no inspection, because the adhesions mean a perforation occurred.
That applies only to adhesions out of order; adhesions in normal arrangement are ordinary growth and the animal is kosher.

47a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rava: two adjacent lung cysts indicate a perforation; a single cyst that looks like two is tested by piercing it, and kosher only if the fluids join.
Rava: a normal lung has five lobes in a fixed arrangement, and any missing, extra, or switched lobe makes the animal a tereifa.
Narrative: a lung with an extra lobe is brought before Mareimar, who rules it kosher, and Rav Aha is surprised by the contradiction with Rava.
Mareimar's reply: the halakha does not follow Rava for an extra lobe aligned with the others, but an extra lobe between the sides is a tereifa.
Narrative: an animal with an extra lobe between the sides is brought to Rav Ashi, who intends to rule it a tereifa.
Rav Huna Mar bar Avya objects: such extra lobes are common in grazing animals, and only an inside-facing extra lobe matters.

47b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A perforation on the back of the lung, however small, makes the animal a tereifa.
Rafram: a lung resembling a wood chip is a tereifa, with several rival readings of what the resemblance means.
Rava: a lung dark like eye shadow is kosher, but one black like ink is a tereifa.
Rabbi Chanina explains that black menstrual blood is really red that has decayed, so blackness signals decay.
A green or red lung is kosher, as shown by the case of Rabbi Natan.
Baraita: Rabbi Natan's account of a red-lunged boy who survived circumcision, showing a red lung can heal.
Second baraita: a green-lunged boy whose blood did not come out also survived, showing green lungs can heal too.
Rav Kahana: a lung resembling liver is kosher, one resembling flesh is a tereifa.
Rav Kahana's mnemonic: the verse forbidding flesh torn in the field, which is a tereifa.
Rav Sama bar Rava: a lung resembling dodder, saffron, or egg yolk is a tereifa.
Asked what the kosher green lung looks like.
It looks like a leek.
Ravina and Rav Yosef give procedures for testing sealed areas and sound-emitting lungs using a knife, a feather, saliva and tepid water.
The sound comes from air between the membranes, so only the inner membrane is perforated.
Ulla, citing Rabbi Yochanan: a lung liquefied like water from a jug is kosher.
This shows Rabbi Yochanan holds an inner deficiency does not count as a deficiency.
Rabbi Abba objects from a mishna: a lung with a missing piece is a tereifa, implying inner deficiency counts.
The mishna means a missing outer piece; both cases are listed to account for Rabbi Shimon's view on small perforations.
Rabbi Chananya is visited while ill, and the sages bring a liquefied lung, which he rules kosher; Rava adds the bronchi condition.
Rav Acha asks how one knows whether the bronchi still exist.
Pour the lung into a glazed vessel: white streaks mean the bronchi remain, making it a tereifa.
Rav Nachman: a partly atrophied lung whose membrane remains is kosher.
A baraita supports this: an atrophied lung with its membrane intact is kosher even if the cavity holds a quarter-log.

48a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If the womb was removed, the animal is kosher.
Narrative: residents of Asia Minor brought a worm-infested liver question to Yavne three times; the Sanhedrin permitted it on the third.
Rav Naḥman's ruling on a lung attached to the chest wall, and Mar Yehuda's version: check for perforation when cysts appear.
How do we perform the examination to tell whether the injury is to the chest wall or the lung?
Rava's procedure: separate the lung with a sharp knife; if the chest wall is not defective, the attachment indicates a lung perforation and a tereifa.
Rav Nehemya bar Rav Yosef tested such a lung by inflating it in tepid water.
Mar Zutra objects that the case should be read as one of Rava's adhering lobes, not a chest-wall attachment.
Rav Nehemya again tests such a lung in tepid water.
Rav Ashi objects: adhering lobes cannot be cleared by such a test, since a scab could hide the perforation.
Did Rav Naḥman really say that a perforated lung with a sealed chest wall is kosher?
Rav Yosef bar Minyumi attributes to Rav Naḥman the view that a perforation sealed by the chest wall is kosher, a contradiction.
No contradiction: the first ruling concerns a lung not in its natural place, the second one growing in its place.
The place of growth is the area where the lobes meet the chest wall on all sides.
Rav Naḥman's ruling: a perforated lung sealed by the chest wall is kosher.
Ravina limits this to a lung tangled in the chest flesh between the ribs.
Rav Yosef asks: if the lung is not tangled, is it a tereifa?
Rav Yosef reasons that the lung is then treated as perforated, so even a tangled one should be a tereifa.
A baraita on a perforated penis that later heals and regains fitness is cited to examine sealing.
What does the baraita's wording exclude, if not a case like a lung sealed by the chest wall?
It excludes a temporary membrane from a wound, which does not seal; chest-wall flesh is a permanent seal.
Rav Ukva bar Chama objects: if chest flesh were perforated, the animal would be a tereifa, so the mishna should list it.
By the same logic, Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on a gallbladder sealed by the liver is also difficult.
The mishna lists only cases where the perforated organ is the one that makes the animal a tereifa.
Rabba bar bar Chana asks Shmuel about a lung that grew cysts full of fluid.
Shmuel replies that the animal is kosher.
Rabba says he agrees, but students doubt it, citing Rav Mattana: pus-filled cysts make it a tereifa, clear fluid does not.
Shmuel defends his ruling: Rav Mattana's rule concerns a kidney cyst, not a lung.
Narrative: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef tries to get Rabbi Yirmeya to rule on cystic lungs in the butchers' market.
Rabbi Yirmeya explains that Rabbi Yochanan sent such cases to Rabbi Yehuda, who permitted them, but Rabbi Yochanan did not hold that way and he is stringent.
Rava recalls walking behind Rav Naḥman in the market.

48b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Narrative: Rav Ami-type sages saw lungs full of fluid or stones in the market and said nothing, so they held those animals kosher.
The Amoraim disagree whether a needle found in a lung makes the animal a tereifa.
Proposal: perhaps the disagreement is whether an inner deficiency counts as a deficiency.
No: all agree an inner deficiency is not a deficiency; they differ on how the needle entered the lung.
Narrative: a needle found in a cut lung is brought to Rabbi Ami, who is inclined to rule it kosher.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects from the mishna on a missing piece: an inner deficiency is a deficiency, so the needle makes it a tereifa.
The lung is sent to Rabbi Yitzchak Nappaha, who is also inclined to rule it kosher.
Rabbi Yirmeya again objects from the same mishna, reaching the same conclusion.
The lung returns to Rabbi Ami, who rules the animal a tereifa.
The sages object: Rabbi Yochanan and his circle ruled it kosher.
Rabbi Ami explains: they saw the whole lung and found no perforation, but he sees only part and cannot be sure.
The Gemara infers Rabbi Ami would have ruled kosher had he seen the whole lung and found no perforation.
But Rav Naḥman says a perforated bronchus makes the animal a tereifa, which seems to contradict that inference.
Rav Naḥman spoke of a needle passing from one bronchus into another, where hard bronchi cannot seal the hole.
Rav Naḥman also says a coil of intestine seals a perforation in another coil, so why not a bronchus?
Rav Ashi: one cannot compare tereifot this way, since where a cut happens decides whether the animal lives or dies.
Narrative: a needle found in the main bronchus is brought before sages, who give no ruling either way.
They refrain because the needle was in the main bronchus and may have entered by the respiratory route.
Narrative: a needle found in a liver; Mar son of Rav Yosef wants to rule the animal a tereifa.
Rav Ashi challenges him: would he rule that way for a needle found in flesh?
Rav Ashi: a needle with its eye facing the stomach came through the gullet and is fatal; one with its eye buried and point outward came through a vessel. Only for a thick needle.
Why is this different from a needle found in the lung?

49a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A needle in the reticulum wall is kosher if it protrudes from one side only, and the eye's direction does not decide the matter.
Food and liquid in the reticulum can push the needle through, so the eye's direction is not evidence of the route.
Narrative: a needle in a liver duct yields conflicting rulings, and Ravina orders restitution to the owner for the discarded meat.
Rav Ashi reports Rav Kahana's rule: a date pit in the gallbladder came through the duct, while an olive pit would pierce it.
Dilemma: does Rabbi Yochanan mean the lung is eaten raw, or only after treatment with substances?
A goose's lung costs more than the whole goose, which suggests treatment is needed before eating.
If the lung is perforated during the butcher's handling, is that attributed to the handling?
Rav Adda bar Natan holds we attribute it to the handling; Mar Zutra disagrees; the halakha follows the former.
Rav Shmuel bar Rabbi Abbahu reports his father's view that the handling is attributed, and rejects Mar Zutra's opposite teaching.
Rav Mesharshiyya: it stands to reason to follow Rav Adda, since perforations are attributed to a wolf.
Worm perforations: Rav Yosef bar Dosai and the Rabbis disagree; the halakha presumes the worm emerged after slaughter. Rabbi Shimon's view is then glossed.
Rav Aha bar Abba cites Rabbi Malokh, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon.
Rav Huna rejects this: Rabbi Malokh the Arab actually held the halakha does not follow Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Zeira reports visiting Rabbi Malokh and hearing him deny that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon.
Rav Beivai asks Rabbi Zeira what further support he has for the opposite.
Rabbi Zeira cites Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ami's tradition that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi ruled for Rabbi Shimon, and the ruling against Rabbi Shimon is noted.
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Nachmani, citing Rabbi Oshaya: priests permitted the fat on the abomasum, following Rabbi Yishmael's tradition.
Where does Rabbi Yishmael help the priests?
A baraita on the priestly blessing: Rabbi Yishmael reads it as priests blessing Israel while God blesses the priests.
Rabbi Akiva's reading: God affirms the priests' blessing for Israel, the verse being taken as referring to Israel.
Where does Rabbi Akiva learn a blessing for the priests?
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak derives it from the promise to Abraham that those who bless Israel will be blessed.
In what sense does Rabbi Yishmael help the priests if Rabbi Akiva agrees they are blessed?
He places the priests' blessing in the same verse as Israel's, so the two receive the same blessing.
The priests permitted the abomasum fat following Rabbi Yishmael's tradition from his forefathers.
A baraita on Leviticus 3:3: the verse forbidding fat on the innards is cited for the disputed fat.

49b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva dispute whether the fat on the abomasum is forbidden under the word all.
The Gemara raises a contradiction with another baraita, where the two Sages' views appear reversed.
Ravin, citing Rabbi Yochanan, says the first baraita's attributions are reversed, so both fats are forbidden to Yishmael and Akiva respectively.
Why reverse the first baraita rather than the second?
The second baraita uses the formula just as and gives textual reasons, so its attributions are likely accurate.
If so, Rabbi Oshaya's claim that the priests followed Rabbi Yishmael seems wrong.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: Rabbi Oshaya meant only that Yishmael gives the lenient view in his forefathers' name, but holds it forbidden himself.
Rav holds kosher fat seals a perforation, while non-kosher fat does not; Rav Sheshet holds both seal.
Does permitted fat of an undomesticated animal seal a perforation, or only attached domestic fat?
Abaye: the innards fat is loose, so it cannot seal even if permitted to eat.
Rava rules on a perforation sealed by non-kosher fat: Rav Sheshet's view and the principle of sparing Jewish money favor leniency.
Rav Pappa objects that Rav holds non-kosher fat does not seal, and this is a Torah prohibition, so the principle cannot apply.
Narrative: a jug maker asks Rava whether honey left uncovered, possibly contaminated by venom, is forbidden.
Rava cites a mishna that only wine, water, and milk are forbidden by exposure, so honey is permitted.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzchak objects that Rabbi Shimon holds exposed honey is forbidden, and a life risk is at stake.
Baraita: Rabbi Shimon says even five liquids, including honey, are subject to exposure prohibition.
The Rabbis dismiss Rabbi Shimon's snake anecdote as an anomaly, and Rava argues for leniency on fish brine and honey.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzchak replies that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar held exposed honey prohibited.
Baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar prohibited exposed honey.
Rav Naḥman's rule: a hat-shaped fat does not seal; Rava reports two abomasum fats, ḥimtza and bar ḥimtza, and the resolution favors the son.
Which is the ḥimtza and which is the bar ḥimtza? A proof from Rav Naḥman is offered.

50a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Challenge: if we forbid this fat and deny it seals, does it fail to seal even where Eretz Yisrael permits it?
The abomasum is bow-shaped: the outer fat is forbidden to all, and the disputed fat on the bowstring is the bar ḥimtza that seals.
Anecdotes of Rav Avya, Rabbi Ami, Rabbi Yannai and Rabbi Ḥanina show how the disputed fat is eaten by taking a handful first.
Narrative: Rabbi Ḥanina tells his Babylonian attendant to cut off all the fat and throw it away.
Baraita: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says intestines perforated but sealed by mucus leave the animal kosher.
What is this mucus?
Rav Kahana: it is the mucus that comes out under pressure when the intestine is scraped with a knife.
Transmission of the tradition from Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Ziera, and Rabbi Yochanan's rulings on tereifot and mourning.
What exactly is the mourning halakha in question?
Baraita: a mourner from a distant or nearby place counts seven days; Rabbi Shimon says a late arrival still counts with the others.
Narrative: a man travels from Babylonia to Eretz Yisrael to learn the halakha from Rabbi Abba.
He asks whether Rabbi Abba really said the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel on tereifot.
Rabbi Abba denies it: he held the opposite, that mucus does not seal.
What about the ruling on mourning attributed to Rabbi Abba?
Rabbi Abba says the opinions conflict on this matter.
Rav Chisda and Rabbi Yochanan hold the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon on mourning; Rav Naḥman disagrees, and the lenient authority prevails.
Rav Shimi bar Chiyya and the Rava episode: intestinal perforations are compared by making new ones and rubbing them, to see whether they match.
Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar let lung perforations be compared, with Rava and the final ruling limiting when this applies.
Abaye and Rava let windpipe sections be compared, and the halakha is ruled broadly with limits.
Ze'eiri: a perforated rectum leaves the animal kosher, since the hips hold it up.
Rabbi Ilai, citing Rabbi Yochanan, says this applies only where the rectum attaches to the hips, even if most of it is perforated.
The sages recount this ruling before Rava in Rav Naḥman's name.
Rava rebukes them: he had warned them not to rely on Rav Naḥman so readily.

50b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Naḥman: a rectum attached to the hips leaves the animal kosher even if removed, if a finger's width remains to grip.
Rav Yehuda reports Natan bar Sheila's testimony and other opinions on which part is the internal rumen.
Opinions of Rav Asi, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak and Rav Aha on locating the narrow place of the rumen.
Opinions of Rabbi Yaakov bar Nachmani, Rabbi Avina and the Eretz Yisrael tradition on the internal rumen.
Rabba bar Rav Huna identifies the internal rumen as the mafrata, which Neharde'a practiced.
Narrative: Neharde'a followed Rabba bar Rav Huna's definition in practice.
Rav Ashi asks Ameimar whether the other definitions of the internal rumen still stand.
Ameimar: all of them fall under the mafrata defined by Rabba bar Rav Huna.
Rav Ashi presses on Rav Asi's narrow-place view and the other opinions.
Ameimar: these explain the same area, and the rest disagree with Rabba, but they are not followed.
Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet on the handbreadth threshold for tears in a large or small animal's external rumen.
Is it not obvious that a majority tear is a tereifa even if under a handbreadth?
No: the rule is needed for a case where a tear slightly over a majority reaches a handbreadth, to show a majority suffices.
Geneiva and Rabbi Asi: a round hole the size of a sela makes it a tereifa; Rabbi Chiyya reports the detail that a hole larger than a sela does.
How much larger than a sela counts?
Rav Yosef: when three date pits, cased or not, can pass through with difficulty or ease, the hole is larger than a sela.
Baraita on a needle in the reticulum: one-side penetration is kosher, both sides is a tereifa, and a drop of blood on the needle matters.

51a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Blood on a perforation tells whether it happened before or after slaughter; a scab shows it was made days earlier, and the burden of proof lies with the claimant.
Why is a needle case different from other perforations where no blood means a tereifa?
A needle gives blood something to cling to, so if none is found the perforation was made after slaughter.
Narrative: Rav Safra tells Abaye about Rav Avira, whose teaching on a one-sided needle seemed to contradict the baraita, and Abaye goes to see him on the roof.
Rav Avira relates the case before Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi: a one-side needle with a drop of blood on the outside, which led to a tereifa ruling.
Abaye says this is just the mishna's case of a perforation to the outside.
The mishna on an animal fallen from a roof; Rav Huna says no concern for shattered limbs if it was left above and found below.
Ravina's kid case: is Rav Huna's rule based on the animal grabbing hold, or on its self-assessment of the jump?
Rav Ashi: it is because the animal evaluates its jump, and that kid did too.
Rav Yeimar holds a ewe dragging its hind legs has rheumatism, not a cut spinal cord, and this is the common explanation.
Ravina objects that it may be a cut spinal cord, making the animal a tereifa.
The ewe was inspected and the cord was cut, but the halakha follows Rav Yeimar since rheumatism is common and cut cords are not.
Rav Huna: rams butting one another are not a concern for shattered limbs, but a fall to the ground is.
Rav Menashei: rams stolen and thrown over a fence are not a concern, but returned by thieves out of fear they are.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: a stick blow along the whole spine is harmless, but one stopping mid-back or with knots is a concern.
Rav Naḥman: the womb does not raise concern for shattered limbs of a calf.
Rava cites a baraita about a one-day-old infant that supports Rav Naḥman.

51b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Suppose a newborn can have shattered limbs: then the ziva ruling would apply, which suggests the newborn is not concerned.
The baraita speaks of a caesarean birth, not one through the narrow birth canal, so it proves nothing.
A baraita: a calf born on a festival may be slaughtered that day, with no twenty-four-hour wait for shattered limbs.
Here too the calf was born by caesarean section; a natural birth requires the wait.
A baraita on a firstborn born on a festival with a blemish, which may be eaten on the festival.
If the animal was born by caesarean, Rabbi Yochanan's view that Rabbi Shimon concedes a caesarean firstborn is not sanctified shows the baraita must mean a natural birth.
The baraita refers to a firstborn that spread its legs and stood immediately after birth, so it is not a tereifa.
Rav Naḥman: an animal thrown to the ground in the slaughterhouse before slaughter is not a concern for shattered limbs.
Narrative: a bull falling in the slaughterhouse is not a concern, since Rav held it digs its hooves into the earth as it falls.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav, and Rav Chiyya bar Ashi rule on animals that fall and stand again, and whether walking afterward matters.
Rav Yirmeya bar Acha and Rav Chisda, citing Rav, rule on how far an animal must move after a fall to avoid inspection.
Ameimar, citing Rav Dimi, and Mar Zutra, citing Rav Pappa, disagree on how far an inspection of a fallen animal must reach.
Huna Mar asks whether the simanim, the windpipe and gullet, need inspection after a fall.
Rav Ashi: the simanim are hard and resist damage from a fall, so no inspection is needed.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel: a bird that swims its body length after a fall is not injured, but this applies only upstream.
A bird falling on a taut or folded garment or a close-knit net is a concern, depending on the surface.
A bird falling on various flax preparations: hard or coarse flax is a concern, while soft, combed or dampening flax is not.
A bird falling on nevara or sifted ashes is a concern, while timaḥta or unsifted ashes are not.

52a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Bird falls on sand, dust, straw, grains and legumes: which surfaces cushion the fall and which cause concern for shattered limbs.
Rav Ashi and Ameimar dispute a bird stuck by one or both wings to a glue board; the halakha is kosher if one wing is stuck and prohibited if two are.
Rules on fractured or dislocated ribs: twelve ribs make a majority, and Ze'eiri, Ulla's ben Zakkai and Rabbi Yochanan give conditions.
Rav: a dislocated rib with its attached vertebra torn out makes the animal a tereifa, even if the spinal cord is intact.
Rav Kahana and Rav Asi ask what the halakha is if one rib on each side is dislocated while the vertebra stays intact.
Rav: are you saying an animal sliced in half is a tereifa? It is a carcass.
But Rav elsewhere also called a sliced animal a tereifa, so why would the opposite rib not make it a carcass?
Rav's tereifa ruling applied to a rib dislocated without the vertebra.
Didn't Rav explicitly speak of a rib and its vertebra being dislocated?
Rav meant a rib with half its vertebra, leaving the opposite rib attached to the rest of the vertebra.
Rav Kahana and Rav Asi's case is then lesser, yet Rav called it a carcass, which conflicts with Ulla's ben Zakkai ruling.
Ben Zakkai's six-rib rule concerns ribs not opposite one another; Rav's case concerns opposite ribs.
Rabbi Yochanan says the tereifa needs a majority of both sides, which forces some opposite pairs, so how is it not a carcass?
Rabbi Yochanan's case has the pestle torn out without the mortar, leaving the spine intact; Rav's case tears out both.
If so, why did Rav Kahana and Rav Asi ask Rav at all?
They had not heard Rav's statement.
Why ask about two opposite ribs rather than the simpler single-rib case?
They wanted one question that answers both cases: a yes on one rib implies two, and a no on two implies the single rib needs asking.
Then asking about two opposite ribs also fails to settle both cases, the same problem.
They judged it better to ask about two opposite ribs, since Rav would become angry at the one-rib question.
But they did ask it, and Rav did not become angry, which is a problem for the explanation.
Rabba bar Rav Sheila, citing Shmuel: a rib ripped from its root, a majority of skull crushed, or a majority of rumen flesh damaged, makes the animal a tereifa.
Did Shmuel really say a ripped rib is a tereifa? A mishna in Oholot seems to contradict it.

52b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: How large must a deficiency in the spine be to matter?
Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute the vertebra count, and Shmuel holds the same dispute applies to tereifot.
The two Shmuel rulings concern different cases: a torn rib without a vertebra, and a missing vertebra without a rib.
How can a vertebra be missing without a rib dislocation?
At the ends of the flanks there are vertebrae with no ribs attached.
Rav Oshaya objects: if Beit Hillel holds one vertebra suffices, the dispute should be listed with the leniencies in Eduyyot.
Rav replies that the question concerned corpse impurity, and the tereifa dispute was not stated in any mishna or baraita.
Shmuel: a skull crushed in its majority makes the animal a tereifa.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether majority refers to height or circumference; left unresolved.
Shmuel: damage to a majority of the flesh that envelops the rumen makes the animal a tereifa.
Rav Ashi asks whether a majority tear along the flesh's length counts, or only a majority removal.
Resolved from the mishna on the internal and external rumen, read through Rabbi Yosei ben Chanina's view that a majority tear of the flesh suffices.
This proof is rejected: Shmuel does not hold Rabbi Yosei's view, and the internal rumen is the woolless area.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: a predator from the size of a wolf upward makes an animal a tereifa, and a hawk or larger makes a bird one.
What does Rav's rule exclude: cats, which are smaller than wolves?
Rabbi Yehuda's mishna requires a lion to make a large animal a tereifa, and Rabbi Ela says his view only explains the Sages.
Rav may hold Rabbi Yehuda disagrees; or everyone agrees a wolf works only on small animals, and Rav excludes cats.
Rav Amram, citing Rav Ḥisda: a cat or mongoose clawing kids or lambs, or a weasel clawing birds, makes the animal a tereifa.
A baraita says cats, hawks and mongooses do not render a tereifa until an inner organ is perforated, which conflicts with Rav Ḥisda.
The hawk point is resolved by bird versus kid cases; Rav Ḥisda follows the Distinguished One, who says clawing matters only where no bystander can save the kid.
Objection: a cat pursuing a hen into a closed room left five drops of venom on the door even with no one present to save the hen.
A cat saving itself counts like saving others; the Rabbis hold a cat's venom does not burn enough to make a tereifa.
An alternative version: the Distinguished One's rule for bystanders is cited, and Rav Ḥisda agrees with the Rabbis about cats clawing unattended animals.
The hen incident again objects that a cat's clawing works even with no one present to save the prey.
Rav Kahana asks Rav a question.

53a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Does a cat render an animal a tereifa by clawing?
Rav: even a weasel, smaller than a cat, does render a tereifa by clawing.
Rav Kahana asks whether cats and weasels, both together, render a tereifa by clawing.
Rav's two answers are reconciled by species and age: birds, adult sheep, and kids or lambs.
Rav Ashi asks whether non-kosher birds other than the hawk render a bird a tereifa by clawing.
Rav Hillel reports Rav Kahana: other non-kosher birds do so, as the hawk's case in the mishna is limited by size.
Doesn't the mishna say only the hawk renders a small bird a tereifa?
Rav Kahana, citing Rav Shimi bar Ashi: a fox does not render an animal a tereifa by clawing.
Rav Dimi's account of a fox clawing a ewe in a bathhouse, judged a clawing case, contradicts that ruling.
An alternative version: Rav Kahana, citing Rav Shimi bar Ashi, says a fox does render an animal a tereifa.
Rav Dimi's bathhouse account is then judged not clawing, which conflicts with that version.
Rav Safra: a dog does not render a tereifa, and Rav Yosef and Abaye give the traditions on what clawing requires, including foreleg, claw, intention and life.
Once unintentional clawing is excluded, is clawing after death also ineffective, obviously?
No: the rule is needed where the predator's claws are severed while still in the flesh, since venom is injected on withdrawal.
Rabba bar Rav Huna, citing Rav: a lion's claw found in an ox's back is presumed to come from rubbing a wall, not from clawing.
Objection: most oxen rub and a rubbing ox does not keep the claw, so the lion clawed it.
Both explanations are possible; the animal stays in its presumptive status, since Rav holds no concern for doubtful clawing.
Abaye: a claw found moist is not ripped out by clawing, so one need not worry, but dry claws or several claws raise concern; Rav and Shmuel dispute doubtful clawing.
Resolving the dispute by presumptions: a doubtful predator is presumed absent or harmless, a quiet predator presumed tamed, and roaring animals presumed merely frightened.

53b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Describes the case where the lion stays quiet while the birds clatter, so the sages disagree about the cause.
Shmuel holds that the birds clatter because the lion is actively clawing them.
Rav holds that the birds clatter from fear of the predator, so clawing is not established.
Ameimar rules that in a case of doubtful tearing the halakha is to be concerned.
Rav Ashi asks Ameimar about Rav's contrary ruling that he had cited.
Ameimar replies that he never heard that ruling and does not hold by it.
Alternatively, Rav retracted his view and conceded to Shmuel on this point.
A story of birds with doubtful tearing sent to Rav, who passed them to Shmuel, who had them strangled and thrown into the river.
If Rav had not retracted he would have released the birds, so the retraction must mean forbidding them instead.
Shmuel's reply: it was Shmuel's own locale, so there was no need to strangle them and they could simply be cast into the river.
Shmuel's rationale: the birds would fly off and survive for twelve months, risking a stumbling block by sale to idolaters.
Further options such as selling to Jews or feeding to dogs were rejected, so the birds were destroyed publicly.
The explanation is that the destruction was meant to publicize the prohibition.
A gosling from Rav Ashi's house came back from the reeds with blood dripping from its wound.
Rav Ashi analogizes: a doubt between a reed and a cat should be handled like a doubt between a dog and a cat.
The sons of Rabbi Chiya teach that a torn animal must be examined opposite the intestines.
Rav Yosef says the teaching of Rabbi Chiya's sons was already explained.
Shmuel's teaching, transmitted from Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus, that a torn animal must be examined opposite the intestines.
Ilfa asks whether a tear affecting the sinews makes the animal a torn one or not.
Rabbi Zeira says Ilfa's question was already resolved.
Rav Chanan bar Rava cites Rav that a torn animal must be examined across the whole body cavity.
Ilfa asks whether this holds even when the sinews are involved.
Rabbi Zeira again says Ilfa's question was already resolved.
Rabbah bar Bar Chana cites Shmuel that when the sinews are loose, the majority of them decides the matter.
Rav Ami asks what the law is for an animal whose flesh has melted.
Rabbi Zeira says Rav Ami's question was already resolved.
Rav Yehuda cites Rav that a torn animal must be examined until the flesh reddens opposite the intestines.
If the flesh has melted, it is regarded as if it were not torn at all.
What is the case of melted flesh?
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua explains: it is when the doctor scrapes it and sets it onto raw flesh.
Rav Ashi recounts a lung brought to Rav Kahana's house that was set properly, as a case in point.
When they lifted the lung it stuck and fell, and it was declared torn based on Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua.
Rav Nachman says a thorn must pierce into the cavity, while for a torn animal the flesh must redden opposite the intestines.
Rav Zevid's version: for a torn animal the flesh must redden opposite the intestines, and in the sinews the sinews themselves must redden.
Rav Pappi relates that Rav Bibi bar Abaye raised a question on this matter.

54a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A perforated gullet makes the animal a tereifa in any amount, while a windpipe needs an issar; the question is how much clawed flesh must redden.
After raising the dilemma, the Gemara resolves it: both count in any amount.
Both the gullet and the windpipe render the animal a tereifa if any amount of flesh reddens.
What is the reason for this ruling?
The venom keeps burning around the hole continuously and widens it.
Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta sat before Rav Nachman and taught that a clawed animal needs examination next to the intestines.
Rav Nachman replies that his teacher Rav taught the examination runs from the hollow to the thigh.
What is the hollow referred to?
If the hollow means the shoulder, it is the same as the intestine area and Rav Nachman would add nothing new.
Rav Nachman means the hollow of the skull up to the thigh, which is a new teaching.
Rav Chiya bar Yosef found Rabbi Yochanan and Reish Lakish teaching that examination is next to the intestines.
Rav Chiya replies that his teacher Rav taught the examination from the hollow to the thigh.
Reish Lakish dismisses the authority of Rav, saying he does not know who he is.
Rabbi Yochanan reminds him of a student who served Rabbi and Rabbi Chiya and was honored, as an example of Rav's standing.
Rabbi Yochanan stresses that this student was the greater of the two and held the more important place in the yeshiva.
Reish Lakish concedes that Rav is remembered for his halakha: a dislocated windpipe that was slaughtered is kosher, since it cannot be slaughtered once dislocated.
Rabbi Yochanan objects that this is not certain and proposes a test: make a new slit and compare the two.
Rav Nachman limits the rule to a case where the slaughterer did not grip the simanim, which keeps Rav's ruling intact.
This is the principle: an animal injured so that its kind cannot live long is a tereifa.
What does this principle add that was not already stated?
It adds the seven tereifot taught in the house of Yosef, including the cases that came before Rabbi Yehuda ben Batira.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Batira rules there are no further tereifot beyond those the Sages listed.
Rav Pappa bar Abba's case of a similar ruling before Rabbi Abba supports the view that no new tereifot may be added.
We see the animal dying, yet we learned that with medicine it can live, so the rule seems contradicted.
Mishnah: these are kosher in a beast; a pierced or cracked gullet is kosher up to a certain amount, which Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel fixes at an Italian issar.
Mishnah continues: a skull dented without piercing the membrane, a heart pierced without its chamber broken, a broken spine with the cord intact, and a liver missing an olive-size piece are kosher.
Mishnah continues: melted matter, pierced pipes, removed spleen or kidneys, a removed lower jaw or womb, and a cut from which the animal was left to Heaven, are listed as kosher.
Rabbi Meir permits these cases while the Sages disqualify them.
Rabbi Yochanan says the listed cases are tereifot exclusively.
Reish Lakish says the listed cases are kosher exclusively.
On what do they disagree, given that they cite the same material?
Rav Mattana's ruling is cited as the basis of the dispute: a hole that is cut out and displaced from its place makes the animal a tereifa.
Rabbi Yochanan restates that these are exclusively tereifot.
The Tanna taught the cases as tereifot, and this is the principle.

54b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Tanna saw that Rav Mattana's dislocated-thigh case seems to fall under the principle that injuries make a tereifa.
What is the reason it should be included?
A dislocated thigh resembles the cases of removed organs, which make a tereifa.
So the Tanna taught these are tereifot to exclude Rav Mattana's case, which is kosher.
Reish Lakish holds that these are kosher exclusively; the Tanna listed the tereifot and then stated the principle.
The Tanna saw that Rav Mattana's case does not fall under the principle, so it is not a tereifa by that route.
What is the reason for this?
A dislocated thigh is unlike perforated, cut or removed organs, so the Tanna taught these are kosher to exclude Rav Mattana's case, which is a tereifa.
Rav Mattana states that a fully dislocated femur head makes the animal a tereifa.
Rava holds the animal is kosher, but if the sinew holding the bone is cut it is a tereifa.
The halakha: even when the sinew is cut the animal is kosher, unless the sinew decomposed.
How much may the windpipe be missing and still be kosher?
Ze'eiri explains the measure: estimate the Italian issar by the Kurdish dinar, which is like a small peruta found in Pumbedita.
Rabbi Chana the money changer reports that Rabbi Yochanan asked him for a Kurdish dinar to measure tereifot, as Ze'eiri said.
Rabbi Yochanan rules that tradesmen need not stand before scholars while engaged in their work.
The Gemara objects from a mishna stating that all tradesmen stand before those bringing first fruits.
Rabbi Yochanan replies that they stand before those bringing first fruits but not before Torah scholars.
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin supports this distinction, praising the mitzva performed at its proper time.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Yosei bar Avin's reason: perhaps the tradesmen stand so as not to make them stumble in the future.
Rav Nachman holds that a measure stated as a sela or issar is treated as slightly more than that measure.
Rava objects to Rav Nachman from a mishna about a rope bed that is pure up to five handbreadths.
A second objection from a mishna about impurity up to ten handbreadths tests the same reading.
A third objection from a mishna on the thin pieces of a clay vessel that sit without being propped.

55a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna sets the measure for a vessel's susceptibility to impurity as holding oil enough to anoint a small child up to a log.
Does up to a log mean below the measure or including it? The Gemara raises the reading that exact measures count as below.
The Gemara seeks proof from the next clause, about a vessel from a log up to a se'ah, which would support the same reading.
The Gemara seeks proof again from the clause about a vessel from a se'ah up to two se'ah.
A baraita explicitly says exact measures count as below, which contradicts Rav Nachman's reading that up to excludes the measure.
The term up to is always read stringently, as Rabbi Yochanan holds, so here it includes the measure, as shown by the rope-bed mishna.
The mishna says a removed spleen keeps the animal kosher; Rava holds that this applies only to removal, and a perforated spleen makes it a tereifa.
Rabbi Yosei bar Avin objects from a mishna on severing organs before slaughter, which suggests the animal itself is permitted even when the spleen was severed.
The animal is in fact prohibited too; the mishna contrasts the parts, or perforation and cutting are separate cases.
The mishna says removed kidneys keep the animal kosher.
Rav holds that disease in even one kidney makes the animal a tereifa, and the Eretz Yisrael version limits this to disease that reached the other kidney.

55b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Mishnah's case of a crevice is introduced as the subject under discussion.
Where exactly is the location of the crevice?
It is the white fatty part beneath the loin.
Rav Nachunya reports the teaching he cites on the mishna.
Rav Nachunya asked all the West's authorities on tereifot, who told him to follow Rakhish bar Pappa's view on a diseased kidney.
The halakha does not follow Rav Avira: a spleen perforated at the narrow end is not a tereifa, but at the thick end it is.
If a layer of spleen as thick as a gold dinar remains intact, the animal is kosher.
The West holds that whatever disqualifies in the lung is kosher in the kidney, a fortiori when the lung is kosher.
Rabbi Tanchuma challenges this as a principle that does not hold generally.
A counterexample: pus is kosher in the lung but unfit in the kidney, and clear water is kosher in both.
Rav Ashi answers that tereifot are compared only to one another, not with a general rule.
Illustration: an animal cut on one side dies, while one cut on the other side lives, and clear water is kosher.
The ruling applies only to clear fluid; turbid fluid makes the animal a tereifa.
Similarly, the clear-fluid ruling applies only where it does not smell, and a foul-smelling one is a tereifa.
A kidney that shrank in its measure is a tereifa at a certain size, with fixed thresholds given.
The Mishnah says the lower jaw removed is kosher.
Rav Zeira limits this: only if the animal can live by being fed, and it is a tereifa if it cannot.
The Mishnah says the womb removed is kosher.
The Tanna clarifies the womb is the bladder, and if it was pierced by Heaven it is kosher.
A baraita: a lung that shrank by Heaven is kosher, but if by human hand it is a tereifa.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says the human-hand rule applies to any person.
Does Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view belong to the first clause, which is lenient, or the last, which is stringent?
A baraita resolves the question: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says even by any person.
Rabbah bar bar Chana found sheep with a shrunken lung, brought them to the house of study, and the one that recovered is kosher by Heaven.
The same case, where the one that did not recover is a tereifa.
The Tanna teaches that Rabbi Meir permits a scab while the Sages disqualify it.
Elazar Sapra and Yochanan ben Gudgada testified that a scab is disqualified.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says Rabbi Meir retracted, so it follows that Rabbi Meir disputed with him about the scab.
A baraita says Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar held there was no dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages about the scab.
Rabbi Oshaya, son of Rabbi Yehuda the perfumer, testified before Rabbi Akiva in the name of Rabbi Tarfon that a scab is disqualified, but kosher if a sela remains.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains: there was no dispute, since Rabbi Meir did not maintain his view.
The master said that if a sela remains it is kosher; where does Rav Yehuda's view on this stand?
Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel: the measure is a sela across the whole spine.
Is a sela measured by length and narrowness combined, or by breadth across the whole spine?
Rabbi Nehorai cites Shmuel that the sela is measured by breadth across the whole spine.
Rabbah bar bar Chana reports the joints view: it is a question of the vertebrae and the navel, transmitted through several sages.
Rabbi Yannai asks whether removing the spine, the navel, or the joints leaves the animal whole; the question is left unresolved.
Rav rules that all the skin protects from a scab except the hoof skin.
Rabbi Yochanan holds that even the hoof skin protects from a scab.
Rabbi Asi asks Rabbi Yochanan whether the hoof skin protects from a scab.
Rabbi Yochanan says it does protect.
Rabbi Asi objects that our teachers taught that these skins count as flesh, including the hoof skin.
Rabbi Yochanan asks him not to annoy him, since he teaches that view as a single opinion.
A baraita: offering a piece of skin from the tail fat outside its place is disqualified without karet, but outside its time is piggul and incurs karet.
Transmitted sayings attribute the view on hoof skin and related skins to several named sages.
The skins counted as flesh for impurity are the hoof skin, the skin of a young calf's head, and the skin of the tail fat.

56a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita continues: a hide of the vulva offered outside its place is unfit without karet, and outside its time is piggul with karet.
The Mishnah lists tereifot in a bird: a perforated gullet, a cut windpipe, or a weasel strike on the head.
The Mishnah continues: a perforated gizzard or small intestines, and singed innards that turned green are unfit while red ones are kosher.
The Mishnah adds: a trampled or crushed bird is a tereifa, but a bird that lived twenty-four hours before slaughter is kosher.
Rav, Shmuel and Levi teach the inspection: insert a hand and check whether nerve tissue rises through the skull hole.
The Gemara objects that the inspection only works on one view, and the other view leaves a hidden perforation.
If the outer membrane was pierced the inner one bursts from fragility, so an intact nerve tissue proves both membranes are whole.
Ze'eiri holds that a weasel-bitten bird cannot be inspected at all.
The Gemara asks what the thin teeth change, since a small amount of nerve tissue would still emerge.
Rav Oshaya explains that the weasel's teeth are fine and crooked, so the hole does not allow nerve tissue to emerge.
Rav Oshaya's letter to Nehardea retracts his view: inspection is by hand, not by nail.
Rabbi Yochanan holds that inspection by nail is also valid, in the dispute of Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Nechemiah.
Rabbi Nechemiah holds one inspects by hand, the other by needle; the hand inspector is the one who uses the hand.
The hand inspector objects that the needle inspector destroys the property of Israel.
The needle inspector objects that the hand inspector feeds Israel carcasses.
The Gemara replies that the animal is not carcass but slaughtered, so the concern is tereifot.
The Gemara resolves that the view permitting hand inspection is that of Rabbi Yehuda.
A baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar in the name of Rabbi Yehuda: hand inspection is permitted, but not nail.
The baraita seems to contradict itself: it says a broken bone without a perforated membrane is a tereifa, yet permits inspection and then rules the opposite.
The Gemara turns to water birds: since they have no membrane, the rule is that the soft membrane is what counts.
Rav Nachman tells Rav Anan that Shmuel and Huna both held that hand inspection makes the bird kosher.
A baraita of Levi lists tereifot in a bird, including a broken bone without perforated membrane, which seems to contradict the rule.
The baraita refers to a water bird with a soft membrane, so the rule is not general.
A case of a hen in the house of Rav Chana, whose bone was broken without perforated membrane, was sent to Rav Matana and declared kosher.
Rav Matana is challenged by Levi's baraita: a bird with a broken bone and intact membrane is a tereifa.
Rav Matana replies that the baraita concerns a water bird with a soft membrane, which has no membrane.
Rav Shizbi inspected by the sun, Rav Yemar by water, and Rav Acha bar Yaakov by hand.

56b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The inspection method is described with a wheat straw drawn over the membrane.
Rav Shizbi says our geese are like water birds, so a broken skull is a tereifa even without a perforated membrane.
The Mishnah on singed innards: Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Yosei ben Yehoshua, says green in any amount makes a tereifa, like a perforation.
Rav Yosef asks Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi what the law is when the liver turned green facing the intestines.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi replies that the bird is a tereifa.
Rav Yosef objects that this should be no stricter than a removed liver with an olive-bulk left, which is kosher.
Rava explains that the bird fell into the fire and the intestines were singed, which is why it is a tereifa.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's hen fell into the fire; Rabbi Elazar HaKappar deemed it kosher when its innards turned green.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi objects from the Mishnah that green innards are unfit.
Rabbi Elazar HaKappar replies that only the gizzard, heart and liver count, since they are naturally red.
A baraita confirms that only the gizzard, heart and liver are relevant for green innards.
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef's hen fell into the fire; sent to Rabbi Abbahu, Rabbi Elazar HaKappar deemed it a tereifa.
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef objects from the Mishnah that red innards are kosher.
Rabbi Elazar HaKappar replies that only naturally red organs count, so red organs that turned green, or green ones that turned red, make a tereifa.
Rav Shmuel bar Chiya cites Rabbi Mani: red organs that turned green and then reddened again after boiling are kosher.
What is the reason?
Smoke entered the organs and changed their color temporarily, so they were never burned.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak holds that red organs that turned green after boiling are a tereifa.
What is the reason for this?
The change of color is revealed in their own nature, so it counts.
Rav Ashi rules that one may eat such organs only when boiled, and we do not impose a flaw on the animal from a doubt.
Rabbi Elazar ben Antigonus, citing Rabbi Elazar bar Yannai, holds that each case requires inspection.
The Mishnah lists kosher birds: a gullet pierced or cracked, or a weasel strike on the head in a place that does not make it a tereifa.
The Mishnah continues: a crop pierced, and Rabbi says even if the intestines came out; Rabbi Yehuda disqualifies a bird whose feather was removed.
Rabbi Simai and Rabbi Tzadok, on a visit to Lod, ruled on a tereifa of the windpipe like Rabbi's view on the crop.
Did they rule this way for prohibition, or for permission, since Rabbi holds the crop view and they do not?
Rabbah, or perhaps Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, says the crop's roof is judged like the gullet.
Rav Bibi bar Abaye says it applies wherever the whole thing is stretched along with it.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak says the rule applies only if the bird did not turn over, but if it turned over it is a tereifa.
The verse He made you and established you is taken to teach that the Holy One made the human frame so that if one part is reversed it cannot live.
Rabbi Meir reads the verse as showing that the whole frame was built in the world, its priests, prophets, rulers and kings included.
A gentile saw a man fall from a roof, his belly burst, and his son slaughtered him in front of him.

57a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A story of a father who fainted and whose intestines were sewn up, so he recovered, illustrating the earlier case.
The Mishnah says a bird with broken legs remains kosher.
Rava inspected a basket of birds with broken legs at the convergence of the thigh sinews and found them intact, so he deemed them kosher.
Rav holds that a dislocated foreleg in an animal is kosher.
A dislocated femur in an animal makes it a tereifa.
A dislocated femur or wing in a bird makes it a tereifa, since the lung may have been perforated.
Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan hold the lung must be inspected, while Chizkiyah holds a bird has no lungs.
Rabbi Yochanan holds a bird does have lungs, thin and red like a rose petal between the wings.
What does it mean that a bird has no lungs?
If Chizkiyah means there are no lungs at all, that is contradicted by seeing them; if they cannot be made tereifot, that is contradicted too.
Levi's baraita lists tereifot in a bird beyond those in an animal, including a broken skull bone, which implies a perforated lung also makes a tereifa.
Chizkiyah means the lung has no special rule for falling or singeing, because most of the ribs protect it.
From Rabbi Yochanan's reply one infers that Chizkiyah holds there are no lungs at all, which seems to contradict his view.
The statement shows Chizkiyah was unfamiliar with chickens, as the West reports in the name of Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Chanina.
Rav Huna cites Rav that a dislocated femur in a bird is kosher.
Rabba bar Rav Huna objects that the Pumbedita scholars cite Rav Yehuda in Rav's name that a dislocated femur in a bird is a tereifa.
Rav Huna replies that each river has its own course, so Pumbedita follows its own custom.
Rabbi Abba found Rav Yirmeya bar Abba inspecting birds at the convergence of the thigh sinews.
Rabbi Abba objects: why so much, when Rav Huna cites Rav that a dislocated femur in a bird is kosher?
Rav Yirmeya cites the Mishnah on severed legs and Rav's own ruling that the same applies to a bird when the thigh sinews are removed.
Rabbi Abba notes this conflicts with Rav's own dislocated-femur ruling, unless dislocation and severance differ.
Rav Yirmeya says Rav clearly distinguishes them: a dislocated femur is kosher, a severed one is a tereifa, and it only seems strange.
Rabbi Abba found Rabbi Zeira teaching that Rav Huna cites Rav that a dislocated femur in a bird is a tereifa.
Rabbi Abba rebukes him: since the master came here, he has been teaching a mistaken ruling.

57b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The speaker reports asking Rav Huna, who said a dislocated femur in a bird is kosher.
The speaker found Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba inspecting birds and cited Rav Huna's ruling that a dislocated femur in a bird is kosher.
Rabbi Yirmeya cites the Mishnah on severed hind legs and Rav's ruling that the same applies to a bird when the thigh sinews are removed.
The speaker objects that Rav contradicts Rav, and Rabbi Yirmeya falls silent.
The speaker suggests Rav distinguishes between a dislocated femur and a severed one.
Rabbi Yirmeya replies that Rav explicitly ruled a dislocated femur kosher and a severed femur unfit.
Rabbi Abba asks Rabbi Zeira what he has heard on the matter.
Rav Chiya bar Ashi cites Rav, and Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi cites Rabbi Yochanan, that a dislocated femur in a bird makes it a tereifa.
Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi says Rabbi Yochanan would have been lenient had he been where Rabbi Chanina was, since Rabbi Chanina ruled a dislocated femur kosher.
Rabbi Chanina had a hen with a dislocated femur, brought before him, and he permitted it and taught it as halakha for his students.
Students say the halakha is not like all these views, but like the case where Rabbi Yosei ben Nehorai asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.
Rabbi Yosei ben Nehorai asked about a reed cauldron's size, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi answered from the Mishnah up to an Italian issar.
Rabbi Yosei objects that a hen in their neighborhood had a cracked reed splint and lived, so the case seems to show recovery.
The reply is that the widely accepted halakha is that a dislocated femur in a bird is a tereifa, so such cases do not decide it.
Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta had a hen whose femur was dislocated, and it was given a reed tube and lived.
This case happened within twelve months as well, and Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta was occupied with matters, so the case is not decisive.
Rabbi Yehuda's view that a bird whose feather was removed is unfit is cited as the target of his activity.
Rabbi Shimon ben Chalafta's hen had a feather removed, was placed in an oven and grew later wings, which seems to show it recovered.
Perhaps Rabbi Yehuda holds that a tereifa may improve; if so, the later wings do not show it was not a tereifa.
What were they occupied with?
The answer comes from a verse: go to the ant, you sluggard, consider her ways and be wise.
A story of a man who wanted to check whether a kingdom was really without a king, and the outcome of his scheme.
Ameimar concludes that the kingdom has no king, since otherwise they would not have needed the decree.
Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi whether the king was present, or whether the decree of the king was in force, or the rule was between kings.
The verse in those days there was no king in Israel, everyone did what was right in his eyes, supports the view that there is no king.
Rav Huna says that twelve months is the sign that a bird is a tereifa.
An objection: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says that a bird that thrives and grows is kosher, while one that deteriorates is a tereifa.
Rabbi says thirty days is the sign of a tereifa, but many survive two or three years, so the view is a tanna dispute.
A baraita: a skull with one long perforation is a tereifa, and many perforations combine to fill a drill's size.
Rabbi Yosei ben Hamshulam recounts a case in Anbul where a skull was dented and a reed bandage was placed, and the animal lived.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar objects that the case proves nothing, since it lived through the summer heat and then died with the cold.
Rav Acha bar Yaakov rules that a bird that gives birth or thrives is not a tereifa, but the halakha is tereifa if not.
Ameimar says these eggs are tereifot.

58a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ameimar holds that the first clutch in the body when the bird became a tereifa is prohibited, while later eggs, fertilized by a kosher male, are permitted.
Rav Ashi objects to Ameimar from a Mishnah saying all agree the egg of a tereifa bird is prohibited because it grew in a state of prohibition.
Ameimar replies that the Mishnah concerns a bird heated by the earth, which was not fertilized by a male.
The Gemara objects that Ameimar could read the Mishnah as about the first clutch, and then the wording grew should have said finished.
The Gemara objects from a baraita on the offspring of a tereifa, where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua disagree about sacrificing it.
Rabbi Eliezer holds that where two causes produce the offspring it is prohibited, while Rabbi Yehoshua holds it is permitted.
If so, the dispute should concern ordinary consumption, not sacrifice, since that is the more basic question.
The sacrifice question is chosen to show how far Rabbi Yehoshua's leniency reaches, even to the altar.
Conversely, the dispute could be about ordinary consumption to show how far Rabbi Eliezer's stringency reaches.
The tanna prefers to emphasize the power of the leniency.
The Mishnah's concession about a tereifa bird's egg is therefore about a bird heated by the earth, with only one cause.
Rav Acha holds with Rav Acha bar Yaakov that a tereifa can lay eggs, so he teaches Ameimar's statement that later eggs are permitted.
Ravina rejects Rav Acha bar Yaakov and holds a tereifa cannot lay eggs, so Ameimar's ruling is stated with the first clutch left aside.
Rav Ashi objects to Ameimar from the same Mishnah, arguing a tereifa bird can produce eggs.
Ameimar replies that the Mishnah concerns the first clutch, and the Mishnah should be emended to read finished.
The Mishnah on a tereifa's offspring is restated for the case where the mother was pregnant and later became a tereifa.
Rabbi Eliezer holds the fetus is part of the mother's limb, while Rabbi Yehoshua holds it is not.
If so, the dispute should concern ordinary consumption, which would show the power of the other side more clearly.
The power of the lenient view is more emphasized, and the parties agree on the egg of a tereifa bird that is prohibited.
The egg of a tereifa bird in the first clutch is prohibited.
What is the reason for this?
The reason is that the first clutch is itself part of the bird.
The halakha: a male bird's offspring is prohibited for twelve months, and a female that does not lay is likewise handled.
Rav Huna says any creature without bone cannot survive twelve months.
Rav Pappa infers from Rav Huna's teaching that Shmuel's case of a cucumber gone bad inside is prohibited.

58b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Dates kept in a jar are permitted after a full year, since worms without bones cannot last twelve months, so worms found must have hatched later.
Rav says there is no one-day mosquito and no one-year fly, since such creatures do not live that long.
Rav Pappa objects to Abaye with a saying about a female mosquito that complained for seven years, implying boneless creatures can survive that long.
Abaye replies that the saying about the mosquito's iron dinars refers to the mosquitoes' own measures and years, not human ones.
A Mishnah on an animal with five legs or only three legs, which is a blemish, is cited as a source.
Rav Huna holds the Mishnah applies only to an extra foreleg or a missing one; an extra hind leg also makes a tereifa, since extra counts as missing.
An animal with two ceca was brought to Ravina, who deemed it a tereifa based on Rav Huna's rule, but kosher if they empty into each other.
A tube from the reticulum to the omasum was found, and Rav Ashi wanted to deem the animal a tereifa.
Rav Huna Mar bar Chiya replies that outdoor animals all have such tubes, so one need not be concerned.
A tube from the reticulum to the rumen was found, and Mar bar Rav Ashi wanted to deem the animal kosher, like the earlier case.
Rav Oshaya objects that such cases cannot be treated alike; a ruling applies only where it was stated.
Natan bar Sheila reports a butcher of Tzippori before Rabbi on two intestines exiting together, which makes a tereifa in an animal and kosher in a bird.
The case concerns intestines exiting in two places; if they exit in one place and are consumed up to a finger, the animal is kosher.
Rav Ami and Rav Asi dispute whether the case requires the intestines to return and be entwined, or not even then.
On the first view the Mishnah's up to a finger makes sense, since the intestines return and are entwined.
On the other view, what does up to a finger mean, and up to a finger from below?
Rabbi Yehuda says a bird whose feather was removed is unfit.
Rabbi Yochanan says Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yishmael say one thing: Rabbi Yishmael holds the feather joins the rest.
Rava explains that Rabbi Yehuda speaks only regarding tereifa where nothing shields, while for prohibition he agrees with the Sages.
Rabbi Yishmael speaks only regarding prohibition, not for tereifa, since nothing shields in that case.
The Mishnah lists kosher cases: blood-seized, smoked, chilled, one that ate a ghoul's poison, or drank foul water.
The Mishnah continues: if it ate deadly poison or was bitten by a snake, it is permitted for tereifa reasons but forbidden for danger to life.
Shmuel holds that an animal fed chalatit is a tereifa, because it perforates its intestines.
Rav Shizbi objects from a baraita listing similar cases, which seems to contradict Shmuel's view on chalatit.
The baraita seems to contradict itself on chalatit, achalatit, and deadly poison.
The contradiction is resolved: one refers to the bones or to the kind of case, and the other to deadly poison.
The deadly poison of animals is the same as the ghoul, and there are two kinds of deadly poison, one for a beast and one for a person.
What is the meaning of tiyah?
Rav Yehuda responds on the meaning of the term.

59a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Identifies the bitter herb as asafoetida, the root of a bitter vegetable.
Rav Yehuda says whoever eats three shekels of asafoetida on an empty stomach has his skin shed from the fever.
Rabbi Abbahu reports his own experience eating one shekel, and how cooling in water saved his skin.
He fulfilled the verse that wisdom preserves the life of its owner.
Rav Yosef says whoever eats sixteen eggs, forty nuts and caper fruit, and drinks honey in summer on an empty stomach, has his heartstrings uprooted.
A young deer, brought to the Exilarch's house with its hind legs cut, was inspected by Rav at the thigh sinews and declared kosher.
Shmuel objects that Rav should not be unconcerned about a possible snakebite before eating it rare.
What is the remedy for such doubt?
Shmuel says to set it in a hot oven, which will reveal a snakebite as the meat falls off the bone.
Shmuel and Rav each cite a verse about the righteous being protected from harm and from hidden troubles.

The Mishnah says the signs of cattle and beasts come from the Torah, but birds' signs do not; the Sages say birds of prey are unclean, and a bird with an extra toe, crop and gizzard peelable is clean.
Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok says any bird that splits its feet is unclean.
Locusts are clean if they have four legs, four wings, and jointed legs covering most of the body.
Rabbi Yosei says the locust is named, and for fish any with fin and scale is clean.
Rabbi Yehuda says a fish needs two scales and one fin, and these are the scales fixed to it and the fins it flies with.
A baraita sets out the signs of cattle, from the verse on split hooves that chew the cud.
Any cud-chewing animal without upper front teeth is clean, and this is the general rule.
The camel chews the cud but has no upper teeth yet is unclean, and the hare and rock badger also chew cud and are unclean, so the rule seems contradicted.
The Mishnah means that an animal without upper teeth, known to chew the cud and split its hooves, is clean, and its hooves should be checked.
Rav Chisda found an animal with split hooves in the desert and checked its mouth for upper teeth to determine whether it was clean.
The camel has teeth, so a camel's young should be the marker, but another animal resembles the camel's young, and this cannot be the rule.
A baraita of the house of Rabbi Yishmael says the verse on the camel teaches that it alone is unclean among cud-chewers, so Scripture singled it out.
Rav Chisda's rule for a hind leg animal: check its hooves, and if split it is clean, if not it is unclean, but one must recognize the pig.
Another animal resembles the pig, so the rule cannot be that simple.
A baraita of the house of Rabbi Yishmael: Scripture singled out the pig, since it alone splits the hoof and is unclean.
Rav Chisda found a hornless animal with split hooves and checked its flesh: if it walks two and then slides, it is clean; otherwise unclean.
Another animal resembles the ostrich-like creature, which is known not to exist, so how does one check it?
Abaye or Rav Chisda says the check is at the edge of the wings of the stinging insect.
The signs of wild animals are stated.
A baraita lists the signs of wild animals, which are included in beasts, and Rabbi Zeira adds a note on the signs.

59b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The signs are given in order to permit the fat of an undomesticated animal, which is otherwise forbidden in domestic animals.
The Tanna's rule: any undomesticated animal with horns and cloven hooves is a kosher wild animal.
Rabbi Dosa says horns alone suffice, while cloven hooves require checking for horns; the keresh with one horn is still permitted.
The Gemara objects that a goat has horns and hooves yet is domestic, so the rule needs layered horns, but a bull has layered horns and is domestic too.
Objections continue: a goat has grooved horns and is domestic, and a gazelle lacks branched horns yet its fat is permitted.
Conclusion: where horns are branched the animal is undomesticated; where not, the horns must be layered, rounded and grooved in an absorbed pattern.
The doubt concerns the karkoz goat, whose status is uncertain, like the goat with a grooved pattern.
A karkoz goat in the Exilarch's house yielded a full basket of fat, and this case is cited as a source.
Rav Achai forbade its fat as domestic, but Rav Shmuel bar Rabbi Abbahu ate it, reading the verse about the belly filled with fruit of the mouth.
The verse from Proverbs 18:20 is quoted for Rav Shmuel's knowledge of the law.
The Sages in Eretz Yisrael ruled the karkoz fat permitted per Rav Shmuel bar Rabbi Abbahu, but asked to honor Rav Achai and not to eat before him.
A baraita: the keresh with one horn has permitted fat, as with the other undomesticated animals.
Rav Yehuda, Rav Kahana and Rav Yosef describe the keresh and the lion and gazelle of Bei Ila'ei by size.
A story: the Roman emperor challenges Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya that God is like a lion, and asks to see the lion of Bei Ila'ei.
The lion of Bei Ila'ei roars from far away and causes miscarriages and falls, and the emperor asks for it to return.
The emperor again asks to see God, and Rabbi Yehoshua says he cannot, so the story ends with that answer.

60a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehoshua makes the emperor look at the sun in summer, and argues a fortiori that if he cannot look at the sun, he cannot see the Divine Presence.
The emperor wishes to prepare a meal for God on the shore, but a wind sweeps away his summer work.
His winter work is washed away by rain, and Rabbi Yehoshua says only the sweepers and floor washers eat it, so the emperor gives up.
The emperor's daughter says God is a carpenter, citing Psalms 104:3, and asks for a distaff to be made for her.
Rabbi Yehoshua prays and she is stricken with leprosy; she sits in the market untangling wool and people pray for her.
Rabbi Yehoshua passes her and asks about the distaff; she asks him to take back the gift, and he replies God gives but does not take.
