Rav Yehuda describes a bull's build as large paunch, hooves, head and tail, and the opposite for a donkey, relevant for sale.
Rav Yehuda holds that the bull Adam sacrificed had one horn on its forehead, citing the verse about a bullock with horns.
The verse uses the plural makrin, which suggests two horns, so the reading seems to contradict the single horn.
Rav Nachman says the word is written makran without a yod, indicating a single horn.
Rav Yehuda holds the horns of Adam's bull came before its hooves, which supports Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds that all of creation was created fully formed, in its stature, knowledge and appearance.
The verse on the heavens and earth and all their host is read as their appearance, supporting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.
Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa expounds Psalms 104:31 as a verse about the prince of the world.
The prince of the world says that when God said to bring forth according to their kinds, the grasses lifted themselves up.
The prince reasons a fortiori: if God wanted mixed kinds, why say kinds for trees, which do not grow mixed.
God replies that all the more so, each one went out according to its kind.
The prince of the world opened and said the verse: may the glory of God endure forever.
Ravina asks whether one may graft two kinds of grass, one on the back of the other.

60b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: What is the halakha according to Rabbi Chanina bar Pappa on mixing kinds after God agreed to the mixed creation? The matter is left unresolved.
Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi raises a contradiction: one verse calls both lights great, while another calls one great and the other small.
The moon complains to God that two kings cannot share one crown, so God tells her to diminish herself.
The moon says she spoke properly and must diminish herself, and God gives her rule by day and by night.
The moon objects that a candle in daylight has no value.
God replies that the moon will count days and years for Israel.
The moon objects that the day too must mark seasons, so she should not be left out.
God replies that righteous people will be named after her, such as Jacob the small and David the small.
The moon is still not calmed, and God says to bring atonement for Him, since He diminished the moon.
Resh Lakish's teaching is cited: the goat of Rosh Chodesh is atonement for God's diminishing of the moon.
Rav Assi raises a contradiction about whether grass sprouted on the third day or before Shabbat.
Grass stood at the gate of the earth until Adam prayed for mercy, so God desires the prayers of the righteous.
Rav Nachman bar Papa's garden did not grow until Rav Assi prayed and rain came.
Rav Chanan bar Rava holds that the split-hooved one is a separate kind with two bellies and two stomachs.
Was Moses a cannon-maker or a catapult-maker? This refutes one who says the Torah is not from heaven.
Rav Chisda tells Rav Tachlifa to write the words of the five lords of the Philistines in the aggadah.
Rabbi Yonatan explains that their chests are five, and Rav Chisda tells Rav Tachlifa to write chest in the aggadah.
This disagrees with Rav, who said the Avvim came from Yemen.
A baraita also says the Avvim came from Yemen, and explains the name as meaning they made the land waste.
Other explanations of the name: they hankered after many gods, and whoever saw them was seized with twisting.
Rav Yosef says they had sixty generations of teeth for each one.
Resh Lakish says many verses are fit to be burned like heretical books, but these are the very body of the Torah.
What is the practical difference, given the verse about the Avvim living in the villages up to Gaza?
Abimelech's oath to Abraham, that Abraham will not deal falsely with his descendants, supports the view of a decree.
God says let the Philistines come out from the Avvim, and let Israel come out from the Caphtorim, similarly.
The verse on Heshbon, the city of Sihon the Amorite, is cited as a source.
What is the practical difference?
God told Israel not to harass Moab, and Sihon was to leave Moab so that Israel could take Sihon's land.
Rav Pappa holds that Ammon and Moab were purified by Sihon, who held their land.
A verse about the Sidonians calling Hermon Sirion and Senir is cited about the mountains of Eretz Yisrael.
A teaching: each nation built a great city and named it after the mountains of Eretz Yisrael, showing their affection for the land.
A verse on Joseph moving the people to cities is cited.
The difference is that Israel should not call their brothers exiles.
The signs of birds were not stated in the Torah.
But isn't it taught that the eagle is listed among the unclean birds, which conflicts with this?

ranges.en: The nesher has none of the kosher-bird signs and is unclean, while doves have them and are clean; so birds are judged by these four signs.
Abaye explains the mishna: the signs of a kosher bird were not stated in the Torah, but come from the Sages' baraita.
Rabbi Chiya teaches that a bird with one kosher sign that is not listed as unclean is kosher, since it is unlike a nesher.
The Gemara objects: why learn from the nesher rather than from doves, which have all four signs and are listed as clean?
If one learned from doves, the other unclean birds listed by the Torah would be unneeded, so the listing shows the lesson is from the nesher.
The Gemara objects: let us learn from the other unclean birds, which have three signs, that a bird with three signs is also unclean.
If so, the crow need not be listed, since it has only two signs; so the listed birds are prohibited and other birds are clean.

61b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Proposes deriving the rule from the crow, then argues the peres and ozniyya would then be superfluous.
Proposes learning from the peres and ozniyya instead, and asks why the nesher would then be needed.
Explains the nesher is mentioned to show a bird with no signs is forbidden, while one with any sign is permitted.
Objects that without the nesher one would derive from peres and ozniyya, but those two verses teach one matter and cannot ground a rule.
Replies that a tradition assigns each sign to one bird only, so the two verses are not a true pair.
Presses that the single sign of peres and ozniyya must also appear in other birds, so the verses form a pair.
Explains the twenty-four birds and their four signs, and that the nesher wording blocks deriving the one-sign rule from peres and ozniyya.
Asks why the doves are needed if the nesher already teaches that a bird with even one sign is kosher.
Rav Ukva bar Hama answers that the doves teach only that they are the sole bird fit for offering, not their kosher status.
Introduces a teaching by Rav Nahman, whose content continues on the next daf.

62a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: States the halakha on one-sign and two-sign birds, depending on whether the person can recognize the non-kosher species.
Asks whether recognizing the crow alone is enough, or whether one must know more than the crow.
Cites a baraita in which Rabbi Eliezer extends the phrase after its kinds to include the zarzir, a non-kosher crow.
Sages object that the people of Kefar Temarta eat the zarzir because it has a crop, so it cannot be forbidden.
Rabbi Eliezer replies that those people too will be judged in the future for their transgression.
Cites the alternative reading, in which the phrase after its kinds includes the white senunit, per Rabbi Eliezer.
Sages object that the people of upper Galilee eat the white senunit, since its gizzard can be peeled.
Rabbi Eliezer again replies that those people will be judged in the future for their transgression.
Explains that Rav Nahman meant one must recognize the crow and every species of crow, not only the well-known one.
Ameimar rules that a one-sign bird is kosher if it does not claw its food.
Rav Ashi challenges Ameimar with Rav Nahman's ruling that one-sign birds may be eaten only after identifying all non-kosher birds.
Ameimar rejects that ruling, since the peres and ozniyya, with one sign each, are not found in settled areas.
Rav Yehuda states that the scratching bird is kosher and fit for a leper's purification, and it is the white senunit.
Ameimar distinguishes two kinds of white senunit and rules like Rabbi Eliezer on the disputed kind.
Mar Zutra restates Ameimar's dispute with the kinds reversed, and rules like the Rabbis on the disputed kind.
Asks what the phrase this is the white senunit adds if the disagreement concerns the yellow-bellied kind.
Answers that the phrase white senunit serves only to exclude the black house senunit.
Rahava, citing Rabbi Yehuda, classifies the tasil as a pigeon and the datzifi and Rehava birds as doves, each fit for different offerings.
Rav Daniel bar Rav Ketina objects from a mishnah that opens with all birds.

62b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Birds disqualify purification water by drinking from it; the pigeon is exempt because it sips without spilling back.
If the tasil were a pigeon, the mishna should have listed it as an exception too.
Rabbi Zeira replies that the tasil spits water back while the pigeon does not, so the distinction holds.
Rav Yehuda rules that the tzutzeyanei doves are fit for the altar, identifying them as the doves of Rechava.
An objection from the leper-hyssop mishna: a modified name disqualifies, so the tzutzeyanei doves should be unfit.
Abaye limits the rule: a name modified before Sinai that the Torah carefully excluded makes the item unfit.
These doves were not renamed before Sinai, so they remain fit despite the later modifier.
Rava offers another resolution: the doves are simply called doves where they live.
Rav Yehuda rules on which grasshoppers and which birds are permitted or forbidden, based on where they are found.
Ravina says those who eat the forbidden grasshoppers are flogged, based on the verse about swarming creatures.
Rav Yehuda rules the tzarda is permitted and the barda forbidden, and the marda is uncertain.
Rav Asi lists eight uncertain bird species whose kosher status is in doubt.
What exactly is the uncertainty about these eight species?
The gizzard of kosher birds peels easily, of non-kosher birds cannot be peeled, and these species peel only with a knife.
The gizzards of these uncertain birds can only be peeled with a knife.
The Gemara objects: a duck whose gizzard would not peel was softened in the sun and then peeled by hand.
Here the gizzard can be peeled only with a knife even after softening, so these birds stay uncertain.
Abaye says the swamp rooster is one of the eight uncertain cases and is the marda mentioned earlier.
Rav Pappa rules the swamp rooster forbidden and the swamphen permitted.
Mnemonic: the verse on Ammonite men and women shows which of the two is excluded.
Mareimar teaches the swamphen is forbidden because it claws and eats its prey, and identifies it as the giruta.
Rav rules the shavor anderafta is permitted and the piruz anderafta forbidden.
Mnemonic: the name of the wicked Piruz marks the forbidden bird.
Rav Huna rules the bunya is permitted and the parva forbidden.
Mnemonic: the name of the sorcerer Parva'a marks the forbidden bird.
Rav Pappa rules the reclining and eating mardu permitted and the bowing and eating mardu forbidden.
Mnemonic: the verse forbidding bowing down to another god marks the forbidden mardu.
Shmuel rules the wine-drinking bird forbidden.
Mnemonic: those who drank wine are unfit for Temple service, which marks that bird.
Shmuel rules the wine-pouring bird forbidden.

63a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The bird called the little wine pourer is permitted.
Mnemonic: the son's strength exceeds the father's, so the larger bird is forbidden and the smaller permitted.
Rav Yehuda lists types of shekitena; the long-shanked red ones are permitted.
Mnemonic: the murzema bird is similar in appearance and known to be kosher.
The little red ones are forbidden.
Mnemonic: a dwarf priest is unfit for Temple service.
The long-shanked green ones are forbidden.
Mnemonic: a mishna on green innards making an animal a tereifa.
Rav Yehuda identifies the shalakh as the fish-scooping bird and the dukhifat as the bird with a bent comb.
A baraita confirms the dukhifat is the bent-comb bird that brought the shamir to the Temple.
Rabbi Yohanan quotes Psalms when he sees a fish or an ant, to show God's justice and provision.
Ameimar permits the laknei and batnei birds, and the sakna'ei and batna'ei birds as well.
Ameimar says the sakna'ei and batna'ei are eaten or not according to local custom.
Does this mean the permissibility of these birds depends on custom?
Yes; the places where they are forbidden have the look-alike peres and ozniyya birds, which causes confusion.
Abaye rules the kevai and kakvai are forbidden, the kakvata permitted, and in Eretz Yisrael it is called taḥveta.
A baraita says the tinshemet is the ba'ut among birds.
Is the tinshemet the ba'ut among birds, or only among creeping animals, since it appears in both lists?
Using the hermeneutic rule of learning from context, the adjacent verses speak of birds, so the tinshemet is a bird.
A parallel baraita says the tinshemet is the ba'ut among creeping animals.
Is it the ba'ut among creeping animals, or only among birds?
Again by context, the adjacent verses speak of creeping animals, so the tinshemet refers to them.
Abaye says the bird-ba'ut is called kifof and the creeping-animal ba'ut is called kurpedai.
Rav Yehuda identifies the ka'at as the kuk and the raham as the sherakrak.
Why is the raham called by that name?
Because when the raham comes to the land, mercy comes to the world.
Rav Beivai bar Abaye says the raham's hissing sherakrak is a sign of rain, and of the Messiah's coming.
The verse in Zechariah on hissing and gathering the people supports the Messiah sign.
Rav Adda bar Shimi objects: a raham sat on a plowed field and hissed, and a stone broke its head.
Mar bar Rav Idai replies that bird was a liar and was punished for false prophecy.
A baraita defines the orev as the crow, including the valley crow and the crow that comes among pigeons.
Is it meant that the particular crow stands before us, so one would know it at once?
Rather, the orev is the black crow.
The Song of Songs verse describing black locks like a crow supports the black crow identification.
The valley crow is the white crow.
Leviticus on a skin mark appearing deeper than the skin links a valley with the color white.
Rav Pappa says the crow that comes among pigeons means its head resembles a pigeon's head, not that it dwells with them.
A baraita defines the netz as the hawk, and the bar ḥireya is included.
What is the bar ḥireya?
Abaye says it is the bird commonly called the shurineka.
Rav Yehuda says the ḥasida is the white dayya.
Why is it called ḥasida?
Because it performs acts of kindness for its fellows by giving them from its own food.
The anafa is the irritable dayya.
Why is it called anafa?
Because it quarrels with its fellows.
Rav says there are twenty-four non-kosher birds, as reported through a chain of transmitters.
Rav Ḥanan asks from where in the Torah the count of twenty-four comes, since Leviticus lists about twenty and Deuteronomy about twenty-one.
If the da'a is added from Leviticus, the count is still only twenty-two.
Rav Ḥisda replies with a teaching from Rav, that the repeated phrase after its kinds indicates additional birds.
The verses in Leviticus and Deuteronomy repeat the phrase after its kinds, which supports the extra cases.
The count then becomes twenty-six, not twenty-four.
Abaye says the da'a and the ra'a are one bird, not two, which brings the count back to twenty-four.

63b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Since Deuteronomy adds to Leviticus, why does each list use a different spelling, and why would the ra'a and da'a be one species?
Even so, the count of twenty-four is still not reached, since the list has twenty-five birds.
Abaye replies that the ayya and dayya are one species, as the ra'a and da'a are, otherwise the wording would be pointless.
Abaye argues from the structure of the two lists that the ayya and dayya must be one species.
If ayya and dayya are one species, why does Deuteronomy write both names?
A baraita says writing both prevents a litigant from disputing the name and eating the bird.
The verse in Deuteronomy lists the ra'a, the ayya and the dayya together, supporting the reading.
A baraita objects: the bird list is repeated in Deuteronomy to add birds, just as the animal list is.
No: the animal list is repeated to add species, while the bird list is repeated only to explain.
Rabbi Abbahu disagrees: the ra'a is the ayya, so the two lists differ from the view just stated.
Why is the ra'a called that?
Because it sees most vividly.
Job 28:7 mentions the eye of the ayya, supporting the identification of the ra'a with the ayya.
A teaching says the ra'a can see a carcass in Eretz Yisrael while standing in Babylonia, so it is the ayya.
If the ra'a is the ayya, must the da'a differ from the ra'a, given the discrepancy in the lists?
Rather, the da'a, ra'a and ayya are all one species, since the discrepancy then has no purpose.
By the same logic, is the dayya distinct from the ayya, and why is the wording different there?
So the ayya and dayya are one species, and by Rabbi Abbahu's view there are only twenty-three non-kosher species.
Isi ben Yehuda says there are one hundred non-kosher birds in the East, all species of ayya.
Avimi taught that there are seven hundred non-kosher fish, eight hundred grasshopper species, and countless birds.
But there are only twenty-four non-kosher birds in the Torah, so countless non-kosher birds cannot be right.
Avimi must have meant that the kosher birds are countless.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says the Torah lists kosher animals because non-kosher ones are more numerous, and non-kosher birds because kosher birds are more numerous.
What is this baraita teaching us?
Rav Huna, citing Rav and Rabbi Meir, says a teacher should be concise, as the Torah is concise.
Rabbi Yitzhak holds a kosher bird may be eaten on a hunter's word, and Rabbi Yohanan requires the teacher to know the birds and their names.
Was Rabbi Yohanan referring to the hunter's teacher the Sage, or the teacher who taught him hunting?
A statement of Rabbi Yohanan requiring familiarity with the birds and their names is brought as proof.
If it means the teacher who was a hunter, that fits; if a Sage, he may know names but not the birds. So the hunter is meant.
A baraita permits buying eggs from gentiles anywhere, without concern for carcasses or tereifot.
But the eggs may come from a non-kosher bird.
Shmuel's father says the baraita refers to a gentile naming a known kosher bird.
Then the gentile need only say kosher bird, so why name the species? Naming lets one compare other eggs, though a dishonest seller could deflect.
Why rely on the gentile, when one could inspect the eggs for signs, as a baraita says for fish signs?

64a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The term refers to fish embryos found inside the fish.
A baraita gives signs of kosher bird eggs: one rounded end and one pointed, with white outside and yolk inside, and a mixed egg is a creeping animal's egg.
The signs are needed only when eggs are already cut and their shape is unknown, or when they are mixed in a bowl.
Yet one may not buy eggs mixed in a bowl from gentiles, since they may be tereifa eggs, so the baraita cannot concern mixed eggs.
Rabbi Zeira holds the egg signs have no Torah-law force, since Rav Asi's uncertain birds would otherwise be easily resolved by inspection.
For what halakha does the baraita teach these signs if one may not rely on them?
The baraita says non-kosher eggs are certain, and kosher-sign eggs may be relied on only when the gentile names a kosher bird, not otherwise.
A statement says a mixed white and yolk egg is certainly a creeping animal's egg, not a non-kosher bird's.
For what halakha is this information needed?
Rav Ukva bar Ḥama says it concerns ritual impurity of an embryo's tissue, provided it is the size of a lentil-bulk.
Ravina objects: it may be a snake's egg, whose carcass does not transmit impurity even when mixed.
Rava says the baraita concerns flogging for eating the embryo tissue, not impurity, based on the prohibition of creeping things.
If so, why specify a non-kosher creeping animal's egg, since eating a kosher bird's embryo also brings flogging?
A baraita cites Leviticus 11:41 on every swarming thing upon the earth as the source of the prohibition.

64b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The rabbinic prohibition on chicks whose eyes are not yet open; the verse is only a support, so no lashes apply.
A baraita permits eggs boiled with non-kosher eggs and unfertilized eggs, and says to discard a drop of blood and eat the rest.
Rabbi Yirmeya and Dostai's teaching: the rest of the egg is eaten only if the blood is on the knot, not the yolk.
What is the reason the whole egg is forbidden when blood is on the yolk?
The decay has spread through the whole egg.
Rav Geviha says a tanna taught the opposite before Abaye, and Abaye corrected it.
From where is it derived that an egg of an impure bird is forbidden by Torah law?
Leviticus 11:16 mentions the bat ya'ana, which is taken to mean the egg of the non-kosher bird.
Perhaps bat ya'ana is simply the bird's name, not an egg.
That cannot be, since Lamentations 4:3 compares the cruel people to the ye'enim in the wilderness.
Micah 1:8 speaks of mourning like the daughters of the ya'ana, which suggests a bird name.
That verse means a mourning like the ya'ana that mourns for its young.
Isaiah 13:21 says benot ya'ana shall dwell there, again suggesting a bird name.
It means they dwell there like the ya'ana that dwells with its young.
Isaiah 43:20 says the jackals and benot ya'ana will honor God, and an egg cannot sing praise.
Both ya'ana and bat ya'ana are written, so both are acceptable names for the bird.
Here the scribe splits the word into two, unlike other animal names, because the scribe divides it that way.

65a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Since the scribe splits the name into two words, the Gemara concludes they are two names, so the egg is forbidden too.
If so, is Chedor Laomer in Genesis 14:4 also two names, since the verse refers to one person?
The scribe may split Chedor Laomer only across words, not across lines, while bat ya'ana may be split even across lines.
The Sages say any bird that claws its prey and eats it is non-kosher.
Rabban Gamliel: a bird that claws and eats is non-kosher, while one with an extra digit, crop and peelable gizzard is kosher.
Rabbi Elazar bar Tzadok's line test: a bird splitting its feet two and two is non-kosher, and three and one is possibly kosher.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar: any bird that catches food from the air is non-kosher.
The tziparta also catches food from the air and is kosher, so the rule cannot be general.
Abaye limits the rule to birds that both catch and eat in the air; the tziparta lands before eating.
Others say a bird that dwells with non-kosher birds is non-kosher, and one dwelling with kosher birds is kosher.
In accordance with whose opinion is this last statement?
Rabbi Eliezer says the zarzir went to dwell with the crow only because they are of the same species.
The 'others say' opinion may be like the Rabbis, who deem the zarzir kosher, since it does not resemble the crow.
The mishna on grasshoppers: four legs, four wings and two jumping legs, with wings covering most of the body, is kosher.
What is meant by most of its body?
Rav Yehuda says most of the length, others say most of the circumference, so Rav Pappa requires both.
A baraita: a grasshopper with no wings yet, which will grow them later such as the zaḥal, is permitted.
Rabbi Elazar bar Yosei reads the word lo in Leviticus 11:21 as not, so even a future-jointed grasshopper is kosher.
What is the zaḥal?
Abaye says it is called askarin in Aramaic.
Leviticus 11:22 is read to identify the arbeh, solam, ḥargol and ḥagav with their species names.
Why does the verse say after its kinds four times?
To include four similar kosher species: the vineyard bird, the Jerusalem yoḥana, the artzuveya and the razbanit.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael: the 'after its kinds' phrases are generalizations, and the named species are details, read together with the prior verse.

65b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The school derives that a species without a smooth forehead, or with one, or with a tail or without, comes before people and is kosher.
From where is it derived for a species with a smooth forehead?
The verse's word solam is the nippul, which has a smooth forehead, and the ushkaf is included with it.
A tailed species is kosher too, since the verse's word ḥargol is the rashon, and the karsefet and shaḥlanit are included.
The derivation continues to a long-headed grasshopper, which is not yet covered by the listed signs.
Compare the three species: they share four legs, four wings, jumping legs and wings covering most of the body, so any such species is kosher even with a long head.
But the tzartzur also has these four signs, so it should be permitted.
The verse's word ḥagav limits the signs, so the tzartzur is excluded and only a ḥagav with all the signs is kosher.
Rav Aḥai refutes the baraita: the four signs are not the only common features, and the inclusion argument can be overturned.
Rav Aḥai says the solam is redundant, so the Torah need not write it and the inference from the other two suffices.
The refutation fails: the arbeh and ḥargol each have a feature the solam lacks, so the solam is needed to teach that long-headed grasshoppers are kosher.

66a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: On what point do the study hall tanna and the school of Rabbi Yishmael disagree?
The study hall tanna reads the jointed-legs verse as a generalization, with the named species as details, so only similar species are kosher.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael reads a generalization, detail and generalization, so any grasshopper sharing one aspect with the named ones is kosher.
How can a generalization, a detail and a generalization be treated together when the two generalizations differ?
The school deduces from such patterns even when the generalizations differ, and this principle is derived from the earlier baraita.
The Master infers that a ḥagav lacking all the signs is excluded by the verse's words after its kinds.
From where would one derive that a grasshopper without all the signs is kosher, since arbeh and ḥargol are written first?
Solam is written to include long-headed grasshoppers, so the words after its kinds teach that a ḥagav must have all the signs.
Why does one baraita call solam the rashon and ḥargol the nippul, while the other reverses them?
Each Sage uses the names customary in his own locale.
The mishna permits fish with fins and scales, and a baraita adds fish that will grow scales later, or shed them after being caught, are permitted.

66b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The akunas, afunas and similar fish-like names are declared permitted.
A mishna teaches that fish with scales must have fins, and fish with fins alone are non-kosher.
If scales alone mark a kosher fish, why does the Torah also write fins?
Writing only scales might be read as fins, which would wrongly permit non-kosher fish, so both signs are written.
If kaskeset means scales as the Samuel verse suggests, why write fins at all?
Rabbi Abbahu says the Holy One made Torah abundant to bestow good upon Israel, expanding some laws beyond need.
A baraita says the positive and negative fish laws both teach that eating non-kosher fish violates a positive and a prohibitive commandment.
Leviticus 11:9 is cited for the permission to eat fish that have fins and scales.
Why is the phrase these you may eat of all in the waters necessary?
It excludes creeping creatures in pits, ditches and caves, which may be drunk from and need not be avoided.
Where did the Torah permit creeping creatures in vessels?
The verse says in the seas and rivers, so creatures found in vessels may be eaten even without fins and scales.
One could say the opposite: fish with fins and scales may be eaten only in seas and rivers, not in vessels.
That cannot be, since Leviticus 11:10 restricts the prohibition of fish without fins and scales to seas and rivers only.
Read the phrase as a generalization and the seas and rivers as a detail, so the restriction does not cover pits and trenches.
This deduction fails because in the waters appears twice, making a generalization, detail and generalization that includes pits.
How can this be a generalization, detail and generalization when the two generalizations sit next to each other?
Ravina says that in the West, Eretz Yisrael, two adjacent generalizations followed by a detail are read as including all similar cases.

67a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The in-the-waters phrase is read as generalization, detail, generalization: flowing water is included, so trenches are forbidden and pits and caves permitted.
Why not read the detail as water that grows on the ground, which would include pits and caves in the prohibition?
Then the phrase these you may eat of all in the waters would be pointless, since vessels would be excluded anyway.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael reads amplification, restriction, amplification, which includes trenches and channels and permits pits, ditches and caves.
Why not include pits and caves for prohibition and exclude only vessels? Then the phrase in the waters again seems pointless.
Perhaps one should reverse the rule: forbid fish in pits and caves and permit those in trenches and channels.
Mattitya bar Yehuda taught that pits and caves hold still water like vessels, while trenches and channels flow, so the reverse does not hold.
Rav Aḥa and Ravina disagree about which verse is the explicit source and which the implicit source for permitting fish in vessels.
What is the reasoning of the one who calls the fins-and-scales verse the explicit source?
That Sage could say the vessel permission is derived from this verse, as stated on the previous amud.
What is the reasoning of the one who calls the no-fins-and-scales verse the explicit source?
That verse proves the other verse permits fish in vessels, since the restrictions apply only to fish in seas and rivers.
Rav Huna says one should not pour beer through a straw at night, lest a creature fall in and the drinker violate Leviticus 11:41.
If so, beer in any vessel should also be suspect, since a creature may climb the side and fall back in.
There the creature's normal growth is to cling to the sides, so it is not considered to have emerged from the liquid.
A baraita permits fish in pits and caves, which is cited as showing that normal climbing of a creature does not make it forbidden.
Perhaps the creature climbed out, became forbidden, and fell back in.
Since that is the creature's normal manner of growth, it does not render it forbidden, and the same holds for beer in a vessel.
Rav Ḥisda cites a baraita on gnats in filtered liquid, which supports the view that only filtered beer need be watched.
Shmuel says a cucumber infested with worms is forbidden by the rule on creeping animals.

67b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Worms in a cucumber attached to the ground are forbidden, because the cucumber counts as part of the earth.
Two baraitot are cited as possible support: one permits worms in produce that is not attached to the ground, the other forbids worms in the roots of trees.
Do both baraitot not concern insects in fruit, so that the contradiction would support Shmuel's view?
No: both concern vegetation attached to the ground, with fruit permitted and tree-borne insects forbidden, and the wording of the second confirms this.
Rav Yosef and Rav Ashi raise dilemmas about worms that emerge from produce or climb onto its roof, and both remain unresolved.
Rav Sheshet says kukeyanei worms in an animal's organs are forbidden, since they came from outside through vegetation.
Rav Ashi objects: if they came from outside, they would also be found in the digestive tract.
Rav Sheisha says kukeyanei are permitted because they originate inside the animal.
Rav Ashi says that is obvious, since worms from outside would appear in the digestive tract.
The halakha is that kukeyanei are forbidden, since worms enter through the snout and bypass the digestive tract; worms in fish are permitted.
Ravina asks his mother to hide the fish's worms so he can eat the fish without seeing them.
Rav Mesharshiyya asks Ravina how this differs from the baraita making worms in animals forbidden, given Leviticus 11:11.
An animal is permitted only by slaughter, so its contained worms stay forbidden, while fish become permitted by gathering, so worms within them start permitted.
A baraita on Leviticus 11:42 assigns the belly-walker to the snake and the four-footed to the scorpion, with inclusions for similar creatures.
Rabbi Yosei ben Durmaskit says the leviathan is a kosher fish, citing Job 41 for its scales and fins.
The closing formula marks the end of the chapter, which begins with the words which are tereifot.

68a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a fetus that extends and withdraws its foreleg is permitted by the mother's slaughter, but one whose head emerged is like a newborn and needs its own slaughter.
Rav Yehuda says in Rav's name that the severed limb itself remains forbidden.
Exodus 22:30 on flesh outside the field makes a tereifa forbidden, so a fetus part outside the womb is permanently prohibited.
The mishna seems to permit the fetus including its limb, which would contradict Rav.
Why does the mishna specify that the foreleg was brought back, if it would be permitted either way?
The ruling applies even without bringing it back; the tanna mentioned it to parallel the head case in the latter clause.
The Gemara restates the mishna's two clauses and notes the tanna taught the first clause with the brought-back detail.
What does the latter clause teach, if not something new?
A Bekhorot mishna: a son after a stillborn whose head emerged alive is not a firstborn for the priests' redemption, but is for inheritance if the head was already dead.
The reason is that the head was dead, so a child born after a living-head birth is not a firstborn even for inheritance.
Perhaps the Bekhorot ruling defines birth only for humans, and the mishna here teaches it for animals.
Human birth cannot be derived from animals, nor the reverse, since an animal lacks the concealed opening and a human face bears the image of God.
A mishna on a placenta partly emerging from an animal makes it forbidden, which suggests the head-birth definition is already taught there.
If the first clause is specific to the brought-back foreleg, why teach the latter clause at all?
As Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak explained, the ruling is needed for the location of the cut, showing the cut point is also forbidden.
A baraita challenges Rav: a foreleg brought back before slaughter is permitted, while one slaughtered first is prohibited.
The baraita adds that a foreleg extended and cut off before the mother's slaughter is impure and forbidden, while the inside part is permitted.

68b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita: Rabbi Meir says a severed foreleg makes the flesh impure as a carcass, while the Rabbis say it is only forbidden as a slaughtered tereifa; the first clause permits the fetus.
Is the first clause not about the limb itself, contradicting Rav? Or if it is the fetus, why does the latter clause prohibit?
Why is the fetus forbidden in the latter case?
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak's explanation applies: the ruling concerns only the cut location on the fetus, and the limb itself stays forbidden even if brought back.
Is that so? A baraita on two hooves of a fetus seems to permit the limb itself, contradicting Rav.
It means the rest of the fetus may be eaten, but not the hooves.
If that is the fetus, why mention the hoof being brought back? And why are there two verses, one for the limb and one for the cut location?
One verse permits the cut location, while the other permits a non-cloven fetus found inside a slaughtered cow.
Rabbi Shimon requires a specific source for this, and Ulla says Rabbi Yoḥanan permits even the limb itself through the mother's slaughter.
Rav Yehuda objects that Rav and Shmuel both hold the limb itself is forbidden.
Ulla replies with reverence for Rav and Shmuel, but follows Rabbi Yoḥanan's view on the boundary verse.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: all flesh permitted within a boundary is included in the tereifa verse, so it becomes forbidden when it leaves, unless it is a sin offering reclaimed.
A baraita objects: second tithe and first fruits are permitted again once returned, so the boundary rule might also permit returned flesh, yet the verse says it is like a tereifa.
Rabba explains the tereifa comparison: once a tereifa cannot regain permission, neither can flesh that left its boundary, so the limb is forbidden, refuting Ulla.
The baraita's premise: second tithe and first fruits regain permission on return, and the question is where this is found in the Torah.
Where do we find that second tithe and first fruits regain permission on return?
Deuteronomy 12:17-18 limits the eating of these to Jerusalem, so by inference they become permitted again when brought back.
In the West they taught the dispute: Rav holds there is birth for limbs, so a limb can never be permitted; Rabbi Yoḥanan holds there is none.
What is the practical difference between these two positions?
The difference appears when a majority of a limb is outside, and whether the inner minority is forbidden.
Dilemmas: if a fetus repeatedly extends and returns its limbs until most of it is outside, or its severed limbs, is it regarded as born?
The Gemara begins to bring a proof from the mishna.

69a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The principle: a severed body part stays forbidden, while a fetus that is not part of the body is permitted by the mother's slaughter.
What new case does this principle add, if the mishna already allows the fetus after severing?
It includes a non-cloven fetus inside a slaughtered cow, which Rabbi Shimon would otherwise forbid if born before the slaughter.
If a sacred fetus extends a limb within the Temple courtyard, is the courtyard its boundary, or only its mother?
Abaye answers by analogy with lesser-sanctity fetuses in Jerusalem: the boundary of a fetus is always its mother.
If a fetus extends a foreleg between the two sisum, do the two cuts combine to make the limb pure?
Rava argues a fortiori: if the first siman helps permit the fetus, it should also help make the limb pure.
If a limb-extended fetus is born alive, does its prohibition pass to its offspring, and what does the case require?
Even a ben pekua fetus raises the question, since a male of this type with a female of another type cannot be permitted by slaughter.
The case concerns the offspring of two such animals: the father's seed may be intermingled through the whole offspring, not limb by limb.
Rabbi Yirmeya says it is obvious the father's seed is intermingled, since otherwise blind fathers would produce blind offspring.
Does the Torah permit only two prohibitions, fat and blood, not a third, the limb outside the boundary, and which Sage holds the view?
Baraita: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda disagree on the sciatic nerve of a fetus, and both prohibitions cannot apply to the same animal.
Is it permitted to drink the milk of a fetus whose limb is forbidden, given that milk is permitted despite being like a limb from a live animal? No resolution is found.
The mishna: severed pieces of a fetus left inside the womb are permitted by the mother's slaughter.
Deuteronomy 14:6 uses the phrase every animal of the animals, which includes the fetus within the mother.
If the phrase includes the fetus, the same wording in the substitution law would consecrate substitutes, which the Temura mishna rejects.
Rather, the fetus is included by the words and every animal, which permits it even when parts are severed.
If so, severed spleen or kidney pieces should be permitted too, yet the mishna forbids them.
Deuteronomy's phrase that it is whole, not lacking, restricts permission to the whole animal, not its severed parts.
If so, a dove-shaped fetus found in a slaughtered animal should be permitted, yet Rabbi Yoḥanan forbids it.

69b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The fetus is permitted only if it has hooves, and a dove-shaped fetus has none.
Then a fetus with non-cloven hooves inside a cow should be forbidden, yet the baraita permits it.
The school of Rabbi Yishmael follows Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai: each phrase of the verse suffices, so even a non-cloven hoof is included.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi says the halakha comes from the phrase an animal in the animal, and the Temura difficulty fits Rabbi Shimon's view on substitution.
From where do we know that the Temura mishna reflects Rabbi Shimon's opinion?
Rabbi Yosei: if one consecrates a leg as a burnt offering, the whole animal is consecrated, and the same holds for substitution.
Who is Rabbi Yosei answering, since Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda would not accept this reasoning?
A baraita says the words that it shall be sacred show only the given part is sacred, against Rabbi Yosei's view.
Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda rule that the animal is sold for burnt offerings and only the limb is sacred, while Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon include the whole animal.
Is Rabbi Yosei answering Rabbi Shimon, as suggested earlier to resolve the Temura difficulty?
No: Rabbi Yosei states his own reasoning without reference to any Sage, so it proves nothing about the Temura mishna.
Mishna on a firstborn: it is consecrated at birth and must be buried if it dies; a fetus cut up before most of it emerges is non-sacred.
Amoraic dispute: Rav Huna holds a firstborn is consecrated retroactively and Rabba holds from that point forward, which settles a sale to a gentile.
A second dispute: a third emerging through the wall of the womb, Rav Huna and Rabba again differ on consecration, following their same lines of reasoning.
Both cases must be taught: otherwise Rav Huna's retroactive view might seem limited to the lenient case, which he would concede to Rabba in the stricter one.

70a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If the dispute were stated only for a fetus emerging through the womb wall, one might think Rabba is strict there alone, so both cases are taught.
Rav Huna's view seems to conflict with the mishna: if a firstborn is consecrated retroactively, its cut limbs should be buried, not cast to dogs.
No: the mishna refers to one who casts each limb to the dogs at once, before any consecration takes effect.
If the limbs are left in place, must each be buried, so why does the mishna not state the case more clearly?
The latter clause means: if the limbs are cast to dogs before a majority emerges, but if left until a majority emerges, they must be buried.
Rava's dilemma: when a minority of a limb emerges with the majority of the fetus, is that minority counted with the limb's majority or the fetus's?
It is obvious that the majority of the fetus is not disregarded in favor of the limb's majority, so the dilemma must be different.
Rava's dilemma in a case where half the fetus emerged but that half holds the majority of a limb.
The mishna's wording that a majority is considered born might resolve Rava's dilemma, unless it means the majority of the whole fetus.
Is the mishna referring to half the fetus emerging with the majority of a limb, so it resolves Rava's dilemma directly?
No: the mishna may mean the majority of the fetus emerged with a limb's minority, teaching we do not disregard the fetus's majority.
Rava's dilemmas: if the fetus was wrapped in a palm bast, a robe or an afterbirth when it emerged, is it consecrated as firstborn?
Emerging in its own afterbirth is natural and not an interposition, so the real dilemma is wrapping in another animal's afterbirth.
Another dilemma: if one wrapped the fetus in one's hands and withdrew it, what if this happened in some circumstance?
If the head emerged first it is clearly consecrated; the dilemma concerns emergence hind legs first with the body wrapped inside.
If a weasel swallowed the fetus, brought it out, and it later emerged of its own accord, is the womb considered opened?
If two wombs were pressed together and a fetus passed from one to the other, is the second fetus consecrated, and the dilemma stands unresolved.
Rav Aḥa asks whether the airspace of a widened womb opening consecrates a fetus that does not touch its walls.
Mar bar Rav Ashi asks whether walls removed from their natural place still consecrate a fetus that emerges against them.
Rabbi Yirmeya asks whether a womb opening thinned by removing its inner layer consecrates the fetus that emerges through it.
Rabbi Zeira says the earlier dilemma, about a cut section of the opening, already resolves the question.
Rabbi Zeira asked Rabbi Asi whether a standing section larger than a breached one, or the reverse, consecrates the fetus.
That dilemma arose only when a breached section is larger, so some womb remains to consecrate; for thinned walls nothing remains, so the fetus is not consecrated.

70b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah rules that a fetus found dead in the womb, touched by the shepherd, is pure for both kosher and non-kosher mothers.
R. Yosei HaGelili dissents: impure within a non-kosher animal, pure within a kosher one.
Asks the reason for the first tanna's ruling.
Attributes the first tanna's position to the reasoning of Rav Ḥisda.
Rav Ḥisda's a fortiori argument: birth-permitting effect implies purity from carcass impurity.
Asks how this halakha is derived from Scripture.
Cites Leviticus 11:39 as the scriptural source.
Expounds the verse by juxtaposing kosher and non-kosher domesticated animals, so the fetus is pure in both.
Introduces R. Yosei HaGelili's opposing view.
Asks the reason for R. Yosei HaGelili's ruling.
R. Yitzḥak cites Leviticus 11:27 about animals walking on paws as his basis.
Explains that the verse refers to animals walking on paws inside a living animal, which are impure.
Objects that a fetus with unsplit hooves inside a cow should then be impure.
Replies that the verse covers only four-footed fetuses inside four-footed mothers, not eight-part hooves.
Objects that a cow fetus inside a camel should then be impure, as eight inside four.
Replies that the word 'whatever' includes a cow fetus in a camel, so Rav Ḥisda's a fortiori is needed here.
Rav Aḥadvoi bar Ami objects that a pig fetus inside a pig should then be impure.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak derives the halakha from Leviticus 5:2 listing carcasses of non-kosher animals.
Asks whether only carcasses of non-kosher animals impart impurity, since the verse seems to say so.
Explains that the verse's object is a fetus, impure inside a non-kosher animal and pure inside a kosher one.
Asks why R. Yitzḥak's proof is needed if Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak's derivation already exists.
Explains that without R. Yitzḥak's proof one would think the whole verse teaches Rav Naḥman's point, so it teaches this additional halakha.
A baraita teaches which carcasses impart impurity, and which do not, based on several verses.
Asks from where ben Azzai derives that a kosher undomesticated carcass imparts impurity.
Ben Azzai cites Leviticus 11:27 on animals walking on their paws as the source.
R. Yonatan objects that the verse says 'among any', not 'any', so the derivation is doubtful.
Ben Azzai replies that the verse is needed to include animals walking on paws inside undomesticated animals.
R. Yonatan asks what R. Yishmael, ben Azzai's teacher, says on this matter.
R. Yishmael derives all these halakhot from Leviticus 11:39, reading behema and ḥayya as inclusive of each other.
Concludes that ḥayya is included in behema and behema in ḥayya, so kosher and non-kosher categories interrelate.

71a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concludes that kosher and non-kosher behema are each included in the category of their kosher or non-kosher ḥayya.
Reports that ben Azzai told the speaker he regretted not having served R. Yishmael.
Asks from where we derive that a ḥayya is included in the category of behema.
Cites Deuteronomy 14:4-5, which lists undomesticated deer and gazelle among the permitted behema.
Explains that the list shows a ḥayya is included in the category of behema.
Asks from where we derive that behema is included in the category of ḥayya.
Cites Leviticus 11:2 which speaks of ḥayya among the behema, so behema is included in ḥayya.
Explains that the kosher ḥayya inclusion concerns the signs of kashrut, cud-chewing and cloven hooves.
Explains that the non-kosher inclusion concerns the prohibition of mating different kinds, per Leviticus 19:19.
Links the non-kosher behema inclusion to the baraita on the sliding-scale offering that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi taught.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi argues that the verse would need only the ḥayya clause, since behema is also called ḥayya.
Asks why an explicit clause about behema is stated if it is already included.
The explicit behema wording is an analogy: impurity of the kodesh-type behema in both verses, as in sacrificial foods.
Explains that the kosher behema inclusion concerns the formation of offspring, which applies to fetal form.
Cites the mishnah in Nidda on the miscarried fetus's form and R. Meir's view that any animal form counts.
The Rabbis hold that a fetus not of human form does not count as an offspring for purity purposes.
Asks why the verse about the non-kosher carcass is needed, if the Rabbis hold a dead fetus is pure.
Answers that the whole verse teaches the sliding-scale offering case taught in the earlier baraita.
Mishnah: a midwife who touches a dead fetus in the womb becomes impure for seven days, while the woman stays pure.
Rabba teaches that an impure item encased in a body does not impart impurity, and a pure one cannot become impure.
Asks from where we derive that an encased impure item does not impart impurity.
Cites Leviticus 11:40 on one who eats a carcass and becomes impure only until evening, implying the swallowed carcass is inert.
Objects that the verse may refer to a carcass no longer fit for a gentile, so the proof is inconclusive.
Replies that according to R. Yoḥanan the proof works, since a carcass fit for a dog still imparts impurity.
According to bar Padda the proof fails, since a carcass unfit for humans may lose impurity for other reasons.
Concedes that a swallowed item may be fit for eating when unnoticed, so the proof stands.
Asks from where we derive that a pure item encased in another body cannot become impure.
Derives it by a fortiori: a sealed vessel does not shield impurity outside it, yet shields the pure item within it.

71b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Argues a fortiori that if a person shields impurity inside him, he should also shield a pure item inside him.
Objects that an earthenware vessel is not comparable to a person, since a person can be impure from outside contact.
Replies that the case concerns contact with the interior, where a vessel may be compared to a person.
Argues that a vessel is in fact stricter, since it becomes impure from impurity in its airspace, so the inference holds.
Asks from where we derive that an impure item entering the body from below, through the rectum, is also encased.
A fortiori: if the body shields impurity entering from above, which is not digested, it should shield impurity entering from below.
Objects that digestion below depends on the chewing and digestion above, so the inference is weak.
Replies that digestion below is nonetheless greater than digestion above, so the inference stands.
Asks from where we derive that an impure item encased in an animal's body does not impart impurity.
A fortiori: a person who conveys impurity while alive still shields impurity inside him, so an animal should shield too.
Objects that an animal is stricter, since its utensils are impure immediately, so the leniency may not apply to it.
Explains that the animal case refers only to utensils on its back, and a person is likewise immediately impure in that case.
Cites a mishnah in Nega'im on how long a person and his garments stay pure in a leprous house.
Rava asks why the statement is necessary, since both halakhot are already learned in a mishnah.
Cites the Mikvaot mishnah on a swallowed impure ring, which does not convey impurity while inside the body.
Explains that Rabba refers to two rings swallowed together, one impure and one pure, which do not affect each other.

72a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that the mishna's midwife case resembles two swallowed rings, yet the mishna rules the fetus renders her impure.
Rabba replies that a fetus is different, since it will ultimately leave the womb.
Rava objects that a swallowed ring will also eventually leave the body, so the distinction fails.
Rava refers the matter to Pumbedita scholars, and Rav Yosef transmits Shmuel's ruling that this impurity is rabbinic, not Torah law.
Asks what Shmuel intended by stressing that the impurity is rabbinic rather than Torah law.
Explains that Shmuel wanted to exclude a reading based on Rabbi Akiva alone, since even Rabbi Yishmael accepts a rabbinic decree.
Asks what the reason for this rabbinic decree is.
Rav Hoshaya explains the decree guards against a fetus whose head emerges and returns unnoticed by the midwife.
Objects that the mother should then also be made impure, since she might miss the head emerging.
Asks what the opinions of Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva are on this dispute.
A baraita on Numbers 19:16 shows that Rabbi Yishmael excludes a fetus, while Rabbi Akiva includes grave covers and walls.
Rabbi Yishmael learns the grave-cover halakha by tradition, and Rabbi Akiva holds the fetus is impure by Torah law.
Asks from where Rabbi Akiva derives that the fetus is impure by Torah law.
Rabbi Oshaya cites Numbers 19:13 as applying to a fetus inside a woman, and Rabbi Yishmael uses the verse for a quarter-log of blood.
Rabbi Akiva consistently holds that a quarter-log of blood from two corpses imparts impurity in a tent, as a baraita teaches.
Asks from where we derive that a quarter-log of blood from two separate corpses imparts impurity in a tent.
Derives it from Leviticus 21:11, where the plural nafshot and singular met combine blood from two people into one measure.
Mishnah on an animal's leg severed before or after slaughter, with Rabbi Meir's view and the Rabbis' view on tereifa impurity.

72b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Rabbis argue by analogy: since a tereifa's slaughter purifies it from carcass impurity, the slaughter of the mother should purify the fetus's limb.
Rabbi Meir objects that a tereifa's slaughter purifies only its own body, not a limb that left the womb.
The mishna asks from where we derive that a tereifa's slaughter renders it pure from carcass impurity.
Compares a tereifa to a non-kosher animal and rejects the comparison by pointing to the born-tereifa case and to slaughter-eligible kinds.
Concludes that an eight-month fetus born alive is not purified by slaughter, since its kind is not slaughtered.
Asks why the impurity of a concealed space does not impart impurity, if Rabbi Meir holds it does.
Cites a mishna in Kelim on garment pieces split after treading impurity, where Rabbi Meir holds impurity passes in a concealed space.
Rabbi Yosei disagrees: the pieces could be impure only through a direct zav contact, so the mishnas cannot be reconciled.
Ulla reconciles the views: Rabbi Yosei disputes only small split pieces, while a piece cut from a large garment is impure at separation.
Ravina offers another reconciliation: a garment is not meant to be cut, while the fetus's foreleg is intended for cutting.

73a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ravina's principle: a foreleg that is destined to be cut off is treated as already cut, so it can impart impurity.
Asks whose opinion this principle follows, suggesting it is Rabbi Meir's.
Cites a mishnah in Mikvaot where Rabbi Meir immerses a handle that will be cut off as if it were already cut.
The Rabbis disagree: the whole vessel, including the handle, must be immersed, so the stand-to-be-cut principle does not apply.
Explains that even the Rabbis accept it for food, where connections are disregarded, so the fetal limb is treated similarly.
Asks why the mishna says the foreleg was severed, if the impurity applies even without severance.
The Rabbis hold that the fetal flesh is impure from contact with a slaughtered tereifa.
Asks whether a slaughtered tereifa imparts impurity.
Answers yes, citing Shmuel's father: the Sages decreed that a slaughtered tereifa disqualifies sacrificial animals by contact.
Cites the Rabbis' analogy: a tereifa's slaughter purifies it from carcass impurity, so the mother's slaughter should purify the fetal limb.
Rabbi Meir objects that if the mother's slaughter purifies the limb, it should also permit it for consumption.
The Rabbis reply that slaughter shields outside parts more than its own body, as a mishnah on fetal and organ pieces shows.
Asks what the Rabbis mean, since the baraita seems incomplete.
Rava reconstructs the missing clause: the Rabbis answer that a tereifa's slaughter purifies without permitting consumption, so the fetal limb is similar.
Rabbi Meir again objects that a tereifa's purification applies only to its own body, not to an outside fetal limb.
The Rabbis reply with the mishnah on fetal pieces versus organ pieces, showing slaughter shields outside parts more strongly.
A baraita repeats the exchange: the Rabbis cite the tereifa analogy, supporting that the mother's slaughter purifies the fetal limb.
Rabbi Meir objects that the hanging limb of an animal is part of its body, so its purification does not extend to a fetal limb.
The Rabbis reply again that slaughter shields outside parts more than its own body, citing the same mishnah.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says the dispute over fetal limbs parallels a dispute over hanging limbs of an animal.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says the dispute concerns only fetal limbs, while for hanging limbs all agree slaughter does not purify.
Asks the reason for Rabbi Yoḥanan's distinction, given the Rabbis' view on fetal and hanging limbs.
Explains that the fetal limb can be rectified by returning to the womb, while a hanging limb cannot be reattached.
Objects from the baraita that Rabbi Meir's reasoning about outside parts undermines Rabbi Yoḥanan's distinction.

73b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Resolves Rabbi Meir's apparent inconsistency by reading the Rabbis' view in Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's version, where both limb types are treated alike.
Notes that the resolution is difficult on Rabbi Yoḥanan's version, since both sides would then be inconsistent with Rabbi Meir.
Restates the dispute as Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish and Rabbi Yoḥanan each framed it, so Rabbi Meir's view is consistent.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina asks the reason for Rabbi Yoḥanan's distinction in Rabbi Meir's view.
Explains that the hanging limb is part of the animal's body, while the fetal limb is not.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef reports Rabbi Yoḥanan: all agree death makes a limb fallen, but slaughter does not.
Asks what case the dispute concerns.
Explains that the case must be a hanging limb, since a fetal limb is already explicitly disputed, making Rabbi Yoḥanan's point needed.
Cites mishnahs on the effect of death and of slaughter on hanging flesh, showing that both treat the limb as not fallen.
Explains that the mishnah's plural rendered susceptible may be read as referring only to the flesh, so the limb's status is open.
Objects that the mishnah's plural form does refer to both flesh and limb, so the reading that only flesh is meant fails.
Asks in what way the halakha is more compelling for one type of flesh than the other.
Explains that flesh attached to a severed limb takes the limb's severe impurity, so the plural teaches it still needs susceptibility.
Rav Yosef says to accept Rav Yitzḥak bar Yosef's report of Rabbi Yoḥanan, which Rabba bar bar Ḥana also holds.
Cites a baraita on Exodus 22:30 treating a limb partly cut from an animal as a limb severed from a living animal.
Rabba bar bar Ḥana reports Rabbi Yoḥanan's explanation of that baraita.

74a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concludes that such hanging limbs are not forbidden by Torah law, so only a rabbinic mitzva to abstain remains.
Rav Yosef reports Rav's ruling via Rav Yehuda: one who eats a hanging limb is flogged.
A Sage objects that Rav Yehuda's version is wrong, since Rav Yitzḥak bar Shmuel bar Marta reports Rav as saying no flogging.
Rav Yitzḥak bar Shmuel bar Marta reports Rav's ruling that one eating such a limb is not flogged.
Rav Huna asks Rav Yosef which version of Rav's ruling they should rely upon.
Rav Yosef explains that the two reports concern different cases: death by other means, versus slaughter, which does not make the limb fallen.
Rava asks from where the principle that death but not slaughter makes a hanging limb fallen is derived.
Derives the principle from Leviticus 11:32 on creeping animals, where death makes the carcass impure, not slaughter.
Rav Adda bar Ahava objects that the verse concerns creeping animals, which need no slaughter, so it cannot teach a slaughter halakha.
Rava replies that since the verse is superfluous for creeping animals, it applies to animals subject to slaughter.
Rav Ḥisda and Rabba debate whether the Rabbis' dispute concerns a fetus alive or dead at slaughter, and cite the eight-month fetus mishnah.
Objects from a baraita that an eight-month fetus born alive refutes the claim that slaughter-eligibility determines purification.
Rav Kahana explains the baraita counts an eight-month fetus as slaughter-eligible inside its mother, so it is not a refutation.
Asks from where the baraita's tanna derives that a tereifa's slaughter renders it pure from carcass impurity.
Derives it from Leviticus 11:39 and Rav Yehuda's report of Rav: 'some' excludes a slaughtered tereifa from carcass impurity.
Rav Hoshaya raises a dilemma: does slaughtering a live nine-month fetus inside the mother permit it?
Explains the dilemma may be raised on both Rabbi Meir's and the Rabbis' views, with the fetus's four simanim possibly sufficing.
Rav Ḥananya resolves the dilemma from the mishnah on a tereifa born from the womb, implying a fetus could be slaughtered inside.
Rava replies that the mishnah refers to a fetus formed as a tereifa from the outset, as with a five-legged fetus.
Mishnah: a fetus found in a slaughtered animal is permitted by the mother's slaughter, unless a live nine-month fetus needs its own slaughter, per Rabbi Meir.

74b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri holds that a live nine-month fetus of a slaughtered mother is permitted, but a fetus found in a torn animal needs its own slaughter.
Rabbi Elazar reports Rabbi Oshaya: the Sages' dispute about a live nine-month fetus concerns only whether it requires its own slaughter.
Asks what Rabbi Oshaya's limitation excludes, and suggests it excludes the fetus's forbidden fats.
Objects that the Sages disagree about the fetal fat and sciatic nerve, citing Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda, so the suggested reading fails.
Restates Rabbi Oshaya's ruling as limited to matters of consumption, excluding only copulation or mixed plowing with the animal.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish holds that blood of the fetus follows the fat's permission or prohibition as each opinion holds.
Rabbi Yoḥanan disagrees: even Rabbi Yehuda, who permits the fat, prohibits the fetal blood.
Rabbi Yoḥanan objects to Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish from a mishnah that prohibits the blood of a fetus but apparently permits its fat.
Rabbi Zeira resolves it: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish meant only that the blood of the fetus is not punishable by karet.
A baraita holds that the blood of exudate is a warning-level prohibition, while Rabbi Yehuda says it is punishable by karet.
Rav Yosef cites Leviticus 17:10 to show that karet for exudate blood follows karet for the blood of the soul, as Rabbi Yehuda holds.
Raises a dilemma: may a ben pekua redeem a firstborn donkey, according to Rabbi Meir and then according to the Rabbis?
Explains that for Rabbi Meir the question need not be raised, since a ben pekua is a full lamb.
Raises the dilemma under the Rabbis' view: is a ben pekua treated like meat in a pot, or still a living lamb that can redeem?
Mar Zutra holds one cannot redeem a donkey with a ben pekua, while Rav Ashi holds one can.
Rav Ashi asks Mar Zutra for his reasoning, which derives donkey redemption from the Paschal lamb by verbal analogy.
Cites Exodus 12:5 and 13:13, the verses on the Paschal lamb and the firstborn donkey, as the basis of the verbal analogy.
Rav Ashi objects that the analogy would require a male, unblemished, first-year lamb, which conflicts with the mishnah.
Mar Zutra responds that the repeated words you shall redeem include lambs that are not so qualified.
Rav Ashi retorts that if the repetition amplifies, it should include a ben pekua too, leaving the analogy with no function.
Raises a dilemma on counting the ben pekua as first or second degree impurity when the mother is impure.
Rabbi Yoḥanan counts the ben pekua as second degree, while Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish treats it like a nut in its shell, equal to its mother.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish objects to Rabbi Yoḥanan from the mishnah on the fetal foreleg impurity.
The Rabbis hold that the flesh has the impurity of contact with a slaughtered tereifa, which the Sages decreed.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish explains his objection: on his view the fetus is impure through the mother, but on Rabbi Yoḥanan's it is not.
Rabbi Yoḥanan replies that the fetus is rendered susceptible by its mother's slaughter, which permits it, per Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Yoḥanan objects from a baraita on a ben pekua that passed through a river, arguing this is unnecessary on Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish's view.

75a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish explains the baraita concerns a dry slaughter, and that it does not follow Rabbi Shimon's view.
Asks who the tanna of the baraita on a ben pekua passing through a river is.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says it is Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's view, since the baraita attributes that position to him.
A baraita reports Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, through Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, that a live ben pekua can become impure as food, against the Rabbis.
Explains that Rabbi Yoḥanan follows his own view, that Beit Shammai and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili agree a live animal can become impure as food.
Recites the mishnah on fish: Beit Shammai, Beit Hillel and Rabbi Akiva differ on when fish become susceptible to impurity as food.
Asks what the difference between Rabbi Akiva and Beit Hillel is.
Rabbi Yoḥanan says the difference concerns a convulsing fish, which Rabbi Akiva holds can already become impure.
Rav Ḥisda raises a dilemma about a fish with tereifa symptoms, which the Gemara leaves unresolved.
Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish disagree on whether the fat of a stillborn fetus is like domesticated or wild animal fat.
Clarifies that the dispute concerns removing the fat of a live nine-month fetus from the womb and eating it.
Rabbi Yoḥanan objects to Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish from a baraita on the fetal fat excluded from sacrifice, asking why a verse is needed.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish replies that the verse teaches that a fetus's fat is not forbidden.
Gives the alternate version: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish objects to Rabbi Yoḥanan from the same baraita on sacrificing fetal fat.
Rabbi Yoḥanan replies that the fetal fat is not sacrificed because, like an offering under seven days, its time has not come.
Rabbi Ami and Rava state the rulings for a live nine-month fetus found in a tereifa, depending on whether one holds with Rabbi Meir or Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Ḥisda gives his own ruling on a live nine-month fetus found in a slaughtered tereifa.

75b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Ḥisda rules that a live nine-month fetus of a tereifa needs its own slaughter, yet is pure from carrying impurity if it dies.
Rava objects that Rav Ḥisda's ruling is inconsistent, and Rav Ḥisda replies that the same problem arises with Rabbi Ḥiyya's baraita.
Rava and Rav Ḥisda each reply that the baraita can be read consistently, by the fetus found dead or by four simanim.
Rabbi Zeira reports Rav Asi's account that Rabbi Yoḥanan endorses the four-simanim halakha of Rav Ḥisda.
Rabbi Zeira asks whether this implies that Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish disagreed with Rabbi Yoḥanan.
Rav Asi replies he does not know, since Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish stayed silent, perhaps waiting or drinking.
Mishnah: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri holds even a live nine-month fetus that plows in the field needs no slaughter.
Asks what difference there is between Rabbi Shimon Shezuri and the first tanna.
Rav Kahana says the difference is whether the fetus stood on the ground, where a rabbinic decree requires slaughter.
Rav Mesharshiyya holds that a ben pekua's offspring from a non-ben pekua mother has no rectification by slaughter.
Abaye and Ze'eiri hold that ben pekua fetuses in particular cases are permitted, and Rabbi Ḥanina rules in line with Rabbi Shimon Shezuri.
Recounts Adda bar Ḥavu's ben pekua mauled by a bear, and Rav Ashi tells him to slaughter it per the first tanna.
Adda bar Ḥavu objects citing Ze'eiri's halakha and Rabbi Yoḥanan's concession about the ben pekua itself.
Rav Ashi explains Rabbi Yoḥanan spoke according to Rabbi Shimon Shezuri, while he himself agrees with the first tanna.
Adda bar Ḥavu persists, citing Rabbi Ḥanina that in any mishnah case Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's view is the halakha.
Rav Ashi replies that he holds Rabbi Yonatan's limit: Rabbi Shimon Shezuri is followed only for the dangerously ill and demai terumah.
Cites mishnahs in Gittin and Demai showing Rabbi Shimon Shezuri's leniency for the dangerously ill and for terumah of demai.

76a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: an animal whose hind leg is severed above the joint, or whose thigh sinews are removed, is a tereifa; a broken bone depends on the flesh intact.
Rav Yehuda, Rav and Rabbi Ḥiyya explain the leg-joint mishnah, and Rabbi Oshaya and Ulla locate the joint by the camel's leg.
Ulla objects to Rav Yehuda: on Rabbi Oshaya's reading the thigh-sinews clause would be superfluous.
Rav Yehuda answers in two cases, but Ulla objects that the mishnah's wording that the leg was severed fully includes the sinews.
Rav Yehuda was silent and had no resolution at that moment.
Rav Yehuda asks himself why he did not offer his proposed resolution to Ulla.
Rav Yehuda reflects that his reading fails, and Rav Pappa teaches the leg-joint explanation in a way that accepts Ulla's view.
Rabbi Oshaya argues it is illogical that cutting higher is less life-threatening than cutting lower on the sinews.
Rav Ashi replies that different tereifot cannot be compared, since different body areas react differently.
Asks which parts are included in the convergence of sinews in the thigh.
Rav Ashi, Rabba bar Rav Huna and Rava son of Rabba bar Rav Huna give differing answers on which sinews are included.
Recounts a Sage who ruled that the convergence includes the arkum sinews, and Rabbi Abba's rejection that this ruling is too stringent.
Shmuel's teaching, transmitted by Rav Ya'akov, places the convergence of sinews where they converge and extends until they are subsumed in flesh.
Asks how far the convergence of sinews extends.
Abaye says it is four handbreadths in an ox.
Asks what the measure is in a small domesticated animal.
Abaye says there is no fixed measure: the sinews count while prominent, hard, thick and white, and not when subsumed in flesh.

76b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rulings on the thigh sinews: Mar bar Rav Ashi's translucent sinews, Ameimar's three-strand majority, birds' sixteen strands, and Rav Yehuda's report of Shmuel.
Infers that Shmuel's ruling contradicts Rabbenai's report of Shmuel, since one remaining sinew would otherwise suffice.
Gives the alternate version of Rav Yehuda's report and Rabbenai's ruling, then the rulings of Rav and Shmuel on broken bones and limbs.
Rav Naḥman objects that Shmuel's ruling may mislead people into thinking a fully severed limb leaves the animal permitted.
Rav Naḥman clarifies that the concern arises only under Shmuel's view, since Rav permits only a break below the joint.
Rulings sent from Eretz Yisrael: the halakha follows Rav that the animal is a tereifa and the limb is impure from carrying.
Rav Ḥisda objects from the baraita on the fetal limb, and Rabba says the mishnah refutes it more conclusively.
Rav Ḥisda replies that the mishnah's blood dispute concerns only the hanging flesh, not the limb.
Rabbi Zeira reports Rav Yirmeya's ruling, that Shmuel retracted in favor of Rav, and a baraita on skin and flesh covering the bone.
Asks how much of a bone must be covered for the animal to be kosher.
Rav Dimi reports Rabbi Yoḥanan requires a majority of width or circumference, and Rav Pappa requires both.
Ulla holds that skin counts like flesh in covering a majority of the bone.
Rav Naḥman objects that the baraita says skin and flesh together, implying skin alone is insufficient.
Ulla replies that the baraita reads skin or flesh, so skin can count.
Gives the variant version: skin combines with flesh to cover a majority of the bone.
Rav Naḥman objects that this makes skin a stringency that completes the required flesh.
Ulla cites a fledgling case, which Rav Naḥman distinguishes because a fledgling's skin is soft and counts like flesh.
Rabba rules that soft sinews that will harden are not a concern, so the case of sinews covering a break is permitted.

77a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Sinews that will harden may still be counted as flesh for the Paschal offering, and the Torah spares people's money.
Rav Pappa objects to Rabba that Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish treats such sinews as not flesh, so the animal is a tereifa.
Asks why Rabba was silent in response.
Cites Rava's ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish in only three specified disputes.
Explains that here Rabbi Yoḥanan retracted in favor of Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, and his earlier view was a lone opinion.
Recounts the case of a bone protruding with a small piece removed, and Rava's ruling that the animal is permitted if skin and flesh cover a majority.
Ravina asks about torn, pulverized or decomposed flesh covering the bone, and what that flesh's status is.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua says decomposed flesh is any flesh the doctor removes to aid healing.
Raises a dilemma about perforated, peeled, cracked or partly removed flesh covering the bone.
Cites Ulla's report of Rabbi Yoḥanan that skin is like flesh as a possible answer to the dilemma.
Refutes the proof: Rabbi Yoḥanan may refer only to places where bone has only skin, not places where flesh belongs.
Rav Ashi recounts the dilemma on a ring-shaped cut, with most of the bone's circumference still covered by flesh.
Resolves it from Rav Yehuda's report of Rav: make an incision with a bone implement so the flesh heals, when the bone holds its flesh.
Mishnah on a placenta found in a slaughtered animal, and on the disposal of a firstborn's placenta and sacred animal placentas.
Asks from where the placenta's permission by the mother's slaughter is derived.
Cites Deuteronomy 14:6 and its wording that you may eat it, excluding a placenta that partly emerged.
Objects that a placenta does not exist without a fetus, so the verse seems unnecessary.
Replies that the verse is a mere support for the halakha, not its source.
Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Nappaḥa raises a dilemma about the ritual impurity of a cooked donkey hide.

77b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraitot teach that a hide and placenta that people do not eat cannot become impure as food, but cooked ones can.
Cites Leviticus 11:39, which makes one impure only through touching the carcass itself, not hide, bones, sinews, horns or hooves.
Rabba bar Rav Ḥana limits that derivation to meat puddings, and explains Rabbi Yitzḥak Nappaḥa's query as about a repulsive donkey hide.
Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yoḥanan dispute whether a placenta partly out of the womb is prohibited when a fetus is inside.
Asks whether Rabbi Yirmeya's report, that Rabbi Elazar's reading is stringent, contradicts this.
Restates Rabbi Elazar's view as a placenta not attached to the fetus inside, and Rabbi Yoḥanan's view, which Rabbi Yirmeya's report confirms.
A baraita following Rabbi Elazar gives the purity and impurity rules for a woman who expels a placenta with an animal fetus.
Mishnah: a firstborn-bearing animal's expelled placenta may be cast to the dogs.
Asks the reason for this ruling.
Rav Ika son of Rav Ami explains that most offspring can be firstborn, so the placenta is not from a firstborn.
Mishnah on sacred animals' placentas, and Abaye and Rava hold the Amorite prohibition covers practices without a medicinal reason.
Objects from a baraita permitting a tree to be painted and loaded with stones, which seems to be an Amorite practice.

78a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The stones weaken the tree during blossoming, so it can bear its fruit.
Asks why the tree is painted red, a practice of the Amorites, if it is permitted.
Explains the paint is applied so that people will see the tree and pray for it.
Cites a baraita on Leviticus 13:45, that one who suffers misfortune should announce it so the masses pray for him.
Ravina identifies the baraita's tanna as the one whose view supports hanging unripe dates on a palm, to bring communal prayer.
Mishnah: the prohibition on slaughtering an animal and its offspring on one day, with each combination of sacred and non-sacred animals inside and outside the courtyard.
