A baraita derives from Leviticus 22:27-28 that the prohibition on an animal and its offspring applies to sacrificial animals too.
Objects that the verse's repetition may limit the prohibition to non-sacred animals, or may extend it to kosher mixed offspring, and Rava begins to respond.

78b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The verse is a paradigm: wherever seh appears it excludes diverse kinds, so seh means sheep or goat only.
The verse says or, which the Gemara reads as including the offspring of diverse kinds.
Asks why or is needed, if not to include, and whether it is needed to separate prohibitions.
Objection: without the or one would be liable only for slaughtering a bull and its offspring plus a sheep and its offspring together.
Reply: separating the prohibitions is derived from the word its offspring rather than their offspring.
Objection that the or is still needed for a different teaching.
Baraita brought in support: a verse saying it and its offspring teaches that one is liable for each separately.
Asks whether the baraita's derivation really comes from the word or.
Answers that the derivation comes from the word it, not from or.
Asks how Ḥananya, for whom it is not superfluous, derives separating the prohibitions without the word or.
Answers that Ḥananya needs no verse for this, since he follows Rabbi Yonatan.
Baraita on cursing parents: the verse teaches liability for cursing either parent alone, per Rabbi Yoshiya.
Rabbi Yonatan holds that the verse implies each parent separately unless the Torah specifies both together.
Asks what the opinions of Ḥananya and the Rabbis are.
Baraita stating the two positions: the Rabbis limit the prohibition to females, Ḥananya extends it to males.
Asks what the reasoning of the Rabbis is.
Baraita's a fortiori argument from the mother bird with chicks, limiting the prohibition to females.
Refutes the inference: the bird case lacks prepared-versus-unprepared equivalence, unlike the animal prohibition.
Reply: the superfluous word it shows the prohibition applies to only one parent, restoring the inference.
Restates the conclusion that the prohibition applies only to females, as with the mother bird.
Proposes a possible refutation: it refers only to the parent to which its offspring clings, excluding the male.
Asks to what refutation the phrase if you wish to say refers.
Explains the refutation: if it denotes a male, the verse's its offspring still excludes the male parent.

79a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ḥananya derives from the verse's it and its offspring that the prohibition covers both a male and a female parent.
Concludes that the prohibition of a parent and its offspring applies to both males and females.
Shmuel rules in accordance with Ḥananya, consistent with his own reasoning in a mishna.
Mishna in Kilayim: Rabbi Yehuda permits animals born of mares with a donkey father to mate with each other.
Shmuel explains that this follows Rabbi Yehuda, who ignores paternity, while the Rabbis count both parents.
Asks who the Rabbis of that dispute are.
The Rabbis are Ḥananya, who considers paternity, so all mules form one species.
Raises whether Rabbi Yehuda is certain of his view or uncertain, and asks what practical difference this makes.
The difference is whether offspring may mate with the mother's species: permitted if certain, forbidden if uncertain.
Asks what the answer is to the dilemma, and turns to a source.
Mishna cited to resolve it: Rabbi Yehuda permits all mares' offspring to mate with each other.
Asks what the circumstances of this mishna are.
Explains that the mishna could refer to two donkey fathers, or to a horse and a donkey father, and asks which.
Argues the mishna teaches the permission for mixed fathers, so Rabbi Yehuda must be certain of his view.
Replies that the mishna may concern two donkey fathers, and the teaching is needed to prevent mixing species.
Baraita: Rabbi Yehuda forbids mating a mule in heat with a horse or donkey and assigns her a mule.
If Rabbi Yehuda is certain, why not mate her with her mother's species, and why does the baraita say of her kind.
The baraita means one may not use horse or donkey species since the mule's mother species is unknown.
Asks why one cannot check the mother species by distinguishing features.
Abaye and Rav Pappa give physical signs of the mother species: voice, ears, and tail.
Resolves that the case is a mule that is mute with its ears and tail cut off, so the species cannot be determined.
Asks what conclusion was drawn from this about Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua: all agree the offspring may not mate with its mother's species, showing uncertainty.
Concludes that Rabbi Yehuda is uncertain about the paternity question.
Rabbi Abba instructs his servant to pair mules with matching voices, ears, and tails, showing he holds paternity irrelevant.

79b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The distinguishing characteristics of species are relied on even against a prohibition mandated by Torah law.
Baraita: the mother and offspring rule applies to hybrids of diverse kinds and to the koy, with Rabbi Eliezer disagreeing.
Rav Ḥisda identifies the koy in the dispute as the offspring of a ram and a doe.
Asks what the circumstances of the koy's birth are.
If a goat mates with a doe, Rav Ḥisda says all agree the mother and offspring rule does not apply to a domesticated animal's offspring.
Proposes an alternative: perhaps a deer mated with a goat and the offspring was slaughtered with its mother.
Rav Ḥisda says all agree a deer mother's offspring is liable when the mother is a goat, so the alternative fails.
Actually the dispute concerns a koy from a goat-doe mating whose female offspring then bore a male koy.
The Rabbis require concern for paternity even for partial sheep, while Rabbi Eliezer ignores the father's component.
Why not say the disagreement is about paternity in general, since the dispute with Ḥananya is about that?
If it were only paternity, even the Rabbis would not apply the sheep rule to partial sheep, so the baraita teaches a new point.
A mishna forbids slaughtering a koy on a Festival and covering its blood, which seems to conflict with this view.
Asks what case the mishna addresses.
If a goat mates with a doe, the koy may be slaughtered and covered on a Festival, since its mother is a deer.
If a deer mates with a goat, the Rabbis' and Rabbi Eliezer's rulings would conflict on covering the blood.
Mishna follows the Rabbis, who are only uncertain about paternity, so they forbid slaughter and covering on a Festival.
Since the Rabbis are uncertain, Rabbi Eliezer must be certain that paternity is irrelevant for this koy.
A baraita on priestly gifts says Rabbi Eliezer exempts a koy hybrid, which seems to conflict with this view.
Asks what type of koy the baraita refers to.
If a goat mates with a doe, Rabbi Eliezer's exemption is consistent since paternity is ignored.
For the Rabbis, why must the owner give only half the gifts and not demand proof of paternity for the other half?
Explains that for the Rabbis the koy from a deer and goat owes half the gifts, the goat half.
If a deer mates with a goat, why does Rabbi Eliezer exempt the owner, rather than making him liable for all gifts?
Rabbi Eliezer is also uncertain whether paternity matters, so he too is uncertain about this koy.
If both the Rabbis and Rabbi Eliezer are uncertain, in what case do they actually disagree?

80a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Rabbis say the word sheep covers a partial sheep, while Rabbi Eliezer requires full descent from domesticated animals.
Rav Pappa concludes the koy cases on blood covering and priestly gifts fit only a deer-goat koy.
Explains that both sides are uncertain about paternity, so the disagreement is whether the partial sheep rule applies.
Rav Pappa finds the slaughter-on-one-day cases with a goat father or a deer father, the offspring of the koy.
Explains the goat-father case: the Rabbis forbid slaughter ab initio, with the sheep rule applying to partial sheep.
Rabbi Eliezer holds the partial sheep rule does not apply, so the deer-father koy may be slaughtered on the same day.
The Rabbis hold lashes apply even under uncertainty, since the partial sheep rule applies to the deer-father koy.
Rabbi Eliezer holds a prohibition exists in the case but no lashes, since it is a definite prohibition only for the offspring.
Explains that uncertainty about paternity means no definite forewarning, so Rabbi Eliezer gives no lashes.
Rav Yehuda says the koy is a separate kind, and the Sages did not decide if it is domesticated or wild.
Rav Naḥman says the koy is the wild ram, and a baraita records a tannaitic dispute with other identifications.
Rabbi Yosei gives the same undecided view as Rav Yehuda, a distinct kind not decided as domesticated or wild.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the koy is a domesticated animal.
Evidence: the house of Dushai raised koy flocks like other domesticated animals.
Rav Hamnuna says forest goats are fit for the altar because they are a kind of goat.
Supports this with Rabbi Yitzḥak's count of ten kosher animals, and goats are not listed among the wild animals.
Rav Aḥa bar Yaakov objects that forest goats may be a wild species not named in the verse.
Relies on the verse's detail and generalization rule, which makes the list of wild animals open-ended.
Responds that the details would be pointless if the generalization were meant, so the list is closed.
Objects that forest goats might be a wild goat, a wild species rather than a domesticated goat.
Further objects that they may be an aurochs or wild sheep, both wild animals.
Ameimar permits the fat of forest goats, which is forbidden for domesticated animals, so he treats them as wild.
Abba asks whether forest goats may be offered on the altar as domesticated animals.
Rav Huna says the disagreement of Rabbi Yosei and the Rabbis concerns only the wild ox.
Mishna and its gloss on the wild ox show all agree forest goats are goats and fit for the altar.
Repeats the objection that forest goats may be a wild goat, aurochs, or wild sheep.
Rav Naḥman cites Ameimar's permission of their fat as showing they are wild animals.
Quotes the mishna on how one slaughters an animal and its offspring.
Rabbi Oshaya says the whole mishna does not follow Rabbi Shimon.
Asks from where this is derived.
The mishna's ruling on sacrifices slaughtered outside, with both disqualified and lashed, shows it rejects Rabbi Shimon's view.

80b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If both sacrificial animals are slaughtered outside, why is the offender liable only for lashes and not for karet?
Mishna case: both non-sacred animals slaughtered in the Temple courtyard are unfit, with lashes for the second.
Given Rabbi Shimon's view that unfit slaughter is no slaughter, the lashes for the second animal seem unexplained.
Asks why the second animal incurs lashes when the first counts as mere killing.
Mishna ruling: for sacrifices slaughtered inside, the first is fit and exempt, the second gets lashes and is unfit.
Sacrifices too are unfit slaughter, since until blood is sprinkled the meat is not permitted, so the mishna's lashes conflict with Rabbi Shimon.
Asks why the second animal gets lashes and is unfit if the mishna follows Rabbi Shimon.
Objects that the conclusion that the mishna does not follow Rabbi Shimon is obvious and needs no analysis.
Explains Rabbi Oshaya needed to state this, since sacrifices slaughtered by Rabbi Shimon's standard would otherwise be fit.
Objects that the second animal should also be flogged for the prohibition of sacrificing before its time, which is not a definite violation.
Baraita: the verse Leviticus 22:23 teaches that all disqualified bulls and lambs violate the prohibition of not being accepted.
Asks whether the mishna lists unrelated prohibitions, since it does not list the prohibition of not being accepted.
Mishna does list unrelated prohibitions, namely the karet and lashes for sacrifices slaughtered outside the courtyard.
Asks why the first animal gets lashes if the lashes for it come from the outside-slaughter prohibition, not the prohibition of an animal and its offspring.
Where no animal-and-offspring prohibition applies the mishna lists unrelated prohibitions, but where it applies it lists only that one.
Rabbi Zeira says to set aside the prohibition of sacrificing before its time, since the verse itself addresses it.

81a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what the reasoning is behind the claim that this prohibition stems from a positive commandment
Leviticus 22:27 says an animal is acceptable as an offering only from the eighth day onward
So the prohibition is derived from a positive commandment, not a negative one carrying lashes
Asks whether this verse is actually needed for the view attributed to Rabbi Aptoriki
Rabbi Aptoriki finds a contradiction between the seven-days clause and the eighth-day clause of the verse
Asks how the two clauses can be reconciled
The night after the seventh day is fit for consecration, while the day from the eighth is fit for acceptance
A second verse in Exodus 22:29 sets out the same positive commandment
Rav Hamnuna reports that Rabbi Shimon held the prohibition on an animal and its offspring does not apply to sacrifices
Asks what the reasoning is for that position
Rabbi Shimon holds that unfit slaughter is not slaughter, and sacrificial slaughter is likewise unfit slaughter
Rava raises an objection from a baraita about slaughtering an animal and its offspring outside the Temple
The baraita states the positions of Rabbi Shimon and the Sages on whether a delayed-time offering violates a prohibition
The baraita is difficult: by Rabbi Shimon's logic the second animal should also incur karet
Rava replies that the baraita is incomplete and gives the corrected wording that resolves the difficulty
Corrected baraita: when both are sacrificed outside, the Sages hold the first incurs karet and the second is disqualified
Rabbi Shimon holds that both animals slaughtered outside incur karet
One outside and one inside: per the Sages the first incurs karet and the second is disqualified and exempt
Per Rabbi Shimon, the second animal in that case is kosher
One inside and one outside: per the Sages the first is kosher and the slaughterer is exempt
The second animal in that case is disqualified and the slaughterer is exempt
Per Rabbi Shimon, slaughtering the second animal outside violates a prohibition
Rava argues that if the prohibition did not apply to sacrifices, the second animal should incur karet too
Rava clarifies that Rav Hamnuna means the prohibition applies to sacrifices but lashes do not
Lashes do not apply because until the blood is sprinkled the meat is not permitted, so the forewarning is uncertain
Following his reasoning, Rava rules a non-sacred mother slaughtered first leaves the later peace offering unpunished
If the peace offering is slaughtered and its blood sprinkled first, the later non-sacred mother incurs lashes, and a burnt offering is exempt

81b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Even if one first offered a burnt offering and then slaughtered a non-sacred animal, he is exempt
Reason: the burnt offering's slaughter is not slaughter fit for eating, so it does not count as a prior slaughter
Rabbi Yaakov reports Rabbi Yohanan's view that consumption by the altar counts as consumption
Asks what the reasoning is for that view
Leviticus 7:18 repeats he'akhol ye'akhel, teaching that there are two kinds of consumption, human and altar
Mishna: Rabbi Shimon exempts one who slaughters a tereifa or forbidden animals, while the Sages hold him liable
Mishna: all agree that a carcass, stabbed animal, or one with its windpipe cut is exempt from the prohibition
Resh Lakish says the liability taught applies only when the first animal was slaughtered for idolatry and the second for food
Rabbi Yohanan rejects this, since even schoolchildren know one receiving two punishments gets only the greater one
Rabbi Yohanan's case: they forewarned him about the mother but not about idolatry, so lashes still apply
Resh Lakish explains that had he been forewarned about idolatry he would be exempt, so he is exempt here too
Rav Dimi's teaching: for unwitting violations of capital or lashes offenses, the dispute over monetary liability is stated
Rabbi Yohanan holds the unwitting offender is liable to pay in that case
Explains each sage's reasoning: Rabbi Yohanan says he sinned unwittingly; Resh Lakish says the lesser offense is exempt
Explains why both cases must be taught, showing each sage's position in the separate scenario
Asks whether the red heifer's slaughter counts as slaughter unfit for eating, as the mishna implies

ranges.en: Resh Lakish, citing Rabbi Yannai's view, holds the red heifer's slaughter is not valid slaughter, and Rav Shemen bar Abba relays Rabbi Yohanan's similar view

Resh Lakish says in Rabbi Yannai's name that the heifer whose neck is broken is not part of the mishna
Asks whether Rabbi Yannai really said this, since he elsewhere admitted forgetting the boundary of prohibition
Rabbi Yannai's own forgotten boundary suggests the heifer's descent to the valley, not its slaughter, is what forbids it

Amoraic dispute on when leper's birds become forbidden, with Rabbi Yohanan and Resh Lakish giving different moments, challenges the view
Asks what the reasoning of Resh Lakish is in that dispute

Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba relays that Rabbi Yohanan gave the resolution, not Resh Lakish, that the heifer is not part of the mishna
Mishna: two buyers of a cow and its offspring; the first buyer slaughters first, and the second must wait a day
Rav Yosef reads the mishna as concerning only a court judgment, not a prohibition on the second buyer slaughtering first
A baraita supports Rav Yosef: a second buyer who slaughters first is diligent and rewarded for eating meat that day
Mishna: slaughtering a cow and then both offspring incurs eighty lashes, while slaughtering the offspring first incurs forty
Mishna: slaughtering a mother and then granddaughter incurs eighty lashes, but granddaughter first then daughter incurs forty
Sumakhos, in Rabbi Meir's name, holds that slaughtering the daughter on the same day as its mother incurs eighty lashes
Asks why lashes apply to slaughtering offspring first, since the verse names the animal itself before its offspring

Explains how the plural verb for slaughter covers two different people slaughtering mother and offspring, each liable for the later act

ranges.en: Challenges the plural wording: the verse is needed for the basic prohibition, so why does the Torah write the plural here

Mishna: one who slaughters a mother, then her daughter's daughter, then the daughter, is liable to lashes
Abaye asks Rav Yosef what the reasoning is for Sumakhos holding that he receives eighty lashes
Asks whether Sumakhos holds generally that eating two olive-bulks of fat in one lapse brings two sin offerings
The mishna teaches Sumakhos's view in this case to show that the Rabbis exempt even with separate animals
Suggests Sumakhos may hold that a single lapse brings one sin offering, so this case would be different
Rav Yosef affirms that Sumakhos holds two olive-bulks in one lapse bring two sin offerings
Asks where Rav Yosef derives this from a baraita on sowing diverse kinds, and whether lashes are given twice
Asks whether the baraita's two lashes involve separate forewarnings, which the nazirite mishna already teaches
Asks which opinion the diverse-kinds baraita follows, since the Rabbis would exempt a second set of lashes
Responds that the baraita follows the Rabbis, who give lashes because he was forewarned before each sowing
The baraita also excludes Rabbi Yoshiya, so it gives no proof about the same prohibition violated twice
Suggests a mishna on the sciatic nerve: eighty lashes for two olive-bulks, while Rabbi Yehuda says forty
Asks what the circumstances are, and whether the two nerves were eaten separately with separate forewarnings
Rabbi Yehuda treats an uncertain forewarning as no forewarning, so the case must be one simultaneous act
A baraita on an uncertain father: striking or cursing one after the other, or both together, to show the uncertain forewarning rule
Rabbi Yehuda holds that sequential acts after uncertain forewarnings are exempt, so the mishna must be simultaneous
Asks who the first tanna is, since the Rabbis would exempt a second set of lashes in the sciatic nerve case
Responds that the mishna follows the Rabbis, and the tanna holds Rabbi Yehuda's view on uncertain forewarnings
A baraita shows the other tanna's view: Rabbi Yehuda holds that an uncertain forewarning counts, deriving from the Paschal offering verse

83a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda holds that the verse adds a positive commandment to burn leftovers, so no lashes apply for the prohibition on keeping them
Rabbi Yaakov says the reason is different: the prohibition involves no action, and lashes apply only to violations involving action
Suggests a sciatic-nerve baraita as a resolution of Sumakhos's view: eighty lashes, while Rabbi Yehuda says forty
Asks what the circumstances are, and why Rabbi Yehuda gives only forty if both acts were separately forewarned
Asks who the first tanna is; if the Rabbis, their view would conflict with their ruling on separate animals
Responds that he ate them separately after two forewarnings, and Rabbi Yehuda's forty applies when an olive-bulk is not reached
Mishna: on four pre-festival occasions the seller must tell the buyer that the mother or daughter was sold that day
Rabbi Yehuda says the duty applies only when there is no interval between sales, and concedes for the groom and bride
Mishna: on those four occasions the butcher is compelled to slaughter, so a bull's death falls on the buyer
A baraita adds that the buyer need not clarify, and may slaughter even if the seller did not inform him
Rabbi Yehuda restates when the seller must inform the buyer on those days
Asks why the mishna specifies the mother to the groom and the daughter to the bride rather than simply one each
Teaches in passing that the groom's household customarily spends more on the wedding, so he takes the larger mother animal
Restates the mishna: on those four occasions the butcher is compelled to slaughter, even against his will
Challenges that the buyer has not yet pulled the animal, so the animal should not yet belong to him
Rav Huna, citing Rav, says the case is one where the buyer did pull and so acquired the animal
If the buyer pulled, why does the mishna's later clause say the death falls on the seller for other days
Rabbi Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak says the buyer did not pull, and the seller acquires through another person for his benefit
Rabbi Elazar, citing Rabbi Yohanan, gives a different explanation: on those days the Sages relied on money effecting acquisition
Rabbi Yohanan says money acquires by Torah law, and pulling is a rabbinic decree against the seller's carelessness
Mishna: the day follows the night for the prohibition on an animal and its offspring, so the offspring may be slaughtered that night
Rabbi Shimon ben Zoma derives this by verbal analogy to the phrase one day in the account of Creation
A baraita attributes the same derivation to Rabbi Shimon ben Zoma, noting that the whole passage concerns sacrifices
Explains why the derivation is needed: sacrifices reverse the night and day order, so one might have assumed the same here

83b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi derives from the verse that a special day needs a proclamation, which underlies the four-occasions rule; chapter ends
Mishna: covering the blood applies in and outside Eretz Yisrael and to non-sacred animals and birds, but not to sacrifices; koy is uncertain
Asks what the reason is that blood of sacrificial birds need not be covered
Rabbi Zeira's teaching: the slaughterer must place earth below and above the blood, derived from the verse about covering with earth
Covering from below is impossible on the altar, and covering from above faces a similar problem, so Rabbi Zeira's reason fails
A baraita shows covering is required even without earth beneath, since blood of a domesticated animal underlies the undomesticated one
Rabbi Zeira's rule on meal offerings explains the exclusion: where proper performance is always impossible, the duty does not apply
Asks why one cannot scrape the altar blood and cover it elsewhere, as the mishna permits for blood spilled outside the pit
Scraping applies to altar-consecrated items; these birds are Temple-maintenance property, forbidden to slaughter, so no covering is required

84a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Challenges that the slaughtered bird of Temple maintenance could simply be redeemed and then its blood covered
Redemption requires setting and valuating before a priest, which a slaughtered bird cannot undergo, so it cannot be redeemed
Asks whose opinion the mishna follows, since both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon lead to contradictions about covering the blood
Rav Yosef reconciles by taking Rabbi Shimon on unfit slaughter and Rabbi Meir on valuation, so no covering is required
Alternatively the whole mishna follows Rabbi Shimon, and the verse's pour and cover wording excludes this blood
Now that this reading is possible, the mishna can concern altar birds, since the verse excludes blood lacking a further step
Mar bar Rav Ashi derives from the verse pairing undomesticated animal and bird that the bird cannot be consecrated
Asks whether the analogy should limit the bird law to species that cannot be consecrated, excluding doves and pigeons
Rejects this: the juxtaposition makes the bird law wholly like that of undomesticated animals, with no species distinction
Yaakov challenges Rava: a deer counts as domesticated for kosher signs, so a domesticated animal should count as undomesticated for covering
Rava replies that the verse equates the blood of domesticated animals with water, which needs no covering
Asks whether one could then immerse impure items in that blood as in water
The verse's exclusionary term shows that only the specified bodies of water purify, excluding blood
Suggests the exclusion only removes liquids not called water, so blood, which the verse calls water, could purify
Two exclusions are written, a spring of water and a cistern of water, and the extra term excludes blood
Argues both phrases exclude other liquids: one for flowing liquids, one for gathered liquids, so blood is not excluded
Three exclusions are written: spring, cistern, and gathering of water, with the last excluding blood
A baraita asks whether trapped birds that are already penned are included in the covering obligation, from the verse on trapping
The word trapping teaches that one should not accustom himself to meat that is not readily available
A baraita derives from Deuteronomy that one eats meat only by appetite and only from one's own flock, not bought goods
Rabbi Elazar ben Azaria sets a scale of meat purchases by wealth, with a weekly meat meal for the richest
Rav urges thrift, and Rabbi Yohanan notes Rav's family was healthy, so ordinary people should buy food promptly
Proverbs 27:26-27 is read to teach that one should provide his own food and sell fields to buy goats for income
Mar Zutra bar Rav Nahman says parents should not accustom children to meat and wine, and Rabbi Yohanan's view begins

84b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Advice: one who wants to grow wealthy should raise small livestock, since such flocks enrich their owners
Rav Hisda reads the word for flocks in Deuteronomy 7:13 as meaning that sheep make their owners rich
Rabbi Yohanan's advice: prefer cups of witches to lukewarm water in metal vessels, unless flavored or boiled
Rabbi Yohanan's advice for a man wishing to squander an inheritance: linen, glass, and unsupervised laborers
Rav Avira reads Psalms 112:5 as telling a person to live within his means and honor his household above that
Rav Eina rules that one who slaughters a wild animal or bird for a critically ill person on Shabbat must cover its blood
Rabba mocks Rav Eina's ruling as astonishing and dismisses it
A baraita states that a koy may not be slaughtered on a Festival, and Rabbi Yosei derives this a fortiori from circumcision
The Sages rebut the a fortiori argument with the shofar on Rosh HaShana in the provinces, which is not decisive
Rabbi Elazar HaKappar refutes the inference: circumcision is not performed on Festival nights, unlike covering the blood
Rabbi Abba notes that Rabbi Hiyya had no refutation of Rabbi Yosei's inference, but Rabbi Elazar HaKappar answered it
The baraita teaches that covering the blood is not required for a definite obligation overriding Shabbat, contradicting Rav Eina
Asks whether the baraita may refer to a healthy person slaughtered for on Shabbat, so the ill-person case still needs covering
Rabbi Yosei's comparison to circumcision shows the case must be one of permitted slaughter, so the baraita challenges Rav Eina
The Sages' rebuttal in the baraita: shofar sounding in the provinces shows the inference is incorrect, as the uncertain obligation overrides a Festival
Asks what uncertain obligation overrides a Festival, since a definite Rosh HaShana case would not bear on koy covering

85a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The shofar refutation concerns uncertain sex, as with a tumtum, who is obligated despite the uncertainty
Rabbi Yosei holds that a definitely female person may sound the shofar, deriving from Leviticus 1:2 that only sons lay hands on offerings
Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon hold that women may optionally lay hands on offerings and sound the shofar without desecrating the Festival
Ravina refutes the Sages: the shofar is definitely obligatory in the Temple even on Shabbat, unlike covering the blood
Rabbi Elazar HaKappar refutes Rabbi Yosei's inference from circumcision by noting its absence on Festival nights
Rabbi Elazar HaKappar meant that circumcision is not in effect at night, unlike covering the blood, and Rabbi Abba notes the refutation succeeded
Mishna: Rabbi Meir obligates covering blood from forbidden animals, while the Rabbis exempt ineffective slaughter and carcasses
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba relays that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi accepted Rabbi Meir's view on mother and offspring and Rabbi Shimon's view on covering
Asks what the reason is that Rabbi Meir holds ineffective slaughter counts as slaughter for mother and offspring

Asks what the reason is that Rabbi Shimon holds ineffective slaughter is not slaughter

Suggests Rabbi Meir could likewise derive from that word that only effective slaughter counts
Rabbi Meir derives terms of slaughter from other slaughter terms, not from the word for preparing
Asks why not derive from the Yishmael verbal analogy of returning and coming in leprosy of houses

Suggests Rabbi Shimon too could derive ineffective slaughter from sacrifices slaughtered outside the Temple
Rabbi Shimon derives non-sacred slaughter only from non-sacred slaughter, since the prohibition is primarily about non-sacred animals
Rabbi Meir replies that the prohibition does apply to sacrifices, so one can derive from sacrificial slaughter outside the Temple
Asks the reason Rabbi Meir requires covering blood in the case of ineffective slaughter
Resh Lakish derives this by verbal analogy of pouring from the blood of sacrifices slaughtered outside the Temple courtyard
Rabbi Shimon replies with the verse's phrase fit for eating, and Rabbi Meir answers that it excludes impure birds

ranges.en: Rabbi Abba says Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon's views on ineffective slaughter each have limited scope, as Meir concedes and Shimon concedes purity

Rabbi Abba's point is needed for Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who follows Meir on mother and offspring but the Rabbis on a fetus

Asks which of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's two rulings on the mother and offspring is the later, definitive one

ranges.en: Rejects the comparison: the students could not drink and bless at once, but covering and slaughtering can be done together by two hands

Rabban Gamliel obligates one who was preempted in covering blood to pay ten gold coins to the slaughterer
Asks whether the ten coins compensate for the stolen mitzva or for the stolen blessing, which affects Grace after Meals
A heretic's argument that separate deities made mountains and wind, rebutted by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi from Amos 4:13
Narrative: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi fasts awaiting the heretic, dines with another, and the cup of blessing is valued at forty gold coins
Rav Aha asks why the mishna's rule of covering only once differs from the rule of returning a lost item even a hundred times

Asks why the bystander is exempt when the wind covered the blood, given a baraita requiring covering for blood absorbed in the ground

ranges.en: Blood mixed with the blood of an undomesticated animal is judged as water, but Rabbi Yehuda holds blood does not nullify blood, so covering applies

The Gemara cites a mishna on sacrificial blood mixed with water or wine, and Rabbi Yehuda's view that blood does not nullify blood

Asks what Rav Yehuda is teaching, since the first two points are already taught in the mishnayot

Rabbi Asi of Neharbil applies Rav Yehuda to blood plasma, and Rabbi Yirmeya holds eating it is punishable by karet with an olive-bulk
A baraita holds liquids from a corpse are pure, except blood-tinged liquid, which imparts impurity in a tent
Raises a contradiction from a mishna on liquids from one who immersed that day, which have the status of liquids he touches

88a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Liquids from an immersed person and from those they touch are not impure, while other impurity sources transmit first-degree impurity to liquids

Sages decreed extra restrictions for a zav, since people do not separate from him, but not for a corpse, from which people keep apart
Baraitot on Leviticus 17:13 derive that blood spurting out or left on the knife must be covered, and Rabbi Yehuda limits this
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says the duty applies only if the blood of the soul was not already covered
Asks what matter the Rabbis, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel actually disagree about
The Rabbis read its blood as all of it, Rabbi Yehuda as any part, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel as the blood of the soul
Mishna: blood may be covered with fine manure, fine sand, lime, or crushed potsherd, but not thick or unprepared materials
Asks what counts as fine sand that may be used to cover blood

Asks what the practical difference is between the two versions of the definition
The versions differ on sand that crumbles by hand: permitted on one reading, forbidden on the other
A baraita derives from earth, with its verse, that manure, sand, crushed stones, and fine flax chaff are also permitted

88b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita continues the list of permitted substances, deriving from the word cover that the verse limits the covering to earth
Asks why the verse is read as a general and specific rule, and why it includes fine sand but not thick sand
Rav Mari rejects that reading: the generalization needs a detail, so the verse requires an absorbing substance, not a vessel
Rav Nahman bar Rav Hisda holds only seed-bearing substances may cover blood, which Rava calls an absurdity
Rav Nahman bar Yitzchak defends the view with a baraita on the desert and the ship, where desert sand is not permitted
Asks how a gold dinar may be ground to cover blood, if only earth or ash is permitted
Rabbi Zeira derives that gold dust is called dust from Job 28:6, so powdered gold counts as earth
Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute whether ashes are called dust, and the Sages add coal dust, stibium, and shavings to the list
The Gemara objects that Rava should apply the same consideration to covering blood as to the ashes and dust of ritual rites
Rava says Abraham's words, I am dust and ashes, earned his children the ashes of the red heifer and the dust of the sota

89a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Abraham's descendants were rewarded with two mitzvot, the fringe thread and the phylactery strap, for refusing the king's property.
Asks how the phylactery strap is understood to provide benefit.
Cites Deuteronomy 28:10 that all peoples see God's name upon Israel, supporting the strap's benefit.
A baraita teaches that the verse refers to the head phylacteries, which bear God's name.
Asks what benefit the sky-blue thread provides.
Rabbi Meir explains sky-blue resembles sea, sky, sapphire and the Throne of Glory.
Exodus 24:10 and Ezekiel 1:26 cited to show the heavens and the throne resemble sapphire.
Rabbi Abba states that stolen property already consumed cannot be returned, even by the righteous.
Genesis 14:24 cited: the young men ate what they took, so it could not be restored.
Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Elazar, says to listen closely to Rabbi Eliezer son of Rabbi Yosei's aggadic teachings.
Deuteronomy 7:7 cited: God chose Israel despite their being the fewest of all peoples.
God says Israel is beloved because they humble themselves even when God raises them up.
God raised Abraham, yet he humbled himself before God.
Genesis 18:27 cited for Abraham's humble self-description as dust and ashes.
Moses and Aaron were also raised, yet they too spoke humbly of themselves.
Exodus 16:7 cited for the humble words of Moses and Aaron.
The humble phrase is recalled, and David is introduced as likewise raised yet humble.
Psalms 22:7 cited for David's self-description.
David called himself a worm and not a man.
Gentile nations differ: God raised Nimrod, who then boasted.
Genesis 11:4 cited for Nimrod's plan to build a tower.
Nimrod's plan is quoted, and Pharaoh is introduced as likewise raised and boastful.
Exodus 5:2 cited for Pharaoh's denial of the Lord.
Pharaoh's denial is quoted, and Sennacherib is introduced.
II Kings 18:35 cited for Sennacherib's boast.
Sennacherib's boast is quoted, and Nebuchadnezzar is introduced as boasting.
Isaiah 14:14 cited for Nebuchadnezzar's claim to ascend above the clouds.
Nebuchadnezzar's boast is quoted, and Hiram king of Tyre is introduced.
Ezekiel 28:2 cited for Hiram's claim to sit in the seat of God.
Hiram's claim to sit in God's seat in the heart of the seas is quoted.
Rava, or in another version Rabbi Yochanan, introduces the next teaching on greatness.
What is said of Moses and Aaron is greater than what is said of Abraham.
Compares the Abraham verse with the Moses and Aaron verse to show their greater humility.
Rava, or Rabbi Yochanan, introduces a further teaching.
The world endures only in the merit of Moses and Aaron.
Cites Job 26:7, the earth hangs on nothing, to match the self-abasement of Moses and Aaron.
Rabbi Ile'a introduces his teaching on the verse.
The world endures only in the merit of one who restrains himself during a quarrel.
Cites Job 26:7, hangs the earth upon nothing, as the verse Rabbi Ile'a interprets.
Rabbi Abbahu introduces his teaching.
The world endures only in the merit of one who makes himself as if non-existent.
Deuteronomy 33:27 cited: the everlasting arms beneath everything uphold the world.
Rabbi Yitzchak introduces his interpretation of a verse.
Asks what the verse written in Psalms means.
Psalms 58:2 quoted as the verse being interpreted.
A person's occupation is to make himself silent like a mute.
Objection: one might think a person should be mute even about Torah teachings.
The verse teaches that one should speak righteous Torah words.
Objection: one who speaks Torah might become arrogant.
The verse adds 'with equity', so even a learned judge must take care in judging.
Rabbi Zeira, or Rabba bar Yirmeya, states a ruling about covering blood.
Blood of a wild animal or bird may be covered with dust of an idolatrous city.
Asks why this is allowed, since the ashes carry prohibited benefit.
Ze'eiri says the ruling concerns only the dust of the ground, not the prohibited ashes.
Deuteronomy 13:17 cited: the city's spoil is gathered and burned, which excludes this dust.
The dust lacks removal, gathering and burning, so it falls outside the prohibited category.
Rava says mitzvot were not given for benefit, so the prohibited ashes may be used.
Ravina was sitting and stating this halakha about covering blood with the ashes.
Rav Rehumi objects to Ravina with a baraita forbidding blowing an idolatrous shofar.
Asks whether the baraita means that one who blew it did not fulfill the obligation.
No: the baraita forbids it ab initio, but if one blew it, the obligation is fulfilled.
Rav Rehumi persists with a baraita forbidding taking an idolatrous lulav.
Asks whether the lulav baraita means one who took it did not fulfill the obligation.
No: forbidden ab initio, but if one took it, the obligation is fulfilled.
Objection: a baraita says a shofar or lulav of idolatry does not fulfill the obligation.
Rav Ashi defends Ravina: covering blood differs from the shofar and lulav cases.

ranges.en: Explains that ash for covering blood needs no minimum measure, unlike an idolatrous shofar or lulav.
Mishna: the sciatic nerve prohibition applies in and outside Israel, to sacred and non-sacred animals, but not to birds.
Mishna: the prohibition applies to a late-term fetus in the womb.
Rabbi Yehuda says it does not apply to a fetus, so its fat is permitted.
Rabbi Meir says butchers are not believed about removing the sciatic nerve.
The Rabbis say butchers are believed about the sciatic nerve and the forbidden fat.
Asks whether it is not obvious that the prohibition applies to sacred animals.
Suggests the sciatic nerve imparts flavor, so the sacred-meat prohibition takes effect on it.
The mishna should have said the sacred-meat prohibition applies to the nerve.
Rather, the tanna holds the nerve imparts no flavor, so only the nerve prohibition applies to sacred animals.
A mishna on a thigh cooked with the nerve shows the nerve does impart flavor.
Rather, the mishna deals with offspring of sacred animals, which are consecrated in the womb.
The tanna holds both prohibitions take effect together, so neither cancels the other.
Can the first clause refer to a fetus? The latter clause implies it does not.
The tanna's point is that the first clause is a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis.
Both prohibitions cannot take effect together, citing a mishna on nazirite impurity from a corpse's olive-bulk.
The olive-bulk clause seems unnecessary, since a whole corpse would obviously require shaving.
Rabbi Yochanan says the clause is needed only for a miscarried fetus whose limbs were not yet joined to sinews.

90a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Evidently the prohibition on sacrificial meat precedes the prohibition on the sciatic nerve.
Even so, the sciatic nerve prohibition takes effect on consecrated offspring, since it also binds Noahides.
Asks whose opinion this reasoning reflects.
Rabbi Yehuda's view does not fit the mishna, which applies the prohibition to both thighs.
The tanna agrees with Rabbi Yehuda that it binds Noahides, but disagrees that it covers only one thigh.
If Rabbi Yehuda's view is that the nerve prohibition takes effect on an already forbidden animal, then the answer fails.
Rather, the mishna speaks of a firstborn, which becomes sanctified only as it leaves the womb.
Alternatively, the mishna speaks of all offspring, which become sanctified only at birth.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Yosef says the nerve prohibition applies only to sacrificial animals that are eaten.
Rabbi Yochanan says the nerve prohibition applies to both eaten and non-eaten sacrificial animals.
Rav Pappa resolves the dispute: one case concerns flogging for eating, the other bringing the nerve up on the altar.
Some say Rav Pappa resolves it differently: one case concerns burnt offerings, the other removing the nerve.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak says the dispute is whether the nerve may be brought up while still attached to the thigh.
A baraita cites Leviticus 1:9 to include bones, sinews, horns and hooves on the altar.
One might think even detached parts are burned on the altar.
Deuteronomy 12:27 cited: only the flesh and blood are offered upon the altar.
If only flesh and blood are offered, one might think the sinews must be removed first.
Leviticus 1:9 cited again: the priest burns all of it, including sinews and bones.
Asks how these verses are reconciled.
Attached parts ascend; if detached, they descend even if already at the top of the altar.
Asks which tanna holds that detached parts descend.
A baraita attributes the view to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and cites Leviticus 1:9 to include detached parts.
Asks how the Deuteronomy verse is then to be understood.
The Deuteronomy verse refers to parts dislodged from the fire: flesh is returned but sinews and bones are not.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says one verse includes sinews and bones, and another excludes anything but flesh and blood.
The verses cited: Leviticus 1:9 includes all, and Deuteronomy 12:27 limits to flesh and blood.
Reconciling them: attached parts ascend, and detached parts descend even on top of the altar.
The Rabbis hold attached parts need no verse, so the inclusive verse is needed only for detached parts.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds that attached sinews and bones, which may be eaten, are brought up.

90b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that the verse is needed for the sciatic nerve still attached to the flesh, which is brought up.
The Rabbis cite Ezekiel 45:15: offerings come only from what is permitted to Israel for eating.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi compares the nerve to forbidden fat and blood, which are offered anyway; the Rabbis distinguish them.
Rav Huna says a burnt offering's sciatic nerve is removed and placed on the ash mound, not left on the thigh.
Rav Hisda objects: is it written that the altar does not consume the nerve? Rather it says the children of Israel do not eat it.
Genesis 32:33 cited: therefore the children of Israel do not eat the sciatic nerve.
Rav Huna holds that the Ezekiel verse bars sacrificing the nerve, since it is not permitted for eating.
A baraita says a burnt offering's nerve is brought up to the altar, which seems to contradict Rav Huna.
The baraita means the nerve is removed on the altar, since the whole leg must be offered intact.
Malachi 1:8 cited: offer a defective or unattractive gift to your governor, which excludes the whole leg with the nerve.
A baraita supports Rav Huna: a peace offering's nerve is swept away, and a burnt offering's is placed on the ash mound.
A mishna is cited describing the ash mound, which held up to three hundred kor of ashes.
Rava says that description is an exaggeration.
A mishna is cited about giving the daily offering water in a golden cup.
Rava says that description is also an exaggeration.
Rabbi Ami says the Torah, Prophets and Sages each sometimes spoke in exaggerated language.
Deuteronomy 1:28 cited: cities great and fortified up to heaven, an exaggeration of the Torah.
The Prophets also spoke in exaggerated language.
I Kings 1:40 cited: the earth rent with the sound, an exaggeration of the Prophets.
Rabbi Yitzhak bar Nahmani relays Shmuel: the Sages exaggerated in three cases, the ash mound, the vine and the Curtain.
A mishna describing the golden vine at the Sanctuary entrance, cited as the vine example.
Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Tzadok says three hundred priests were needed to move the vine.
A mishna on the Curtain is cited: its thickness, weave, size, cost and the three hundred priests who immersed it.
The mishna teaches the nerve prohibition applies to the right and left thighs.
The mishna is not in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, who says only one thigh's nerve is forbidden, the right.
A dilemma: does Rabbi Yehuda consider the right thigh obvious, or is he uncertain between the two?
A mishna on Paschal offering leftovers is cited, asking why sinews are listed separately and burned.
Rav Hisda resolves it: the sinews of the neck are listed, and the mishna follows Rabbi Yehuda's single thigh view.
If Rabbi Yehuda is uncertain, both nerves must be burned; if the right is obvious, the left may be eaten.
Rav Ika bar Hanina: the right thigh is obvious, but here the nerves were identified and then mixed together.

91a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Ashi says the burning ruling concerns only the fat around the nerve, which is permitted but treated as forbidden.
Ravina says the ruling concerns the outer nerve, following Shmuel's teaching transmitted by Rav Yehuda.
Shmuel holds there are two nerves: the inner one is forbidden by Torah law, the outer one only by rabbinic law.
A mishna is cited on eating an olive-bulk from each thigh: Rabbi Yehuda gives forty lashes, others eighty.
If Rabbi Yehuda is uncertain, the forewarning is uncertain, so he should not impose any lashes.
A baraita on an uncertain father shows Rabbi Yehuda does not count an uncertain forewarning.
This tanna follows the other tanna of Rabbi Yehuda, who holds an uncertain forewarning does count.
Exodus 12:10 is cited: leftover sacrificial meat is burned, and one is not flogged for leaving it over.
Rabbi Yaakov says the reason is that leaving meat over is a prohibition without an action, so no flogging.
A baraita on eating two nerves from two animals: Rabbi Yehuda gives forty lashes, the first tanna eighty.
From the baraita's wording, both nerves must be from the right thigh, so it is obvious to Rabbi Yehuda.
If the right nerve is obvious to Rabbi Yehuda, why does he give only forty lashes?
Here the nerve is less than an olive-bulk, and Rabbi Yehuda requires an olive-bulk for flogging.
Asks what the reason is that only the right thigh's nerve is forbidden by Torah law.
Rava cites Genesis 32:33: the definite article refers to the most important thigh, the right.
The Rabbis hold both thighs are forbidden, and the article excludes only the outer nerve.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says the verse shows the angel wrestled in a way that reached the right thigh.
Genesis 32:26 cited: the angel wrestled with Jacob.
The angel hugged Jacob, his hand reaching to the spoon of his right thigh.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nahmani says the angel appeared as a gentile, placed to Jacob's right.
Rav Shmuel bar Aha says in Rava bar Ulla's name the angel appeared as a scholar, placed on the right.
The Rabbis hold both thighs are forbidden, since the angel came from behind and struck both.
Asks what the Rabbis derive from the phrase as he wrestled with him, since it is needed for another reading.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi says the dust of their feet rose to the throne of glory.
Nahum 1:3 cited: the clouds are the dust of God's feet, matching the wording as he wrestled.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains the name: the nerve departed from its place and rose.
Jeremiah 51:30 cited: their might has left them and they became as women, supporting the nasha wordplay.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina asks about the meaning of a verse in Isaiah.
Isaiah 9:7 cited: a word sent to Jacob and fallen upon Israel, read as the sciatic nerve.
The word sent to Jacob refers to the sciatic nerve, whose prohibition spread to all of Israel.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina asks about the meaning of another verse.
Genesis 43:16 cited: Joseph told the steward to slaughter and prepare the meat.
Joseph had the nerve removed before the brothers, a practice that applied before the Torah to Noahides.
Genesis 32:25 cited: Jacob was left alone.
Rabbi Elazar says Jacob stayed for small pitchers, showing the righteous value property and avoid stolen goods.
Genesis 32:25 cited: a man wrestled with him until the break of dawn.
Rabbi Yitzchak says a scholar should not go out alone at night, as Jacob was injured then.
Rabbi Abba bar Kahana says the source for that instruction is the same verse.

91b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ruth 3:2 cited: Boaz winnowing barley at night, the basis for not going out alone at night.
Rabbi Abbahu cites Genesis 22:3: Abraham waited until morning to set out, so a scholar should not travel at night.
The Rabbis cite Genesis 37:14: Jacob sent Joseph during daylight, showing a scholar should not go out alone at night.
Rav cites Genesis 32:32: Jacob stayed the night and left in the morning.
Rabbi Akiva recounts asking Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua in the meat market about the sun shining on Jacob.
Asks why the sun shone only for Jacob, since it shone for the whole world.
Rabbi Yitzhak says the sun shone early for Jacob because it had set early for him.
Genesis 28:10-11 cited: Jacob left Beersheba for Haran and encountered the place.
Jacob thought he should have prayed at the place of his fathers, and the land contracted for him.
Genesis 28:11 cited: he encountered the place.
God says the righteous man came to His lodging, so the sun set early to make Jacob stay overnight.
Genesis 28:11 and 28:18 cited: he took stones, then one stone, a contradiction.
Rabbi Yitzhak explains that the stones gathered into one place and were absorbed into one rock.
Genesis 28:12 cited: Jacob dreamed of a ladder set on the earth.
Asks how wide the ladder was.
It was eight thousand parasangs wide.
Genesis 28:12 cited: angels ascending and descending, in plural forms.
The plural forms indicate two angels ascending and two descending at once.
When they met, four angels were in one place, so the ladder had to be that wide.
Daniel 10:6 cited: an angel whose body was like Tarshish.
Tarshish is two thousand parasangs, and angels gazed at Jacob's image above and below.
Genesis 28:13 cited: the Lord stood over him.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish says the verse is hard to utter, since God is depicted as shielding Jacob like a father.
Genesis 28:13 cited: the land upon which you lie, I will give to you.
Rabbi Yitzhak explains the promise: God folded all of Eretz Yisrael under Jacob so his children could conquer it.
Genesis 32:27 cited: let me go, for the dawn has risen.
Jacob asks the angel whether he is a thief or a gambler who fears dawn.
The angel says he is an angel who had not yet had the time to sing praise until now.
Rav's teaching: three groups of angels recite the Holy each day, each saying a different part of the verse.
A baraita objects: the Jewish people are dearer than the angels, who sing praise only rarely.
Deuteronomy 6:4 cited: Israel mentions God's name after two words.
The angels mention God's name only after three words.
Isaiah 6:3 cited: holy, holy, holy is the Lord of hosts.
The angels do not sing above until Israel sings below.
Job 38:7 cited: the morning stars sang together, referring to Israel and the angels.
Rav's version: one group says holy, another holy holy, and a third holy holy holy is the Lord of hosts.
An objection: Ezekiel 3:12 has Blessed, the name of God, as the third word.

92a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara answers that the ofanim say the verse, and the three-word permission was extended to shorter praise.
Hosea 12:5 cited: Jacob strove with an angel, prevailed, wept and made supplication.
Asks who became master over whom, since the verse does not say.
Genesis 32:29 cited: you strove with angels and men and prevailed.
Jacob became master over the angel, since the angel is the one who wept.
Asks who wept to whom, since the verse does not say.
Genesis 32:27 cited: let me go, for the dawn has risen.
The angel wept to Jacob, since the verse says he struggled with him.
Genesis 32:29 cited: you have striven with angels and with men.
Rabba says the angel hinted to Jacob that two princes would come from him, one in Babylonia, one in Eretz Yisrael, and exile.
Genesis 40:10 cited: in the vine were three branches.
Rav Hiyya bar Abba says in Rav's name the branches are three proud princes, and the sages look to Rabbana Ukva and Rabbana Nehemya.
Rava says the branches are three angels who plead for Israel in each generation.
A baraita: Rabbi Eliezer says the vine is the world, the branches the patriarchs, the blossoms matriarchs, clusters the tribes.
Rabbi Yehoshua objects: a dream shows only what will be in the future, not the past.
Rabbi Yehoshua says the vine is the Torah, the branches Moses, Aaron and Miriam, and the clusters the righteous.
Rabban Gamliel says the verse needs Rabbi Elazar HaModai's explanation, which places all of it in one place.
Rabbi Elazar HaModai reads the vine as Jerusalem, the branches as Temple, king and High Priest, and clusters as libations.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi reads the vine as Torah, the branches as the well, pillar and manna, and the clusters as libations.
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba reads the vine as the Jewish people, a reading supported by Psalms.
Psalms 80:9 cited: you plucked a vine out of Egypt and planted it.
The branches are the three pilgrimage festivals, and the blossoms show the time for Israel to multiply.
Exodus 1:7 cited: the children of Israel were fruitful and multiplied.
The blossoms show the time for Israel's redemption.
Isaiah 63:3 cited: I have trodden the winepress and redeemed My raiment.
The clusters show the time has arrived for Egypt to drink the cup of punishment.
Rava explains the three cups in Pharaoh's dream as three cups of punishment for Egypt.
Rabbi Abba tells Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba that Rav interpreted these verses the same way.
Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish likens the nation to a vine: homeowners support, scholars are grapes, ignoramuses are leaves.
This is why they asked from there to pray for the leaves, since without leaves the grapes could not survive.
Hosea 3:2 cited: so I bought her for fifteen pieces of silver and barley.
Rabbi Yohanan says the word kira means a sale, as in Joseph's burial in the grave Jacob acquired.
Genesis 50:5 cited for the word kariti, a purchase, in the same sense as the fifteen.
The fifteen refers to the fifteenth of Nisan, the redemption date, and silver to the righteous.
Proverbs 7:20 cited: he has taken the bag of silver with him, referring to the righteous taken away.
The barley counts forty-five righteous individuals in whose merit the world exists.
Asks whether thirty are in Babylonia and fifteen in Eretz Yisrael, or the reverse.
Zechariah 11:13 cited: I took the thirty pieces and cast them into the house of the Lord.
Thirty are in Eretz Yisrael and fifteen here in Babylonia.
Abaye says most of the fifteen Babylonian righteous are in the synagogue under the upper room.
Zechariah 11:12 cited: they weighed my hire, thirty pieces of silver.
Rabbi Yehuda says the thirty are righteous among the nations, in whose merit the nations endure.
Ulla says the thirty are the mitzvot the descendants of Noah accepted, but they keep only three.

92b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continues Ulla's point: the gentiles' three mitzvot, and that a bird has no sciatic nerve prohibition.
Asks: we see a bird does have a protrusion on its thigh, so why no prohibition?
Rabbi Yirmeya's dilemma: does the nerve status follow the individual animal or the species? Left unresolved.
The mishna's fat is permitted according to everyone, Shmuel says.
Asks: which fat? If it is the nerve's fat, the tanna'im already disagree about that.
The tanna'im disagree about this, as a baraita shows.
A baraita: Rabbi Meir forbids the nerve and fat of a late-term fetus, Rabbi Yehuda permits them.
Rabbi Elazar, citing Rabbi Oshaya, explains the dispute concerns a nine-month fetus, following each sage's general view.
Perhaps Shmuel refers to the fat of the nerve itself, where the tanna'im also disagree.
A baraita on scraping the nerve: Rabbi Meir cuts out the fat from its source, Rabbi Yehuda only to the flesh.
Shmuel refers to the nerve's fat, which Rabbi Meir holds is permitted by Torah law but forbidden by rabbinic law.
A baraita quoted: its fat is permitted, but the Jewish people treat it as forbidden.
Asks whether this baraita must be Rabbi Meir's view, permitted by Torah law and forbidden rabbinically.
This cannot be Rabbi Yehuda's view, since Rabbi Meir would forbid it by Torah law too.
A baraita: one scrapes around the nerve and its fat is permitted.
Scraping is Rabbi Meir's view, so he must hold the fat is permitted by Torah law and forbidden rabbinically.
Rav Yitzhak bar Shmuel bar Marta says Rav holds the Torah forbade only the tendril-like fibers.
Rav holds the Torah forbade only the tendrils of the nerve, which are not food.
Ulla says the nerve is like wood, yet the Torah makes one liable for eating it.
Abaye says the halakha follows Ulla, which is reasonable.
Rav Sheshet cites Rav Asi: the strands of veins in forbidden fat are forbidden, but no liability.
Here too the Torah says the nerve, not its tendrils, so the same reasoning applies.
Restates the principle: strands of veins in the fat and in the kidney are forbidden, but no liability.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Hiyya disagree on whether the white kidney fat is forbidden.
Rabba and Rabbi Yohanan scrape the white fat from the kidney.
Rabbi Asi cuts it from the surface of the kidney but does not scrape it out.
Abaye says the halakha follows Rabbi Asi, citing Shmuel's teaching transmitted through Rav Yehuda.

93a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Fat covered by flesh is permitted.
Leviticus 3:4 read as covering only the fat above the loins and kidneys, not the fat inside them.
Rabbi Abba, citing Rav Yehuda and Shmuel, says the fat covered by flesh is permitted.
Asks: is that so, given Rabbi Abba's statement that the fat under the loins is forbidden even when covered?
Abaye: in a live animal the limbs separate at the joints, so the loin fat is not covered by flesh and stays forbidden.
Shmuel holds the omasum and reticulum fat, the coccygeal fat and the veins of the foreleg are forbidden, with karet.
Rav Safra and Rava each object that the Torah does not forbid meat or prohibit blood in this way.
The veins are forbidden because they are filled with blood, so salting or roasting them removes the prohibition.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, says the fat on the top cubit of the small intestine must be scraped away.
Rav Yehuda says the five sinews of the tail are forbidden as fat, and must be drawn out warm or scraped.
Abaye, or Rav Yehuda, says three of the five strands are forbidden for fat and two for blood.
Asks what difference it makes whether a strand is forbidden for fat or for blood.
Blood-strands can be made permitted by cutting and salting them, while fat-strands cannot be rectified.
Rav Kahana, or Rav Yehuda, lists five membranes, three for fat and two for blood.
Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya peels a spleen's membranes for Levi, cutting only the upper surface.
Rav Huna bar Hiyya says Rav's teaching, transmitted through Rav Yirmeya bar Abba, prohibits only the membrane on the upper surface.
Rav Yirmeya bar Abba holds the Torah prohibits only the membrane on the spleen's thick upper surface.
Levi asks: did Rav Hamnuna not teach that the spleen membrane is forbidden without karet?
Asks what the baraita means: if it is the upper membrane, why is there no karet?
Rav Huna bar Hiyya tells Levi: if the baraita is taught, it is taught, and he cannot dispute it.
Rav Hamnuna cites a baraita: the spleen and kidney membranes are forbidden, but no karet.
But a baraita says one is liable to karet for the spleen and kidney membranes.
The contradiction is resolved: one baraita concerns the upper thick part, the other the other part of the spleen.
The same resolution applies to the kidney membrane: upper and lower parts.
Rav Ami and Rav Asi dispute whether crushed testicles still attached to their cords are permitted.

93b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the two views on crushed testicles: one sees them as severed limbs, the other as merely weakened.
Rabbi Yohanan tells Rav Shemen bar Abba the crushed testicles are permitted.
Proverbs 1:8 cited: do not forsake your mother's teaching, so he should refrain from eating them.
Mar bar Rav Ashi: goat testicles are permitted until thirty days, then depend on whether they contain semen.
Asks how one can know whether the testicles contain semen.
Red streaks in the testicles mean they are forbidden; without them they are permitted.
Rav Aha and Ravina disagree on three cases, and the halakha follows Ravina except in these three.
Explains the three cases: salting or roasting removes blood, coals may draw it out or harden it inside.
On removing hair by ashes: the head is permitted if blood can flow out through the neck or nostrils.
Some say the head is permitted if placed on its nostrils or the slaughter point, or if opened to let blood out.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, says the inner nerve is forbidden by Torah law, the outer only rabbinically.
But a baraita says the inner Torah-forbidden nerve is next to the flesh.
But a baraita says the outer nerve is next to the bone.
Rav Yehuda: this refers to where butchers cut the leg open, where the outer nerve is closest to the bone.
If a butcher leaves forbidden fat, Rav Yehuda says a barley-grain amount makes him liable, Rabbi Yohanan an olive-bulk.
Rav Pappa: they do not disagree, since one speaks of flogging and the other of removing him from being a butcher.
Mar Zutra's resolution, and the halakha: an olive-bulk for flogging, a barley grain for removing the butcher.
The mishna: butchers are not deemed credible about the sciatic nerve, says Rabbi Meir; the Rabbis say they are.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Abba says Rabbi Yohanan said the Rabbis retracted to say butchers are credible.
Rav Naman's question is answered: earlier, scraping was arduous, so butchers were not credible; later they were.
Some teach the latter clause as including the forbidden fat: the Rabbis say butchers are credible about both.
Rabbi Yohanan says the Rabbis retracted, and Rav Naman says today butchers are credible.
Earlier they followed Rabbi Yehuda, so butchers were credible; later Rabbi Meir, so they were not, until they forgot his view.
The mishna's view on the fat: Rabbi Meir says butchers are not credible about the nerve and the fat; the Rabbis say they are.
Mishna: a Jew may send a whole thigh with its nerve to a gentile, because the nerve's place is visible.
Asks what case the mishna means: if butchers do not announce a tereifa sale, it would be forbidden to buy from gentiles.

94a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Since no one buys a cut thigh from a gentile, the whole thigh may be sent only where sales are announced, and not otherwise.
Option one: where tereifot are announced, a whole thigh may be sent, since Jews could tell gentile cutting apart.
Option two: where tereifot are not announced, a cut thigh is forbidden as a decree against sending it in front of a Jew.
A third reason: sending it deceives the gentile, and Shmuel forbade deceiving people, even a gentile.
Shmuel's ruling is only inferred, not stated, from an incident: he rebuked his attendant after paying a ferryman.
Asks why Shmuel was angry: the gift was a tereifa chicken, or diluted wine given in an undiluted vessel.
If it is inferred by Shmuel's view, what does that prove, since the anger may have another cause?
Shmuel may have been angry simply because the attendant disobeyed his instructions.
A baraita: Rabbi Meir forbids insincere invitations, gifts a person will refuse, and opening sold wine barrels for a guest.
Asks: but Ulla visited Rav Yehuda, who opened sold barrels for him.
Rav Yehuda told Ulla beforehand, or Ulla was especially dear to him, so he would have opened them regardless.
A baraita forbids bringing a nearly empty wine jug to a mourner, or filling it with water; a crowd makes it permitted.
A baraita forbids selling a sandal from a natural death animal as slaughtered, for deception and snakebite danger.
A baraita forbids sending wine with oil floating on top; a host who could not provide oil hanged himself.
A baraita: guests may not give food to the host's children without the host's permission.
A story of three guests and three eggs: the child died, then the mother and father died as well.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says three Jewish souls were killed over this matter.
Asks what this statement teaches, since three deaths are already obvious from the incident.
It teaches that the entire baraita is taught by Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.
A baraita on sending a thigh: a whole thigh needs no sciatic nerve removal; a cut one does, and gentiles need none.
Two reasons not to sell a gentile unslaughtered or tereifa meat: it deceives him, and he may resell it to a Jew.
Similarly, one may not ask a gentile to buy meat for him from a Jewish butcher, for two reasons.

94b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Restates the baraita's two reasons for not selling a gentile unslaughtered or tereifa meat, and the no-removal case.
Asks what case this is: if it is where sales are announced, why need the nerve not be removed from a cut thigh?
It must be where sales are not announced, where a Jew would not buy from a gentile.
The middle clause gives two reasons: it deceives the gentile, and he may resell to another Jew.
If it is where sales are not announced, no Jew would buy, so the latter clause makes no sense; it must mean where they are announced.
The latter clause about buying meat with a dinar would then be pointless where sales are announced, so it fails the same test.
Could the first and latter clauses refer to unannounced places, while the middle clause refers to announced ones?

Rava objects that a permitted item that absorbs will eventually become forbidden, so one eats the forbidden.
Rava distinguishes between items that can be tasted to nullify and those that cannot.
Rav Papa objects that a Persian could taste it, and points to the mishna on cooking in a pot.
Cites the mishna on a pot in which meat was cooked, which may not be used for milk, and the teruma rule.
Explains that teruma is tasted by a priest, but for meat in milk there is no taster, so the Persian is hypothetical.
Reports Rav and Shmuel disagreeing on whether fish that were cooked in a dish may be eaten with sour milk.
Rav holds that such fish are forbidden because they impart flavor, while Shmuel holds they are permitted.
Clarifies that Rav's view was not stated explicitly but only implicitly.
Narrates that Rav visited Shimi bar Chiya's house, where a fish dish was served after his son had eye trouble.
Relates that R' Elazar stood before Shmuel, who was served fish in a dish and ate it with sour milk.
Rav asks whether Shmuel withdrew his ruling.
Shmuel replies that he does not hold that view and asks not to be bothered.
Narrates that Rav Huna and Rav Chiya bar Ashi were seated across the river, and Rav ate fish in sour milk.
Relates that Rav was served figs and grapes mid-meal and ate them without a blessing.
Rav rebukes his companion that the orphan's master did so, and the companion replies similarly.
Rav replies that he holds like Shmuel, and then that he holds like R' Chiya.
Quotes R' Chiya's baraita that bread exempts all kinds of food and wine exempts all kinds of drink.
Reports Chizkiya citing Abaye that fish cooked in a dish is permitted to be eaten with sour milk.
Holds that a radish cut with a knife used on meat is forbidden to eat with sour milk, referring to radish.

112a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that sharp pickled items absorb flavor, so cucumber and radish dishes differ in what is permitted.
States that bread soaked in these items is fine, as the flavor is permitted.
Rav Dimi asks Rav Naḥman whether a jar of salted food may be placed beside a jar of vinegar.
Rav Naḥman replies that it is forbidden because of the vinegar.
Rav Dimi reports Rav Naḥman's reply that it is permitted.
Asks what distinguishes the case where one eats from the salted jar, and what the reason is.
Explains that the forbidden item has its prohibition present in its substance, while the other does not.
Narrates that a young pigeon fell into a jar of vinegar, and Rav Chinena, son of Rava of Pashronia, permitted it.
Rava asks who is wise enough to permit a case like this, and whether Rav Chinena's view is correct.
Explains Rav Chinena's reasoning from Shmuel's teaching that salted food is like hot food.
Limits that rule to cases where the food is not edible because of its salt, while this vinegar is edible from its salt.
Adds that this applies to raw food, while roasted food needs a peel, and seasoned food is forbidden whole.
Reports Rav Naḥman citing Shmuel that a loaf cut with a knife that touched meat is forbidden to eat.
Qualifies the rule as applying to cases where the meat is fattened, flavored or fattening, but not to a flat bread.
Reports that Shmuel threw the loaf to his dog.
Rav Huna reasons that whichever way the rule goes, it applies to all people equally.
Holds that Rav Huna is an exception, since his mind was at ease, and Rava ate it and called it meat wine.
Rav Naḥman citing Shmuel holds that one should not place a vessel under meat until the reddish color is gone.
Asks how we know this rule.
Cites Mar Zutra in the name of Rav Pappa that the rule applies until the smoke rises.
Rav Ashi objects that the lower part may have reached the upper part, which is not the case.
Rav Ashi holds that the only remedy is to throw in two lumps of salt.

112b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Acha son of Rav Ika objects to Rav Ashi, citing Shmuel that a loaf cut with a knife touching meat is forbidden.
Explains that the case is different, since the knife's pressure in cutting releases the flavor.
Rav Naḥman holds that fish and fowl salted together are forbidden to one another.
Asks what the case looks like: in a vessel without holes, fowl with fowl is also forbidden.
Explains that in a perforated vessel even fish and fowl are permitted, since the fish releases its juices first and the fowl absorbs them afterward.
Narrates that Rav Mari bar Rachel salted raw meat from a slaughtered animal together with meat of a non-kosher animal, and brought the case to Rava.
Rava cites the verse on unclean animals, and concludes that their sauce and brine are forbidden.

113a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Proposes deriving the answer from Shmuel's ruling that salted food is like hot food and pickled food like cooked food.
Replies that from Shmuel one would only infer the rule for meat, not for brine and sauce.
Raises a baraita: a clean fish salted with an unclean fish is permitted, which seems to refer to both being salted.
Notes that the latter clause, marked by its wording, shows the first clause concerns cases where both are salted.
Clarifies the baraita: a clean fish salted with an unclean fish is permitted, and asks how this works.
Explains the baraita as one where the clean fish is salted and the unclean one is bland, which is the sensible reading.
Asks whether the latter clause is taught to exclude the reading that the first clause covers only one salted item.
States that if both are salted, the combination is forbidden.
Explains the baraita teaches the latter clause to reveal that the first clause still permits even when both are salted.
Brings a proof from the latter clause: an unclean salted item with a clean bland one is forbidden, implying both salted is permitted.
Explains that the baraita repeats its pattern in the latter clause, so the reversed case is also taught.
Gives a mnemonic for the rule about the meat that is salted and then placed in the pot.
Shmuel holds that meat does not lose its blood unless salted and rinsed thoroughly.
Rav Huna holds that the baraita teaches salting then rinsing, while another version teaches rinsing then salting.
Reconciles the views: one case has the butcher cut the meat and the other did not.
Narrates that Rav Dimi of Neharde'a salted meat with coarse salt and shook it out.
Rav holds that blood is not retained in the intestines, and Shmuel adds the dispute over how meat is placed.
Shmuel holds that salted meat may be placed only on a perforated vessel.
Asks why Rav Sheshet salted two bones, and what the reason for doing so is.
Explains the reason is not that one bone separates while the other absorbs, but that the other has no effect.
Shmuel states in the name of R' Chiya that breaking an animal's joint before it dies makes the meat heavy and robs people and absorbs blood.
Asks whether the case is only forbidden because it absorbs blood in the limbs, or also forbidden for him; the question is left unresolved.
Mishna: one who brings a fowl together with cheese onto the table does not transgress a negative commandment.
Concludes from the mishna's formulation that eating fowl with milk is forbidden by Torah law.
Reinterprets the mishna: bringing the fowl onto the table with cheese does not lead to transgressing the prohibition.
Mishna: meat of a clean animal with milk of a clean animal is forbidden to cook and to benefit from, while with an unclean animal it is permitted.
R' Akiva holds that beasts and fowl are not included in the Torah prohibition, citing the verse about a kid in its mother's milk.
R' Yosei the Galilean derives from two verses that fowl is excluded, as it has no mother's milk.
Asks from where these rules are derived.
R' Elazar derives the rule from the verse about Judah sending the kid of the goats.

113b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains that the verse about a kid of goats, read as a general term, includes cow and sheep, as another verse shows.
Repeats the principle that a general kid includes cow and sheep, and that the verse teaches this.
Holds that two written verses that come together do not teach anything by themselves.
Asks how this works for the view that they do teach, and what other reading there is.
Shmuel expounds several inclusions and exclusions from the repeated kid verses, such as milk, the dead animal, and the afterbirth.
Asks why three kid words are written when the Gemara expounds six.
Shmuel holds that a prohibition takes effect on a prohibition, and the blood and afterbirth are not part of the kid, so the verses are divided.
Objects that Shmuel also said that a prohibition does not take effect on a prohibition, which seems contradictory.
Cites Shmuel in the name of R' Elazar: a priest made impure who eats impure teruma is not liable to death, derived from the verse about profaning.
Explains that a prohibition takes effect on a prohibition, and that the verse in the teruma case is an exception.
Explains that Shmuel holds a prohibition does not take effect on a prohibition, and the kid case is an exception.
Notes that these are the positions of the speakers and their teachers.
