Rav Acha bar Ami asks Rav whether one who cooks a kid in milk from a goat that never nursed is liable.
Rav replies that Shmuel needed to state in its mother's milk, not male milk, since a male is not a candidate for inclusion, but this one is.
Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi disagree on whether one who cooks milk in milk is liable to lashes.
Proposes that the dispute concerns whether a prohibition takes effect on a prohibition.
Rejects that reading: all agree on eating, and the dispute is only whether one is flogged for cooking.
Explains that the dispute on cooking follows whether cooking is a single prohibition, so the Torah used the term cooking.

114a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concludes that since one is not flogged for eating, one is also not flogged for cooking.
Notes that some say all agree one is flogged for cooking, and the dispute concerns eating.
Explains the two views: one holds no prohibition takes effect on a prohibition, the other holds the Torah used the word cooking for eating.
Argues that if one is flogged for cooking, one is also flogged for eating, and the two Sages' views do not really conflict.
Cites a baraita: cooking blood, bones, or sinews in milk is exempt, but cooking forbidden items such as the piggul, notar or impure is liable.
Explains that the baraita's author holds a prohibition takes effect on a prohibition, so cooking in milk water is exempt.
Supports Resh Lakish from the mishna that milk water is like milk and diluted oil is like oil.
Resh Lakish holds that mishna is only for qualifying seeds, and that milk water is not like milk for cooking meat.
Asks from where we learn that the prohibition covers cow and sheep, not only the mother's milk.
Gives a kal vachomer: if the mother is forbidden with her young by mating, then a cow and sheep forbidden by mating are forbidden by cooking, so the verse is needed.
Asks why the verse is needed if the derivation follows from this argument.
Rav Ashi explains the derivation may be refuted at first, so one must bring it from the mother's slaughter, not the cow's.
Cites a baraita: milk of the mother is forbidden, and by kal vachomer, the older sister's milk is forbidden with cooking.
Asks again why the verse is needed in that case.
Rav Ashi again explains that the derivation from the mother's slaughter is needed, so the verse is required to teach the mother's milk.
Derives that the younger sister is also forbidden from the older sister and the mother by kal vachomer.
Concludes that a sister's flesh and cooking in milk share the same prohibition, so the derivation is valid.
Asks why, if the younger sister is included, the verse about the mother's milk is needed.
Cites a baraita: the verse about the mother's milk is needed to exclude others from the prohibition.

114b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: States the case of the mother herself cooked in her own milk.
Gives a kal vachomer: where one fruit with another fruit is not forbidden by slaughter, a fruit with its mother is, so the verse is needed for cooking.
Asks why the verse is needed if the derivation already follows.
Rav Achadvoi bar Ami analyzes the case of a mule and a horse and other pairs, to show why the verse is needed to forbid cooking.
Rav Idi bar Avin and Rav Ashi argue from mixed seeds and from the difference between one body and two bodies, concluding the verse is needed.
Rav Ashi derives from the verse that meat with milk is forbidden for eating, and that cooking is also forbidden by the general term.
Asks why, if the general prohibition covers all forbidden things, the verses for eating and for benefit are distinguished.
R' Avahu, citing R' Elazar, explains that each prohibition on eating also includes a prohibition on benefit, unless the verse specifies otherwise.
Cites a baraita on carrion: the stranger and the gentile differ in giving and selling, and R' Meir holds both cases are forbidden.
R' Yehuda holds the words are read as written, so a stranger receives by giving and a gentile by selling.
R' Meir explains the verse is needed to give priority to giving to the stranger over selling to the gentile.
R' Yehuda holds that the verse is not needed for that priority.
Gives the reasoning: one is commanded to keep one alive and the other is not commanded to do so.
Gives a mnemonic listing the mishna's cases such as Sabbath, plowing, mixed seeds, and sending away the nest.
Asks, then, whether the derivation can be made otherwise.

115a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Holds that Sabbath labor is not forbidden to be done on the Sabbath, since it is an abomination of God.
Quotes the verse that the Sabbath is holy to you, and that its work is not holy, which shows the Sabbath is distinct.
States that plowing with an ox and donkey, and muzzling an ox, are not forbidden, as they are abominations to God.
Reasons a fortiori: if Sabbath work is permitted, then mixtures of seeds are clearly permitted.
Shows from the verse on vineyard mixtures that mixtures of seeds are permitted, since the verse singles out the vineyard case.
Objects that the vineyard mixtures may be forbidden for eating and benefit, while seed mixtures are forbidden for eating only.
Cites the verse on animals and fields: animal mating and field sowing are linked, so the offspring of each is permitted.
Asks how we know that mixing animals themselves is forbidden.
Explains that the Torah forbids the animal and its young, and sending away the nest is permitted, as the Torah did not say it leads to a stumble.
States that the Torah did not say to send away the nest to cause stumbling.
Resh Lakish derives from the verse on the Passover offering that meat with milk is forbidden, with cooking on its own counting as a distinct cooking.
Asks which combination is meat with milk.
R' Yochanan replies in response to the question.

115b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Introduces the teaching that R' stated, using the word like this.
R' reasons that the verse about meat in milk may be read as applying to any forbidden item in the Torah, not only meat and milk.
Explains the principle that a teaching is derived by the thirteen exegetical rules, deducing from the matter itself.
Asks what the verse speaks of.
Answers that it speaks of two kinds, and would otherwise have applied only to eating, so the verse teaches benefit too.
Derives from the verses on holiness that R' holds the prohibition also covers benefit, following R' Eliezer's exposition.
Cites the school of R' Yishmael: the verse on carrion teaches that one may not cook or sell it.
Cites a baraita: the verse about kid in its mother's milk teaches three prohibitions, for eating, benefit, and cooking.
Cites Issi ben Yehuda: meat with milk is forbidden by the verse linking holiness with the prohibition on the torn flesh.
Argues a fortiori from orlah, which is forbidden for benefit though no sin was done in it, to meat in milk.
Objects that the plowing example could show otherwise, since sin was done with those animals and yet they are permitted.
Asks why the orlah case should not prove it instead, and why the mixture of seeds is the one to derive from.
Rav Ashi suggests the carrion case proves it, since it is forbidden for eating and permitted for benefit.
Rav Mordechai relays the teaching of Resh Lakish: one can refute a derivation from its own matter, but not from outside.
Asks why the mixture-of-seeds case cannot be refuted, since it too has big ground.
Rav Mordechai relays Resh Lakish's view that a refutation of the derivation counts only when both cases are the same.
Rav Mordechai repeats the teaching in Resh Lakish's name for the case of all the items.

116a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Sets out the rules for when one may refute a derivation by an analogy, from one matter or from several.
Objects that the mixture of seeds case cannot be refuted by the vineyard case, since vineyards lacked the time of growth.
Rav Adda bar Ahava says the vineyard mixture was forbidden originally, and the time of growth was before the rooting.
Rav Shemaya bar Zeira raises an objection from the mishna on a perforated pot placed in a vineyard, which depends on whether it adds two hundred.
Abaye explains that two verses are written, so the case is resolved by whether one planted the seed originally or it was added.
States that the mishna does not follow this tanna, as a baraita teaches otherwise.
Cites a baraita of R' Shimon ben Yehuda in R' Shimon's name: meat with milk is forbidden to eat and permitted to benefit from.
Introduces R' Akiva's view that beasts and fowl are included in the prohibition.
Explains that R' Akiva holds one prohibition takes effect on another, so the verses are read to include all, excluding beast and fowl.
Presents R' Yosei the Galilean's view that the verse states the prohibition, with no exception for beasts.
Asks what the difference is between R' Yosei the Galilean and R' Akiva.
Explains that R' Yosei holds that the beast prohibition is Torah law, while R' Akiva holds it is rabbinic.
Offers that the difference lies in fowl: R' Akiva holds beasts and fowl are rabbinic, while R' Yosei holds fowl is not forbidden even rabbinically.
A baraita reports that in R' Eliezer's place they cut wood to make charcoal, and in R' Yosei's place they ate fowl in milk.
Narrates that Levi visited Yosef Rishba's house, where a dish of fowl in milk was served, and he said nothing.
R' asks Levi why he did not rebuke them.
Levi replies that this is Rav Yehuda ben Batyra's place, and he had taught according to R' Yosei the Galilean's view that fowl lacks milk.
Mishna: the cheese of a gentile, or of a carcass, is forbidden, but one who lays the cheese on the skin of a kid is permitted.

116b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Cites a baraita: a cheese-maker's kid that nursed from a forbidden animal is forbidden, but a kosher one is permitted since its milk is gathered in its stomach.
Asks whether a gentile's kid is not in fact a carcass.
Rav Huna answers the case is one of buying a kid from a gentile, where we fear it nursed from a forbidden animal.
Objects from a mishna that one buys eggs from gentiles without concern for carrion or torn animals, so the concern is only for impure animals.
Asks why impure animals are a concern while torn animals are not, since impure ones are common.
Explains that the rabbis decreed where the buyers keep their distance but not where they cannot check, so the rule is practical.
Shmuel holds that a gentile's slaughtered kid is a carcass, as the baraita states one thing.
Objects that Shmuel did not say so, since Shmuel said the cheese of gentiles is forbidden because it is set in the kid's skin.
Explains that the prohibition is because the cheese is set in a carcass's skin, while the kid itself is permitted.
Resolves the contradiction: one case is before the return of the animal and one after it.
Gives the baraita's remaining ruling that a kosher milk-bearer that nursed from a torn one is permitted.
Objects from the first clause that a gentile's kid is forbidden, and Rav Chisda says it looks like one eating carrion, with slaughter involved here.
Rava objects that this is a fortiori: if one permitted the carcass's milk, one would come to eat it, and a torn slaughtered animal would be permitted too.
Rav Yitzchak, citing R' Yochanan, resolves the difficulty: one case is before the return and one after, and the mishna remains unchanged.
R' Chiya bar Abba cites R' Yochanan: one may set in the milk of carcasses, but not in the milk of a gentile's slaughter.
R' Shimon bar Abba objects that this follows R' Eliezer, who holds a gentile's intention is idolatry, and asks whose view it is.
On the return of Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak, R' Yochanan rules one may set in both, and the halakha is that one may not set in the skin of a carcass.
Explains that one may not set in the skin of a carcass; the milk gathered in its stomach is only extra fluid.
Mishna: a difference in stringency applies to milk versus blood, and milk is more stringent than blood in its prohibition.

117a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishnah: misuse and forbidden-fat liability apply to blood-free kosher domestic animals; blood is stricter in other respects
Asks where these rulings about misuse and the fat are derived from
Rabbi Yannai derives misuse liability for peace-offering fat from the bull verse, linking it to the sin-offering bull
Rabbi Chanina objects that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi already derived it from the verse about all fat belonging to God
Abaye defends Rabbi Yannai's derivation as necessary to include the diaphragm and kidneys, which the other verse omits
Rav Mari argues that if a sheep tail counts as fat, it should be forbidden for eating
Rav Zevid replies that forbidden fat is only what appears equally in ox, sheep and goat, excluding the tail
Rav Ashi explains the tail is called a fat tail but is not simply fat
The Gemara objects that by this logic benefit from the tail would not incur misuse liability either
Concludes that Rav Zevid's explanation is the correct one
Mishnah continues: unlike fat, benefiting from blood does not incur misuse liability
Asks from where this blood rule is derived
Ulla's derivation from the word 'to you' and the school of Rabbi Yishmael's derivation from 'to make atonement'
Rabbi Yoḥanan derives the same rule from the repeated word 'it is', comparing before and after atonement
Objection: 'it is' could equally mean the blood is subject to misuse both before and after atonement
Response: no item whose mitzva was performed remains subject to misuse, so the objection fails
Counterexample: the removal of altar ashes has its mitzva performed yet still involves misuse liability
Ash removal and the High Priest's Yom Kippur vestments are exceptions, two verses coming together, so no general rule follows
Difficulty: if the vestments are exempt only per the Sages, why is ash removal not a general paradigm for R' Dosa
Ash removal and the red heifer are two verses coming together, so they share an exception that cannot generalize
Asks whether this answer holds for the view that two verses together do teach a shared rule to other cases

117b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why three separate verses are needed if each one only excludes a single prohibition from blood
Each of the three verses excludes blood from one category: notar, misuse, and impurity, but not piggul
Piggul needs no verse, since a mishna teaches that anything whose blood can release it incurs piggul liability
Closing formula of the chapter, followed by the opening words of the next mishna on what is in the chapter
Mishna: skin, gravy, stomach, sinews, bones, hooves and horns join to convey food impurity but not carcass impurity
A slaughtered impure animal sold to a gentile conveys food impurity but not carcass impurity until it dies
Until the animal dies or its head is cut off, it conveys food impurity only, not carcass impurity
Rabbi Yehuda holds that a gathered piece of meat with an olive's bulk in one place is liable
The Gemara cites a baraita that establishes the distinction between light and severe impurity for seeds and fruits
Asks from where we know this distinction
The school of Rabbi Yishmael derives it from the verse on seeds sown in the way of people, with their husks
Seeds are not kept for severe impurity, as the baraita concludes
Asks from where we know that a carcass with no olive's bulk of flesh is not kept for severe impurity
The Sages derive it from the verse on the carcass, excluding a skin with no olive's bulk of flesh

118a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: One might think touching flesh from behind does not convey impurity, but the verse says it does
Asks what the mishna's wording is meant to teach
Raba explains the mishna is missing words, and the skin is completed to an olive's bulk by the flesh
Derivations that skin with an olive's bulk is not excluded, and a mishna on what conveys impurity as a hand or guard
Asks where these inclusions of hands are written
Two verses on seeds and on carcasses include the hands, which the Torah derives from the wording of each
Hands and guards need no verse to be included or excluded, the principle is set out
A kal vachomer from the hand shows the guard joins to convey impurity, so why is it written
Proposes the alternative that a hand excludes and a guard includes, reversing the roles
Rejects that alternative: the reading cannot stand, since the roles are fixed as before
Asks whether exiting needs to be derived once entering is already established
Proposes that a hand excludes, a guard includes, and points out a superfluous hand in the verse
The verse on the oven and stoves includes the handles, supporting the scheme of inclusion
Asks which of the verses would then be superfluous
Working out the a fortiori comparisons between seeds, ovens and carcasses by their impurity and transmission
Objection: deriving seeds from the others fails, since seeds convey impurity only once prepared
Rav Huna's answer: fruits not made susceptible resemble an oven whose work is unfinished
The objection is renewed: the others convey impurity without touch, so seeds should too, and so for food
Asks why the carcass hand is needed at all if it bears no relation to the carcass
Proposes relating it to an ordinary hand instead, while the carcass hand is still needed
Had the carcass not been written, one would say the case is governed by the analogy, so the verse is needed
Objection: just as those do not convey impurity to a person, a carcass should not either
Resolves that the carcass hand and guard serve as a kal vachomer that excludes and includes by the hand

118b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Proposes that if the carcass guard is irrelevant, the ordinary guard should be the one that enters and joins
Asks why the carcass guard is needed at all, if the hand was written for entering
Objects: if the guard is meant for joining, the reasoning fails, since it would not join
A kal vachomer from the hand shows the verse was needed to teach entering and exiting, so the ordinary guard is similar
Principle that where a verse can be expounded it is expounded, and Rav Chaviva's view on the carcass guard
Rav Yehuda bar Yishmael objects: a pomegranate pit joins for impurity, so why read the verse as covering all seeds
Three verses are cited, one each for seeds, trees, and meat, eggs and fish
Rav and Rabbi Yoḥanan state their positions on whether a hand conveys impurity and whether it conveys susceptibility
Asks what the two positions actually disagree about
Explains the disagreement as one about whether a verse is expounded before or after its face, or about reasoning
A baraita is cited supporting Rabbi Yoḥanan: hands convey both impurity and susceptibility, just as detachment matters
Rav holds a hand needs at least an olive's bulk and a guard at least a double measure, while Rabbi Yoḥanan differs
A baraita objects: two bones with half-olives each join to an olive, so how can two bones join

119a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks how Rav reads the ruling, specifically whether it concerns the hand
Objects that on the hand reading the first clause is difficult, and on the guard reading the second is
Offers resolutions: the mishna concerns the guard, or the hand, depending on whether one follows the first Tanna or Rabbi Yehuda
A baraita: Rabbi Yehuda says a clump with an olive's bulk of meat conveys impurity throughout, others say a double measure suffices
Asks again how Rav interprets the same ruling
Objects that on the hand reading the second clause is difficult, and on the guard reading the first is
Resolves the difficulty by aligning each position with one of the Tannaim, and Raba explains the measure is stated because the clump is a guard case
Rabbi Ḥanina holds the given measure is a fixed measure, while Rabbi Yoḥanan denies it is a measure
Explains the double measure is given because the first Tanna mentioned a measure, so the others do too
Baraitot on bean sauce and on the verse about seeds, showing that a seed's husk and its use determine impurity
Rav Oshaya asks whether the case is different, to resolve the earlier baraita

119b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what the case of two guards on each other is, and whether a guard can sit on a guard at all
Objects that the mishna's clause on onion skins shows a guard on a guard is not counted as one wrapping
Rav Oshaya asks whether a guard that eats a piece of the case joins when each shields only itself
Baraitot on bean sauce and on the seed verse, read as showing that hand and guard both bear on the case
Objects that the upper clump needs the lower one, but the lower one does not need the upper, since an olive's bulk eats in one spot
Explains the case by the wheat of Shimon ben Shetach, where a single wheat grain is likewise counted
A baraita with two bones and two half-olives, where Yehuda ben Nekosa cites Rabbi Yaakov on bones joining to an olive
Resh Lakish holds bones join only when they are a hand, while Rabbi Yoḥanan says even a thread counts as a hand
Rabbi Yoḥanan objects to Resh Lakish from a skin case, and Rav Acha bar Yaakov extends the objection to tefillin
Explains the objection was misplaced: Western sources say a hole the ink passes through is not a hole, and the case turns on the hand
Asks where Rabbi Elai's ruling about husk threads was stated and what those threads are for
Rabbi Elai explains the threads serve as a guard, as is reasonable, and another version says the same
Objects that if the matter were about the hand, one thread would serve no purpose
Rabbi Elai's comparison between threads and husks is cited, together with the mishna on husk-threads of ears
Rabbi Elai's ruling on the threads between the husks is restated, and another version of the teaching is noted

120a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: skin, gravy and stomach join together to convey food impurity
Resh Lakish limits the joining to a bone that acts as a guard, while Rabbi Yoḥanan says any object acts as one
Resh Lakish asks whether a guard can sit on a guard, and Rav Acha presses the point with tefillin
Rav Acha's point was misplaced: in the West any hole the ink passes over is not counted as a hole
Rabbi Yoḥanan objects to Resh Lakish: the fleshy part should convey impurity by guard, not by hand
Rabbi Elai's ruling on the threads of husks is cited as an analogy for the guard reading
Asks what gravy is
Raba answers that gravy means fat
Abaye objects that the gravy itself should convey impurity, so why does the ruling require it to congeal
Explains that gravy on vegetables counts for purposes of settling the mind, whereas here joining requires it to congeal
Rabba explains kipa as a kind of mustard, a spice
Abaye objects that the kipa itself should convey food impurity
Rav Pappa answers that kipa means a spice, as the mishna there shows
Mishna: one who wraps blood and eats it, or licks fat and swallows it, is liable for karet
Explains that wrapping blood and eating it is an eating only because wrapping counts as an act of consumption
Resh Lakish's verse covers drinking, supported by a baraita on chametz, where drinking it makes one liable for karet
Explains the baraita on chametz by the bread of affliction and by whether matzah lacks drinking
Resh Lakish's verse of nefesh is cited again, with a baraita on a clean bird carcass that is drunk
Objects that if drinking is covered, sun-steeping should also count, but it rots rather than is consumed
Kal vachomer arguments on why fat, chametz and carcass each need their own verse, given their differing status
Objects that each verse could be derived from the others, and that priests received fat of beasts from the altar
A baraita cites the impure items, their gravy and their kipa, as ruled forbidden
Asks why the rule needs to be taught at all, if the case can be learned from the others
Analogy: since the Torah wrote the case, the sentences cover the same measure of an olive's bulk, as in the other case

120b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that creeping things could be the source, but they convey impurity from a minute amount, so the derivation fails
A baraita: the liquids that come out of terumah, first fruits, sanctified items and other produce are of the same kind as those fruits
Asks from where we know this
Objects that the derivation may come from the others, but those are prohibitions that come on their own, which differs
Rabbi Yosi derives from the word bring that the first fruits themselves are brought from the produce of grapes and olives
Objects that first fruits, unlike other offerings, require recitation and placement, so no derivation follows
Derivations from the verse on terumah and first fruits, and a mishna on which fruits are liable, with the disagreement set out
Rabbi Eliezer's position that liquids from all kinds of produce follow the same rule, versus Rabbi Yehoshua's narrower reading
Rabbi Yehoshua's reasoning that only oil and wine extend the rule, supported by mishnayot on first fruits and on the forty stripes for orlah

121a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara again brings a derivation for orlah from the wording on fruit and first fruits
Asks what the word clump means
Rabbi Yoḥanan says the clump is a kind of bone-marrow, Resh Lakish says it is meat the knife expelled
Objects with a verse from Job calling physicians worthless, which bears on whether the clump can heal
Resolves that the verse concerns what has no healing power, so the disagreement is about the clump in the mishna
A baraita from Rabbi Yehuda: a gathered clump with an olive's bulk in one place incurs liability
Rav Huna says this applies only if one gathered the clump together
Explains that on Resh Lakish's view the liability arises only at an olive's bulk, and the disagreement is among the Sages
Rabbi Yoḥanan holds the clump also joins, while Resh Lakish holds only meat expelled by the knife joins
Asks what the case of meat expelled by the knife actually is
Explains the case: if one intends it, it is impure even alone, and if not, it is nullified
Rabbi Avin and Rabbi Mesha give opposing views on whether part of the clump was intended or expelled
A mishna on the snout and claws, citing the principle that the snout is wood
Rabbi Elazar, Rav Pappa and Rabbi Elazar on lower parts and horns, and Rabbi Asi on the slaughter of impure animals
Asks why preparation is needed at all, if the item's end is severe impurity
Explains that whatever ends up conveying severe impurity needs no preparation, and the seed verse makes the same point
Baraitot from the school of Rabbi Yishmael on seeds and from Rabbi Yosi on why a clean bird carcass needs intention but not preparation

121b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Hezekiah holds that since the item can be dragged and reduced below an olive's bulk, it is treated accordingly
Objects that Hezekiah could not have said this, since the case of two cuts or most of two cuts still twitching was taught
Hezekiah and Rabbi Yoḥanan disagree on whether a slaughtered animal that still twitches counts as limbs or as dead
Objects that the animal has left the category of living without yet entering the category of dead
Restates the case of two cuts still twitching, with Hezekiah ruling it is not limbs and Rabbi Yoḥanan ruling it is
Rabbi Elazar says to hold Rabbi Yoḥanan's view, as Rav Oshaya taught, and a long baraita on impure animals slaughtered by gentiles and on what may be eaten
Rabbi Elazar asks whether the knife's delay in the animal or its trampling makes a difference
An old man cites Rabbi Yoḥanan that the animal needs preparation, and Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak explains that preparation means checking the knife
Rabbi Zeira asks Rav Sheshet whether the animal's impurity protects the absorbed parts inside it
Rav Sheshet answers that it conveys food impurity and protects, but does not convey carcass impurity
Abaye holds it does not protect the absorbed parts, and Rav Huna holds that two halves of olives on the skin nullify each other

122a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the view that a skin does not nullify is attributed to Rabbi Yishmael or to Rabbi Akiva
Explains that by Rabbi Yishmael the skin nullifies only when a living animal expelled the clump, not a knife
A baraita: Rabbi Yehuda says a gathered clump with an olive's bulk in one place is liable, and Rav Huna says this is when it was gathered
Objects that if a knife-expelled clump is not nullified by Rabbi Yishmael, Rav Huna's view must fit Rabbi Akiva, which is obvious
Explains Rabbi Akiva's reasoning: the skin nullifies the clump only when it is expelled by a knife, as the closing clause shows
Mishna lists skins that are impure or pure, and Ulla states that the skin of a human is pure by Torah law
Explains the rabbinic decree making the skin impure: a person might turn his parents' skins into rugs
Ulla's ruling is repeated with differing mishna versions, and the disagreement is whether the opening or closing clause is the Torah-based impurity
Asks in what the Sages disagree about the skin of a pig
Positions on whether the skin of a soft camel is one that needs to be carried, and when its time to be carried arrives
Abaye asks whether a camel whose time to be carried has not arrived but was carried is soft, which is left undecided
Rabbi Yishmael bar Abba cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that it applies while the animal has not been carried
Ravin bar Ḥinnana cites Ulla that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's teaching concerns the time the camel has not been carried
Rebukes the speaker that one point was enough, and points to the difference between the pious of Babylon and the strong land of Israel
Ulla holds the calf's head skin is impure until the calf is a year old, while Rabbi Yoḥanan holds until it nurses
Asks how Ulla can say a year old and nursing together

122b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether Ulla spoke of a calf that nurses or of one a year old, and whether Rabbi Yoḥanan agrees
Explains Ulla's view covers both nursing and not nursing, while Rabbi Yoḥanan requires a year old and nursing
Cites a teaching of Rabbi Yoḥanan that the rule holds while the calf nurses, as the wording shows
Resh Lakish asks Rabbi Yoḥanan whether the calf's head skin conveys impurity
Rabbi Yoḥanan says it does not convey impurity
Resh Lakish objects that the mishna itself teaches the calf's head skin is like flesh, so it should convey impurity
Rabbi Yoḥanan replies not to annoy him with a single-opinion wording, since he teaches it as a baraita
Baraitot on the skin under the tail of a burnt offering, and on the many tannaitic views of which skins count as flesh for impurity
Asks what the hoof-house skin is
Rav reads it literally as the hoof-house, while Rabbi Ḥanina says it is the ridge sold together with the head
Baraita on the verse listing unclean creatures, which includes their skins as flesh, with Rav's point on the tanashmet
Objects that the tanashmet is in the Tanna's list, but our Tanna does not teach it
Rav Sheshet explains the Tanna follows Rabbi Yehuda, who relies on the view about the lizard
Mishna: skins prepared or used for walking are pure; whether a skin walked on is required for the rule
Objects with a baraita from Rabbi Ḥiyya that the ear of a donkey is pure even without walking
Rulings on the measure of walking used for work, for kneading, prayer and washing hands, namely four miles

123a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Positions on whether one who walks behind, or less than a mile, must return to a place for the measure of work, citing Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina and Rav Acha
A baraita on a legion moving from place to place: a house entered by it is impure, and Rabbi Yishmael's skull is an example
Mishna: one who flays an animal, pure or impure, must flay enough to lay the hide on a mat, and Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri disputes the neck skin
Asks what Rav's view is on the point after which the flayed skin is no longer connected
Rav holds the flayed skin is pure, while Rabbi Asi holds a handbreadth adjacent to the flesh is impure
Objects with a baraita: one who touches the flayed part is pure, so even a handbreadth next to the flesh should be pure
A second baraita: skin opposite the flesh is impure, while a handbreadth adjacent to the flesh is pure
Explains the case concerns the first handbreadth, since the Tanna sets the grip measure at a handbreadth
Objects that another baraita says two handbreadths are needed for a grip
Abaye answers that the measure is a doubled handbreadth, and a baraita says so too
Mishna: a garment begun to be torn is no longer connected once most of it is torn, and so is pure
Rav Nachman, citing Rabbah bar Avuh, limits the rule to a garment worn on the day of immersion, and gives the reason for the decree
Rabbah gives two answers to the question, the first being the concern that people would say a day-old immersion counts

123b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Elazar bar Rabbi Shimon's decree on a bird burnt offering: the rule is enacted lest one fail to do most of the act
Rav Yosef objects that a decree about a garment torn after immersion would apply equally, and asks why the decree is needed for the flayer
Explains that touching impurity is purified just as a Torah-level impurity is, so the same reasoning applies here
Asks what case we are dealing with here
If it is a rabbinic impurity, pure and impure go as expected, but a Torah-level impurity applies to a torn animal that was slaughtered, per Shmuel's father
A baraita from Rabbi Dostai bar Yehuda in the name of Rabbi Shimon: skin of creeping things joins only when fully flayed, not a camel, but the neck skin
Rav Huna and Resh Lakish on whether a skin with enough left to be stretched joins, and Rabbi Yoḥanan disputes the skin's connection
Rabbi Yoḥanan objects to Resh Lakish from a baraita on a skin used for thongs and sandals, with the impurity of the knife
Asks why the case cannot be read as the skin becoming connected
Explains the skin connects only where it is needed openly, namely at a corner that is reached by way of its surroundings
Rav Yirmeyah objects with a baraita on flaying an animal with enough left to lay on a mat, asking why the skin does not connect
Rabbi Avin translates the baraita, distinguishing the first handbreadth from the second
Rav Yosef objects with Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Nuri's view that the neck skin does not connect
Abaye suggests reading the second clause, and explains the dispute concerns a guard made to tear off by itself
Positions on whether a guard made to come loose on its own counts as a guard
Rabbi Yirmeyah objects from the rule for an oven that became impure: it is divided into three and the attached parts are dragged

124a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Meir holds the oven need not be dragged and need not reach the ground, but only cut down from inside by four handbreadths
Asks why it cannot be said that an attached part that stands is simply the rule
Raba explains the point was that the rabbinic rule does not require the dragging to reach the ground, and states the actual ruling
Mishna and baraita on an impure oven: divide it into three and drag the attached part, with Rabbi Meir's view on cutting it down
Objects that a baraita says an oven's start of four and remainder of four are impure, which contradicts the earlier ruling
Explains the Sages' measure as a handbreadth, based on the way ovens are made, and separates a made oven from a cast one
Asks what purpose a remainder of most of a handbreadth serves
Abaye explains that a large oven's remainder counts when most of it is left, and the four-handbreadth ruling applies to smaller ovens
Rav Huna, citing Rabbi Yishmael bar Rabbi Yosi, and Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yoḥanan disagree on whether a skin counts as a guard
Rabbi Yoḥanan objects to Resh Lakish from a baraita on a skin used for thongs and sandals, and asks why it does not count
Explains the case is one where the object is needed for a zav to sit on
Mishna: a skin with an olive's bulk of flesh is impure by carrying but not by touch, per Rabbi Yishmael, while Rabbi Akiva disagrees; Ulla reports Rabbi Yoḥanan's view
Rav Nachman rejects Ulla's report of Rabbi Yoḥanan, and Rav Oshaya finds Rav Nachman dismissing Rabbi Yoḥanan's teaching
Restates the second clause of the mishna on two half-olives and Rabbi Yoḥanan's view on the knife-expelled clump
Rav Nachman presses whether the teaching is in the second clause, and says he would not accept it even from Joshua ben Nun
Ravin reports it was taught in the first clause, and the difficulty is resolved as Rav Pappa said

124b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Bar Pada and Rabbi Yoḥanan disagree on whether a skin rolled up touches again and again from the front, or not at all
Rabbi Yoḥanan's consistency: Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Dosa ben Harkinas agree, citing the mishna on tent impurity and entering the house
Rabbi Dosa aligns with Rabbi Yishmael, so the Sages align with Rabbi Akiva on the point of touching and returning
Objects that Rabbi Akiva purifies only the skin, so he would not purify the case generally
Rabbi Akiva purifies only the skin, while elsewhere he counts the case as impure, as the second clause and his reasoning show
Rav Ukva bar Chama objects from the verse on carcasses that two half-olives on skin should convey impurity by carrying
Rabbi Akiva's exposition of the words touch and carry, showing what each verse brings into its category
Raba explains the rule: what enters the category of touch in every direction does not enter that of carrying, and the reverse
Rav Oyya asks whether Rabbi Yishmael holds that a flat unsealed case takes impurity, since it can touch from the front
Dismissive exchange: the raven flew off, and Raba says it is not the same Rav Oyya that the speaker praised in Pumbedita
Ulla states that two half-olives skewered on a stick remain pure even if carried all day
Gives the reason from the verse: carrying applies only to what is carried all at once
Asks why two half-olives on a case convey impurity by carrying, when the case is not actually carried
A baraita: Rabbi Akiva agrees about two half-olives skewered on a stick and moved, and the same applies to the flat case
Rabbi Eliezer's view that one who carries is like one who moves, and the disagreement on the terms, opening the next mishna on the dead animal's carcass

125a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: the clump of consecrated items conveys impurity whether sealed or pierced, while the clump of a carcass or creeping thing conveys impurity by touch only when pierced
Derivation from the verse on touch and carrying: what enters the category of touch does not enter carrying, and vice versa
Touch conveys impurity but overshadowing does not
Asks what the case is, to see whether a bone with an olive's bulk could convey impurity by overshadowing in a tent
Objects that if overshadowing conveys impurity with an olive's bulk of flesh, then a bone with marrow or a bone reaching outside should too
Rav Yehuda, son of Rabbi Ḥiyya, states that marrow inside does not make a bone reach outside, as a teaching
Asks in what case this was established, since then consecrated items should convey impurity and the clump should too
Explains the first clause concerns less than an olive's bulk and the second an olive's bulk, and the ruling teaches that inside marrow does not reach outside
Mari bar Avuh, citing Rabbi Yitzchak, rules that bones of consecrated animals that served as a base for forbidden meat convey impurity to hands
Abaye explains: marrow inside that reaches outside does count, and the case is one that is split, following Rabbi Elazar's distinction on length and breadth
Rabbi Yoḥanan says a bone with an olive's bulk and marrow inside that reaches outside counts, and asks what the clump touching in the mishna overshadows
Asks why the clump of carcass and creeping thing are pure when not pierced
Rabbi Binyamin bar Gidal, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan, explains the case as marrow that rattles beside a corpse, which conveys impurity when pierced
Rabbi Avin cites a mishna on touching half an olive and overshadowing half an olive, and asks whether they join
Objects that if they are two names they should not join, but the mishna says anything under one name joins and is impure
Asks what is meant when it is one name, and whether the second clause should be read instead

125b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna rules that one touching half an olive-bulk of corpse flesh under an overlying item remains pure.
If contact and tent impurity are one concept, why is he pure? The first clause of the mishna seems difficult.
Rabbi Zeira explains the mishna concerns impurity pressed between two chests with no handbreadth gap, so it counts as touching all.
Who is the tanna who calls overlying by a tent the term touching?
It is Rabbi Yosei, who holds that a tent counts as touching.
A baraita from Tosefta Oholot states Rabbi Yosei's view that a full ladle of corpse dust imparts impurity by contact, carrying and tent.
Carrying and tent cover all the dust, but touch does not, so the touching reading seems impossible.
Rather, the Gemara concludes that noge'a must refer to overlying, as the baraita implies.
How can noge'a mean overlying when the baraita also separately teaches touching and overlying?
Abaye answers there are two kinds of overlying: low overlying counts as touching, high overlying is merely a tent.
Rava says that according to Rabbi Yosei even a tent overlying impurity above one handbreadth counts as touching.
What is the case of a mere tent, a structure spreading impurity from source to person?
Rava states where he derives his view from.
Baraita on bundles and grilles between floors, and on a netting over a corpse, where holes in the netting determine impurity.
What is the case? If the netting is below one handbreadth, why is one not opposite a hole pure, like a dressed corpse?
Rather, the netting is above one handbreadth, and Rabbi Yosei calls overlying touching in that case.
Abaye defends his view: the netting is low, and it differs from a dressed corpse because the spreader intended to remove it.
Hidden impurity under a low overlying should break through, so one not opposite a hole should also become impure.
From where do you say that Rabbi Yosei holds hidden impurity does not break through?
Mishna of Oholot 4:2 on a chest compartment with an opening under one handbreadth supports that hidden impurity does not break through.
Impurity typically exits a place but does not typically enter, so the chest counts as a separate tent.
Rabbi Yosei deems the house pure because the impure item can be removed in halves or burned in place.
The latter clause of the mishna, with the chest at the entrance facing out, is cited as support for the same principle.

126a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: To which halakha of the mishna does the baraita refer? Could it mean the latter clause about a chest in the entrance?
If it meant the latter clause, the first tanna would also deem it pure, so Rabbi Yosei's ruling would not be distinctive.
The first tanna holds the house is impure, either because impurity typically exits its place or because hidden impurity breaks through.
Rabbi Yosei objects that impurity need not exit and can be removed in halves, and that hidden impurity does not break through, which contradicts his other ruling.
A mishna in Oholot 11:7 about a dog that ate corpse flesh and lies on a threshold is brought as a source.
Rabbi Yosei's position in that mishna: look where the impure item lies relative to the lintel.
Rabbi Elazar's position: look at how the dog lies, whether its mouth or its rear is inside or outside the house.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira holds the house is impure in either case, since impurity can exit through mouth or rear.
Is Rabbi Yosei's statement not referring to a dog lacking a cubic handbreadth opening, so that he is answering Rabbi Meir?
Therefore, one learns from it that Rabbi Yosei holds hidden impurity breaks through and ascends.
Rava defends Rabbi Yosei: he holds hidden impurity does not break through, and his criteria concern the adjacent empty space, not the dog.
Rav Aha son of Rava says Rava's explanation is explicit in the mishna, which says to look at the empty space adjacent to the impurity.
Who is the tanna who disagrees with Rabbi Yosei that overlying and touching are one category?
It is Rabbi Shimon, as a baraita teaches that he holds these two methods of transmitting impurity differ.

126b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: three sources of impurity derive from a corpse; each of two imparts in two ways, and the third imparts in none of the three.
A full ladle of dust imparts impurity by carrying and in a tent, but not by contact, since one cannot touch all of it at once.
Where does contact impurity apply to the dust, since it does not apply to the dust alone?
A bone the size of a barley grain imparts impurity by carrying and contact, but not in a tent, a halakha from Sinai.
Where does tent impurity apply to the bone, given that it does not apply to the bone alone?
A grave cover and grave wall impart impurity by contact and in a tent, but not by carrying, also a halakha from Sinai.
Where does carrying impurity apply to the cover and wall, given that it does not apply to them alone?
Mishna turns to the sealed thigh bone of an unslaughtered carcass or creeping animal, which is pure to touch.
Baraita on Leviticus 11:39 and 11:31: touching is impure only where the flesh can be touched, and pure where it cannot.
Rabbi Zeira objects to Abaye: an animal still in its hide should then not impart impurity, since its hide cannot be passed through.
Abaye replies that animals have many orifices, such as eyes, nostrils and mouth, through which the flesh can be touched.
Rav Pappa objects to Rava: a fat-covered kidney of a carcass should not impart impurity by contact either.
Rava replies that many sinews emerge from the kidney that one can touch, so it does impart impurity.
Does a thigh bone intended for perforation but not yet perforated count as lacking the necessary action, so it stays sealed?
Rav Oshaya resolves it: an unperforated bone is not lacking the action, and if intended to be perforated it imparts impurity immediately.
Mishna: an egg of a creeping animal with embryo tissue is pure while sealed, but impure if perforated to any size.
Mishna: a mouse half flesh and half earth makes one who touches the flesh impure, and one who touches the earth pure.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that one who touches the earth adjacent to the flesh is also impure.
Baraita: the verse deems the egg and thigh bone of a creeping animal sources of impurity, as the term impure ones includes them.
Baraita: the egg imparts impurity only if embryo tissue developed, since the verse says creeps, like the creature itself.
Baraita: a perforated egg or bone imparts impurity only where the flesh can be touched, as the verse says touching.
How large must the perforation of an egg or thigh bone be for one touching it to become impure?
It must be the width of a hair strand, since one can touch the inside with a strand of one's hair.
Mishna's case of the mouse half flesh and half earth is restated for discussion.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds that impurity arises only if the flesh developed along the whole mouse, and some apply this to Rabbi Yehuda's latter clause too.
Explains that the two versions differ: one reads the ruling for the first clause, the other only for the latter clause per Rabbi Yehuda.
Baraita on Leviticus 11:29: the verse's mouse might include a sea mouse, but a weasel-based inference suggests only land mice.
Second baraita reasoning: the word mouse covers any animal so named, including a sea mouse, but the phrase upon the earth excludes it.
If the halakha comes only from upon the earth, one might think a mouse that descends to sea stays impure, which the verse excludes.

127a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The verse that creeps indicates that creeping animals impart impurity anywhere they creep, including the sea, so upon the earth excludes a sea mouse.
Alternative reading: the word creeps means any animal that breeds imparts impurity, while one that does not breed does not.
On that reading, a half-flesh half-earth mouse is excluded because it generates from the earth and does not breed.
Logical inference: the verse deems a weasel and a mouse impure, so mouse covers any animal of that name, even a half-earth mouse.
Alternative inference: just as a weasel breeds, mouse refers to a breeding mouse, which excludes the spontaneously generated one.
The verse among the creeping animals includes the spontaneously generated mouse, and upon the earth excludes the sea mouse.
A Sage suggests Rava read the verse differently: the phrase upon the earth teaches that a creature becomes pure only if it descends to sea.
Rava rejects this: since the sea is also a place of impurity, location in land or sea makes no difference.
Why does the baraita read upon the earth as excluding a sea mouse, when it is needed to exclude a floating source of uncertain impurity?
The phrase upon the earth appears twice: one instance excludes floating uncertainty, the other excludes the sea mouse.
Baraita: the verse's great lizard after its kinds includes the arvad, the nefilim and the salamander among the creeping animals.
Rabbi Akiva would exclaim at this verse on the diversity of creatures living in sea, land, fire and air, each dying if moved.
Baraita: every animal on land has a counterpart in the sea, except the weasel, which exists only on land.
Rabbi Zeira cites Psalms 49:2 as the verse behind this, since dry land is called ḥeled because the weasel lives only there.
Rav Huna holds the beavers of Neresh are not from the settled area, so eating them is not liable to lashes.
Rav Pappa says the people of Neresh are wicked and should be excommunicated, citing Jeremiah 22:29.
Rav Giddel reports Rav's warnings about travelers from Neresh, Nehar Pekod and Pumbedita, who may steal or rob.
Rav Huna bar Torta reports seeing locals in Va'ad crossbreed a snake and a great lizard, producing an arvad.
Rabbi Shimon the Righteous explains that God will punish the crossbreeders with the arvad, a creature He did not create.
The Gemara objects: animals whose gestation periods differ cannot reproduce together, so a snake and great lizard should not produce offspring.
Rav says it was a miracle within a miracle that these different creatures could reproduce.
The Gemara explains the miracle within a miracle was a calamity, a punishment for the wicked people.
Mishna: a limb or flesh partly severed but hanging from a live animal is not treated as severed; it becomes impure as food only if susceptible.

127b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a slaughtered animal's hanging limb becomes susceptible via its blood per Rabbi Meir, but not per Rabbi Shimon, who requires another liquid.
Mishna: if the animal died unslaughtered, the hanging limb imparts impurity as a severed limb but not as carcass, per Rabbi Meir; Rabbi Shimon deems it pure.
Gemara infers the hanging limb imparts food impurity but not carcass impurity.
What are the circumstances? If the limb can heal it should not be susceptible even as food, and if it cannot heal it should impart carcass impurity.
The mishna concerns a limb that cannot heal; carcass impurity is unique and applies only once the limb fully falls, per Leviticus 11:37.
Baraita: a limb connected by a hair-thin strand is not a carcass until it falls, but still counts as severed for food impurity.
This supports Rav Hiyya bar Ashi's report of Shmuel: figs dried on the tree are severed for impurity but attached for Shabbat.
Baraita: cabbage and gourd dried on the plant are not susceptible to food impurity, but if cut while moist they are.
Does it enter your mind that cut and dried produce is susceptible to food impurity, when it is merely wood and inedible?
Rabbi Yitzhak says the baraita concerns produce cut while moist in order to dry it, which is susceptible even though it will become inedible.
Explains the suggested support: if produce and its stems were both dried it is obvious, so the baraita must mean only the produce was dried.
The Gemara rejects that reading: the baraita concerns full drying, and the stated rule is needed for the latter clause about moist cut produce.
A baraita challenges Shmuel: a fruit on a broken branch is detached in all matters, so dried fruit on a tree should be attached in all matters too.
The Gemara rejects the challenge: the cases differ, since the dried fruit on the tree is attached for Shabbat but detached for impurity.
Mishna case restated: an animal slaughtered and its hanging limb.
On what principle do Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon disagree?
Rabba says they dispute whether an animal is a handle for its limb: Rabbi Meir says yes, Rabbi Shimon says no.
Abaye explains the dispute as whether the hanging limb is one and the same with the animal, depending on whether it is grasped with the animal.
Rabbi Yohanan also holds Abaye's explanation of the dispute about a small part hanging off a larger part.
Rabbi Yohanan raises a contradiction between two statements of Rabbi Meir, and a mishna in Tevul Yom 3:1 contradicts the view that the small part is one with the whole.

128a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Meir holds the small and large pieces are one only if the large piece rises with the small, which seems to contradict his mishna ruling.
Rabbi Yohanan resolves the contradiction by saying the attributions of the opinions in Tevul Yom are reversed.
Perhaps Rabbi Meir distinguishes the impurity of one who immersed that day from other impurities, so there is no contradiction?
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi teaches that contact rules are the same for the impurity of one who immersed that day and for all other impurities.
Perhaps Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi does not distinguish, while Rabbi Meir does, so the two statements of Rabbi Meir do not conflict?
Rabbi Yoshiya clarifies Rabbi Yohanan's point: per Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi there is a real contradiction in Rabbi Meir, so the attribution is reversed.
Rava explains the dispute: both agree an animal is a handle for its limb, but disagree whether a handle renders attached food susceptible.
Rav Pappa explains the dispute as whether susceptibility can take effect before the owner designates the meat as food.
A baraita on Rabbi Akiva's teaching about fat of a village animal, which needs designation but not contact with liquid, supports the dispute.
Rabbi Yehuda recounts Rabbi Akiva's endive ruling, which required contact with liquid after designation for food, and Akiva's later retraction.
Rav Pappa concludes that Rabbi Meir follows Rabbi Akiva's original teaching, and Rabbi Shimon follows his retracted teaching.
Rav Aha son of Rav Ika explains the dispute as whether blood wiped off between the two simanim counts as blood of slaughter.
Rav Ashi explains the dispute as whether slaughter itself, not the blood, renders the limb susceptible, given the meat is still forbidden.
Rabba raises a dilemma: does a living animal with a partially severed limb, touching impurity, transmit impurity to the limb as a handle? Unresolved.
Abaye cites the Okatzin 2:9 mishna on a cucumber planted in a flowerpot, which becomes pure when it grows over the edge to the ground.
Rabbi Shimon asks what the cucumber's impurity is, and holds the inside part stays impure and the outside part stays pure.
Based on Rabbi Shimon, Abaye asks whether the part outside the flowerpot is a handle transmitting impurity to the part inside. Unresolved.
Rabbi Yirmeya cites the ruling that one who bows to half a gourd forbids only that half, as the sages held.
Based on that ruling, Rabbi Yirmeya raises a dilemma about the handle question for the gourd's halves.

128b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Does the forbidden part of an idolatrous gourd, touching impurity, make its permitted half impure as a handle? Unresolved.
Rav Pappa cites Okatzin 3:8: a fig branch mostly detached from the tree is attached for Rabbi Yehuda, while the Rabbis depend on whether it can be reattached.
Rav Pappa asks whether a reattachable branch, bearing a second branch that cannot be reattached, transmits impurity as a handle. Unresolved.
Rabbi Zeira cites Nega'im 13:2 on a stone in the corner of a shared wall, where the stone's share is treated separately during removal.
Does half of the shared stone act as a handle to transmit leprous impurity to the neighbor's house? Unresolved.
Mishna: a dead animal's hanging flesh becomes susceptible only through contact with liquid, and the hanging limb imparts impurity as a severed limb.
What is the difference between the impurity of a limb from a living animal and that of a limb from a carcass?
The difference concerns flesh separating from the limb: from a living-severed limb it is pure, but from a carcass limb an olive-bulk is impure.
What verse teaches that a limb severed from a living animal imparts impurity?
Rav cites Leviticus 11:39 with the phrase min habehema, read as from an animal, to include a limb torn from a live animal.
How can Rav read the verse that way, when min habehema is needed for a baraita: a tereifa slaughtered is not a carcass for impurity?
The double phrase min habehema teaches two conclusions, so one word would not suffice.
If the verse teaches that a limb from a living animal imparts impurity, it might also teach that flesh from a living animal does.
A baraita rejects this: the verse says death leaves no replacement, so a limb is impure while flesh regrows, per Rabbi Yosei.
Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi derive from animal whether a part with sinews and bones, or with flesh too, imparts impurity.
What is the practical difference between Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Akiva? It is the leg joint, which has sinews and bones but no flesh.
What practical difference is there between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili?
Rav Pappa says the difference is the kidney and the upper lip, which impart impurity per Rabbi Yosei but not per Rabbi Akiva.
A baraita on creeping animals, citing Leviticus 11:32 and the word dead, gives the same three opinions, with Rabbi Yosei HaGelili excluding flesh.
Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi derive from creeping animal whether parts with sinews and bones, or flesh too, impart impurity.
What is the practical difference between Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Akiva, and between Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, for creeping animals?
Explains the case for creeping animals and why the halakha must be taught for both living animals and creeping animals, since their impurity rules differ.
Baraita: one who severs an olive-bulk of flesh from a living-severed limb makes it impure as food only if designated as food before contact.
Narrative: Rabbi Asi did not attend the study hall and found Rabbi Zeira, to ask what was discussed there.
Rabbi Zeira asks what difficulty Rabbi Asi finds, prompting him to explain.
Rabbi Asi cites the baraita that if flesh was designated for a gentile before severing, it is impure, which he finds difficult.

129a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Principle: contact with impurity in a concealed part of the body does not render an item impure, so the flesh under the hanging limb stays pure.
Rabbi Zeira reports that Rabbi Abba bar Memel explained the baraita as Rabbi Meir's view, who holds concealed contact does impart impurity.
Rabbi Asi rebuts: that answer does not fit, since Meir distinguishes impurity that requires susceptibility, and unsusceptible flesh is exempt from concealed contact.
Rava suggests the baraita may concern flesh that was rendered susceptible before being severed from the limb.
Rabba bar Rav Hanan asks why the flesh needs susceptibility, since it is part of a limb that already carries the severe carcass impurity.
Rava replies that the principle applies only within food impurity; here the flesh served as wood as part of the limb, so it needs susceptibility.
Rava's principle applies to other cases: a leaven mass designated as a chair becomes a seat subject to treading impurity.
Abaye holds the seat's impurity is rabbinic, but the Gemara responds that it is Torah impurity, since the leaven then served as wood, not food.
The same reasoning applies to an idolatrous food offering that imparts tent impurity: it was not food then, but served as wood.
The same applies to food connected to vessels, such as dough on a kneading bowl, which imparts vessel impurity by Torah law as wood.
Rav Pappa cites Okatzin 3:3 on fat of a carcass that covers the kidney, which Abaye treats as rabbinic impurity for food.
The Gemara responds that the fat imparts carcass impurity by Torah law, since it served as a protective wood-like part of the kidney.
Rav Mattana cites a baraita on a house roofed with seeds, which becomes pure, but the Gemara again says the seeds imparted impurity by Torah law as wood.
Mishna: Rabbi Shimon deems the hanging limb of a dead animal pure, against Rabbi Meir.
Whichever way you look at it, Rabbi Shimon's ruling is difficult: whether or not death makes the limb fallen, it seems it should be impure.
Rabbi Shimon refers to the first clause, where the hanging limb imparts food impurity only once susceptible, and is not susceptible otherwise.
Restates that Rabbi Shimon deems the hanging part pure.
What is the reason for Rabbi Shimon's opinion, according to Rabbi Yohanan?
Rabbi Yohanan cites Leviticus 11:34: the repeated phrase food which may be eaten means food one can feed to others, including gentiles.

129b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Food that cannot be fed even to gentiles, such as a live animal's limb or flesh, is not called food.
Rabbi Zeira challenges Rabbi Yohanan's reasoning: Rabbi Shimon may hold that an attached limb counts as attached, not that it is non-food.
Rabbi Zeira recalls the Okatzin 3:8 fig-branch mishna and the reasoning for Rabbi Yehuda's attached-status view, which parallels Rabbi Shimon.
Rabbi Asi says Rabbi Yohanan is explaining Rabbi Shimon's view on the middle clause, that slaughter blood did not render the limb susceptible.
Rabbi Yohanan cites Leviticus 11:34: food that can be fed to others is food, while flesh of a living animal is not called food.
Rabbi Zeira questions this again: Rabbi Shimon's middle-clause reasoning may rest on a handle explanation or a different principle.
Rabbi Asi says Rabbi Shimon is really speaking of the latter clause, about flesh rather than the limb, which is not susceptible.
Rabbi Yohanan repeats his Leviticus 11:34 reasoning as support for Rabbi Shimon's view on the latter clause.
Mishna: a human's partially severed limb and flesh are pure while hanging; Rabbi Meir holds the limb imparts impurity as a living limb, while Rabbi Shimon deems both pure.
The Gemara challenges Rabbi Shimon's latter-clause ruling: whether or not death makes the limb fallen, it seems the limb should be impure.
Rabbi Shimon speaks generally of a limb separated from a corpse, inferring from Rabbi Meir that corpse limbs impart impurity only with an olive-bulk of flesh.
Baraita: Rabbi Eliezer holds a living limb imparts impurity, and Rabbi Yehoshua argues a fortiori that a corpse limb also does.
Rabbi Yehoshua adds that Megillat Taanit forbids eulogy on Minor Passover, so the a fortiori logic applies to corpse limbs; Rabbi Eliezer keeps his tradition.
What is the practical difference between the impurity of a limb from a living person and that of a limb from a corpse?
Eduyyot 6:3: Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Nehunya ben HaKana and Rabbi Yehoshua dispute whether a separated olive-bulk of flesh or a barley-grain bone is impure.
Gemara concludes that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon differ on the same cases, with Rabbi Shimon following Rabbi Yehoshua that both bone and flesh are pure.
Chapter-closing marker, ending the chapter of the skin and the gravy.

130a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: gifts of the foreleg, jaw and maw apply in and outside the Land, inside and outside the Temple, to non-sacred animals only.
The mishna cites an a fortiori argument from the breast and thigh, then Leviticus 7:34 limiting the priest's due to that matter alone.
Mishna: sacred animals with a permanent blemish before consecration are redeemed and still owe firstborn and gifts, and may leave sacred status.
Mishna: if the blemish came after consecration, the animals are exempt from firstborn and gifts, and their offspring and milk stay forbidden.
The Gemara explains the verse's word them restricts the gifts, since otherwise one would infer sacred animals owe gifts.
Why is the a fortiori inference needed at all, and can it be refuted by what is unique about non-sacred animals?
Successive a fortiori proposals from male animals, goats, old goats and purchased or orphaned animals are each refuted by what is unique to them.
The Gemara responds that sacred animals enter the pen to be tithed like non-sacred ones, so an a fortiori argument does apply to them.
A reverse a fortiori: sacred animals, not owing gifts, owe breast and thigh, so non-sacred animals owing gifts should owe them too.
Deuteronomy 18:3 says this shall be the priests' due, so only the foreleg, jaw and maw go to priests from non-sacred animals.
The Gemara objects: the verse's this implies the reason, and breast and thigh must be waved before the Lord inside the Temple, which non-sacred animals cannot do.

130b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rejects the idea of waving breast and thigh inside the Temple, since that would bring non-sacred animals into the courtyard; so the verse is not needed for that.
If so, why does the verse need to state this is the priests' due?
Verse is needed for Rav Hisda's ruling: one who damages or eats gifts of the priesthood need not pay a replacement, since only the items themselves are due.
What is the reason for Rav Hisda's ruling?
Either the word this limits the gift to those items, or the gifts are money with no claimants, so no priest can sue over them.
A baraita reads the verse's mishpat as judgment, and asks whether that means priests may claim gifts in court, which would contradict Rav Hisda; it is answered that judgment concerns distribution.
Rav Shmuel bar Nahmani cites Rabbi Yonatan and II Chronicles 31:4 to show gifts are not given to an am ha'aretz priest.
A baraita on Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira reads this as limiting the judgment language to the foreleg, jaw and maw, excluding breast and thigh.
If the baraita concerns extracting gifts through judges, it implies priests can claim them in court, contrary to Rav Hisda.
Here the gifts came into the priest's possession while untithed, and this tanna treats unseparated gifts as separated, so taking them is theft.
A mishna of Pe'a 5:4 has a poor man take gleanings and pay a poor person afterward, per Rabbi Eliezer, apparently against Rav Hisda.
Rav Hisda says the mishna teaches an attribute of piety, and Rava objects that the tanna says explicitly he will pay, so the halakha is not like Rabbi Eliezer.
The objection comes from the latter clause: the Rabbis hold a poor homeowner exempt, implying a wealthy one must pay poor claimants.
Rav Hisda replies that even a wealthy homeowner need not pay, and the Rabbis' obligation is an attribute of piety.
A baraita from Leviticus 22:15 says a priest's rights to produce begin at separation, so eating untithed produce is not payable in court.
If one who eats after separation must pay, why should one pay, unlike the case of damage to gifts, which Rav Hisda exempts?
The Gemara responds that the same logic applies here, to explain the distinction.

131a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The tanna holds unseparated gifts count as separated, so a priest seizing untithed produce gains rights and the consumer must pay.
A baraita on the king's household seizing a threshing floor requires tithing the grain, implying tithes can be claimed as money, against Rav Hisda.
The seizure there differs, since exemption from tithing would benefit the owner; the baraita does not imply a claim in court.
A mishna on a butcher's sale of a cow's innards: gifts of the priesthood must go to the priest, which seems to contradict Rav Hisda.
Why must the buyer give the maw to the priest, when such damage to gifts is exempt per Rav Hisda?
A baraita lists nine items that are a priest's property, two of which a priest may claim when a convert's property was stolen and the thief lied under oath.
The list means a priest may use these to buy slaves, lands and Torah scrolls, and creditors and divorced wives can take them, per Bikkurim 3:12.
A Levite snatched gifts from children delivering them to priests; Rav says the Levite should not be allowed to take them from them.
What does Rav maintain: if Levites are part of the people, why not take their gifts, and if not, why would they be exempt?
Rav is uncertain whether Levites are called part of the people, so he exempts them, since the burden of proof rests on the claimant.
Rav Pappa was teaching this halakha in Rav's name.
Rav Idi bar Avin objects to Rav Pappa with a baraita listing four poor gifts from a vineyard, three from grain and two from trees.
The baraita explains that these gifts give the owner no discretion and must be left for all the poor, while poor man's tithe does allow discretion.
Leviticus 19:10 cited as the source for the peret and olelot gifts, which must be left for the poor and stranger.
Deuteronomy 24:21 cited, with Rabbi Levi reading after you as referring to forgotten clusters.
Pe'a for the vineyard is derived by verbal analogy from the olive verse, read via Rabbi Yishmael's school as not taking all its splendor.
The baraita teaches that three gifts from grain are left for the poor, beginning with the gleanings.

131b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The baraita cites Leviticus 23:22 and Deuteronomy 24:19-20 as the sources for the forgotten sheaves and pe'a left for the poor.
The baraita cites Yishmael's school on Deuteronomy 24:20 for pe'a and forgotten fruit, and states that owners have no discretion over these gifts.
What is the reason the owner has no discretion over these gifts?
Leviticus 23:22 is cited: leaving is written for them, so even a poor owner must leave them and the court may take them from him.
Baraita: the poor man's tithe distributed within the house gives the owner discretion, unlike the field gifts.
What is the reason for this halakha?
Giving is written for it, so it is actively given to the poor rather than left in the field.
Rabbi Ile'a derives by verbal analogy from to the stranger that a poor owner must also separate the poor man's tithe from his own produce.
Rav Idi bar Avin argues the baraita implies gifts are removed from Levites to priests, so Levites count as part of the people, contrary to Rav.
The baraita refers not to the foreleg, jaw and maw but to a similar gift, namely first tithe.
But first tithe is given to the Levite, so why would it be removed from him?
A baraita: teruma goes to the priest and first tithe to the Levite per Rabbi Akiva, but Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya gives first tithe to the priest too.
Did Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya say first tithe goes exclusively to priests, and is it removed from Levites?
Even if Ezra penalized Levites, one can ask whether first tithe is taken from them to give to priests, which seems to go too far.
The baraita refers instead to first sheared wool, which is not from the people, so Levites must give it to priests.
A baraita states that items of sanctity are removed from Levites for priests, while the foreleg, jaw and maw are not, so Levites are not part of the people.
A baraita: an Israelite slaughtering for a priest or gentile is exempt, implying liability when slaughtering for a Levite or Israelite.
The Gemara rejects this inference: the baraita says only that slaughtering for another Israelite creates liability, so Rav's uncertainty stands.
If slaughtering for a Levite creates no liability, why does the baraita not say so explicitly?
A baraita explicitly says a Levite slaughter is liable, which seems a conclusive refutation of Rav's uncertainty.
Rav could reply that the baraita is a dispute between tanna'im over whether Levites are part of the people.
Baraita on Leviticus 16:33: the atonement verses list the sanctum, the Tent, the altar, courtyards, priests, the people and the Levites.
Another baraita: the verse's he shall make atonement also refers to Canaanite slaves owned by Jews.
The tanna of the second baraita holds Levites are part of the people, so the phrase covers slaves; the first tanna holds they are not.
If this is a dispute between tanna'im, why is Rav uncertain? Could he just follow one of them?
Mareimar rules that the halakha follows Rav's uncertainty about Levites, so Levites cannot be compelled to give these gifts, and follows Rav Hisda on damage.
Rava objects to Ulla's practice of giving priestly gifts to a priest's daughter: her meal-offering remainder is eaten, but a priest's is not.
Rava presses that Leviticus 6:16 says a priest's meal offering is not eaten, so the daughter's should not be either.
Ulla replies to Rava, my teacher, responding to the objection.

132a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ulla's proof: Aaron and his sons are written in the meal-offering passage, and the repeated priest in Deuteronomy 18:3 includes a priest's daughter.
Several sages, including Rav Kahana and Rav Pappa, partook of priestly gifts on account of their priestly wives.
Ravina reports Mareimar's rulings: Levites are uncertain about gifts, Rav Hisda's damage rule stands, Ulla's daughter rule stands, and Rav Adda bar Ahava's Levite rule applies.
Baraita: gifts apply to a hybrid and to a koy, and Rabbi Eliezer exempts a hybrid of a goat and doe because a doe is not domesticated.
The Gemara asks whether the dispute about a goat-doe hybrid really turns on paternity, since both sides are uncertain about it.
The dispute is whether the obligation applies to a sheep and even to a partly sheep animal, with the Rabbis including partly sheep.
If Rabbi Eliezer exempts the hybrid, why should the Rabbis not have the priest take only half, leaving the owner to prove the other half is exempt?
Rav Huna bar Hiyya says the Rabbis mean the owner is obligated in half the gifts.
Rabbi Zeira objects with a baraita: a koy has domesticated and undomesticated traits, and Rabbi Eliezer exempts its owner from gifts.
If the Rabbis require half the gifts, why does the baraita not say so explicitly?
Because the tanna taught that the fat and blood are forbidden, and half of an item cannot be forbidden while the other half is permitted.
Ravin reports Rabbi Yohanan: per the Rabbis a koy owes all the gifts, since the verse's ox and sheep phrases include the hybrid and the koy.
If Rabbi Eliezer exempts the koy and hybrid, why does he need the ox or sheep phrase, and how do the Rabbis derive the division?
What does Rabbi Eliezer do with the phrase from them that perform a slaughter?
He uses it for Rava's ruling: a priest claims gifts from the butcher even if the animal belongs to another.
Mishna: a blemished firstborn mingled with one hundred non-sacred animals, slaughtered by many owners, exempts all from gifts; a single slaughterer exempts one.
Mishna: one who slaughters for a priest or gentile is exempt, and an Israelite partnering with a priest or gentile must mark the animal as jointly owned.
Mishna: if an Israelite buys innards from a butcher, the purchaser gives the maw to the priest, deducting its value only when bought by weight.
Why does the Gemara need the firstborn rule of two-sided claim: why not let the priest claim each slaughterer from two sides?

132b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Oshaya: a priest may generally issue such a claim, but here the priest already received the firstborn unblemished and sold it blemished, so he cannot claim it again.
Mishna: one who slaughters a priest's animal for the priest, or a gentile's for a gentile, is exempt from the foreleg, jaw and maw gifts.
Why does the mishna not simply say that a priest or gentile is exempt from the gifts?
Rava explains the wording shows the priest's claim is against the butcher, so a priest butcher slaughtering for an Israelite owes the gifts.
Rava cites Deuteronomy 18:3: from the people, not the priests, and from them that slaughter includes even a priest who is a butcher.
The host of Rabbi Tavla, a priest short of money, is advised to partner with Israelite butchers, who would then be exempt from gifts.
Rav Nahman still obligates the butcher to give gifts, and tells the priest to pass gifts to a priest or lose Rabbi Tavla's support.
Rabbi Tavla asks Rav Nahman why he rules against the mishna.
Rav Nahman cites Rabbi Aha bar Hanina quoting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: a priest butcher is exempt for two or three weeks, then becomes obligated.
Rabbi Tavla asks Rav Nahman to apply Rabbi Aha's exemption to this priest for the first weeks.
Rav Nahman replies that the exemption applies only when no butcher shop was set up, and this priest already set one up.
Rav Hisda declares excommunication on a priest who does not separate gifts for another priest, and the Huzal butchers have stood under it twenty-two years.
What is the halakha in this case of Huzal butchers excommunicated twenty-two years, given a baraita that one is not punished indefinitely for transgressions?
Rabba bar Rav Sheila means the court fines them without forewarning for refusing gifts for so many years.
Rava fined a man by taking his thigh, and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak fined one by taking his cloak, to give to priests.
Is that so? Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef said in Eretz Yisrael the gifts are divided bone by bone, each shared by two priests.
In Eretz Yisrael the case concerned a large bull, so each share was substantial, unlike smaller animals.
