Rabbi Yohanan rules that one may not eat an animal whose gifts are not yet separated, but the halakha does not follow him.
Rav Hisda rules gifts may be eaten only roasted and with mustard, as kings eat, based on Numbers 18:8.
Rav Hisda rules a priest must know all twenty-four gifts to receive one, and the Gemara notes this is not quite right.
Baraita of Rabbi Shimon: a priest who does not believe in the Temple service has no share, from the word hamakriv in Leviticus 7:33, and fifteen rites are listed.

133a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A baraita lists the rites stated to the sons of Aaron, including water for a sota, the heifer's neck, leper purification and the Priestly Benediction.
A priest who does not believe in these rites has no portion, which by inference means a believing priest keeps his portion even if inexpert, contradicting Rav Hisda.
Rav Huna says in Rav's name that the veins in an animal's jaw are forbidden, so a priest who cannot remove them should not receive the jaw.
The Gemara notes this need not be a concern, since roasting, cutting and salting drain the blood from the jaw.
Rava reports Rav Yosef's question on seizing gifts, resolved by Deuteronomy 18:3: that they shall give means the owner gives, so seizing shows contempt for the mitzva.
Abaye recounts that he seized gifts at first, then stopped after learning this and the sons of Samuel's sin, and took only what was offered.
Abaye took gifts offered on the eve of Yom Kippur only to affirm his priestly status, since he otherwise refrained from taking gifts.
The Gemara challenges Abaye: he should spread his hands for the Priestly Benediction all year, and answers that his study schedule prevented it.
Rav Yosef rules a priest may grant his expected gifts to a poor Torah scholar neighbor, even before receiving them, if the priest is well known.
Rava and Rav Safra visit Mar Yohana's house, where Rava takes the tongue gift from the attendant to eat with mustard, while Rav Safra refuses.
Rav Safra dreams of Proverbs 25:20, a verse of a garment in cold weather and vinegar upon niter, which is read as chastisement.
Rav Yosef tells Rav Safra he acted rightly, since the permission covered only a priest granting gifts by choice, not an attendant under pressure.
Why were they read this verse, if Rav Safra did right?
The reading was aimed at Rava, who ate the gifts against Rav Yosef's ruling, and he was rebuked so no direct message came to him.
Abaye asks Rav Dimi what the plain meaning of that verse is.
Rav Dimi says it refers to one who teaches an unworthy student, like a garment or vinegar on niter, useless to such a student.
Rav Yehuda cites Rav: one who teaches Torah to an unworthy student falls into Gehenna, supported by Job 20:26 and Joel 3:5, with yera sarid read as such a student.
Rabbi Zeira cites Rav: teaching an unworthy student is like throwing a stone to Markulis, supported by Proverbs 26:8 and 19:10.
Mishna: one who enters a partnership with a priest or gentile must mark the animal.
Is one obligated to mark the animal even in partnership with a gentile?
A baraita contradicts this: one partnered with a priest must mark, but one partnered with a gentile or slaughtering disqualified consecrated animals need not mark.

133b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains the case as a gentile sitting in the butcher shop, making partnership evident, unlike the mishna's case.
Asks why a priest sitting in the shop still requires marking the animal.
Replies that people would assume the priest is in the shop only to buy meat.
Objects that the same reasoning would let people assume the gentile is only buying meat.
Offers an alternative: the gentile sits by the safe, which evidently makes him a partner.
Asks again why marking is required when the priest sits by the safe.
Replies that people would think the butcher trusts the priest to guard the safe.
Objects that the same reasoning would apply to a gentile sitting by the safe.
Says Jews rarely trust gentiles; alternatively, a gentile partner yells at the seller while a priest defers.
Quotes the baraita: disqualified consecrated animals need no marking since their owner is exempt.
Objects that the disqualified consecrated status would not be evident, since such animals are treated like ordinary meat.
Cites a mishna stating disqualified consecrated animals are sold and weighed like non-sacred meat.
Explains the baraita refers to firstborn and tithe animals sold inside the house, barred from the market.
Rav Huna holds that partial ownership of the head, leg or innards exempts only the matching gift.
Ḥiyya bar Rav holds that partnership in any one part exempts the Israelite from all the gifts.
Raises an objection to Ḥiyya bar Rav from a baraita about a priest's partnership in a tiny share.
Asks whether the baraita really means exempt from one specific gift and liable for the rest.
Replies that the baraita means the Israelite is exempt from all the gifts.
Asks why the baraita would not state explicitly that the Israelite is exempt from all the gifts.
Cites another baraita stating the butcher is obligated for the rest, refuting Ḥiyya bar Rav.
Rav Ḥisda explains the baraita misled Ḥiyya bar Rav, thereby upholding his view.
Cites a baraita: all twenty-four priestly gifts were given by generalization and detail, under a covenant of salt.
Lists the twenty-four gifts by where they are consumed: the Temple, Jerusalem, and the Land of Israel.
Explains the baraita counted foreleg, jaw and maw as one because they are similar, not because they form one gift.
Raises a dilemma: if a priest owns the head, does the Israelite owe the jaw, following obligation or principal part?
Cites baraitas on sheep sheared by an agent and on buying wool or parts before the gift arises.
Concludes that liability follows the gift-bearing limbs, so the Israelite is obligated, as the baraita implies.
Mishna: a priest who sells an animal but keeps the gifts leaves the Israelite exempt from giving them.

134a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects with a baraita holding that a priest's stipulation that the gifts be his is void, so the Israelite owes them to any priest.
Explains that on the condition is not a term of retention, unlike except in the mishna, so the stipulation is void.
Objects with another baraita where the gifts stay with the priest when he stipulates they are his.
Resolves that the two baraitot disagree on whether on the condition is a term of retention.
Mishna: a buyer of innards must give the maw to the priest, deducting its value when bought by weight.
Rav holds the priest may claim the maw from the buyer, and from the butcher too if the butcher did the weighing.
Rav Asi holds that even if the butcher weighed the innards, the priest may claim the maw from the buyer alone.
Suggests the Sages disagree about Rav Ḥisda's ruling on whether the owner may collect from either party.
